speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The resolutions which I introduced on the occasion of my Budget speech were yesterday approved by the Committee of Ways and Means, and afterwards concurred in by the House. I now beg leave to introduce a Bill No. 169, entitled an Act to amend the Customs tariff, 1907, founded upon those resolutions.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On the Orders of the Day being called:

I desire to rise to a question of privilege. The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Fisher) and the hon. member for North York (Mr. J. A. M. Armstrong) yesterday brought to the attention of the House an article in the Toronto Globe of Wednesday, the 29th April, asserting that certain members of the Government were outspoken in their opposition to the Canadian Northern railway deal as announced by the Government. I was not in the House when the matter was brought up by the hon. member for Brant, otherwise I would have joined him in denying the accuracy of that statement. My own name was mentioned among others, and I take this first opportunity of denying that there is any reason or foundation for such a statement. On the contrary, I think the transaction has been handled in a most businesslike and thorough manner by the Government, and in the only manner in which it could be properly handled. The agreement will have my most cordial support.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My attention has been called to a report in to-day's issue of the Montreal Gazette and in certain other newspapers By inadvertence an erroneous impression has been created as to what I said yesterday during the discussion of certain steel items in the tariff. The report is as follows :
That there may he some further revision of steel duties required to meet the existing conditions in Canada, particularly as regards structural steel, was intimated by Hon. W. T. White to-night, during the discussion of the steel items in the tariff schedules. Mr. White said that the bridge manufacturers and allied interests in particular were naturally deeply interested in this question, and would have representations to make which might result in some further changes. The nature of these he did not indicate.
I shall read from ' Hansard ' what I said. I was speaking of the resolution under which the Governor in Council is authorized, when satisfied that rolled iron or steel angles, beams, channels, and other rolled shapes or sections of iron or steel weighing 120 pounds and less per lineal yard are manufactured in substantial quantities in Canada from steel made in Canada, to direct that there be substituted for tariff item 379 in schedule A to the customs tariff, 1907, the following:

379. Rolled iron or steel angles, beams, channels, and other rolled shapes or sections, of Iron or steel, not punched, drilled or further manufactured than rolled, weighing over one hundred and twenty pounds per lineal yard, n.o.p. not being square, flat, oval or round shapes, and not being railway bars or rails per ton-British preferential, $2; intermediate, $3 ; general, $3.
I explained to the House that the effect would be that on structural steel, from 35 pounds per lineal yard up to 120 pounds per lineal yard, the general rate of $7 per ton would be imposed. That is now the Tate on structural steel up to 35 pounds per lineal yard. The item which I have read will not become effective until the Governor in Council so directs, after being satisfied that rolled iron or steel angles and the other products mentioned are manufactured in substantial quantities in Canada. What 1 said, in answer to my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), was:
X am in hopes that within the next year and a half or two years plants will be established at the Sault, and possibly at New Glasgow, Sydney and Hamilton, capable of manufacturing structural steel up to 120 pounds per lineal yard. As soon as the Government is satisfied that structural steel up to that weight can be manufactured in Canada, the increased duty will come into effect. It is possible that some other adjustments of the tariff may have to be made by reason of that change when it comes into effect. For instance, the manufacturers of bridges are interested in this duty upon structural steel.
Of course, it was not in my mind that a change would be made in the $7 per ton duty which this item imposes. I said that when the change comes into effect it is possible that some other adjustments of the tariff will have to be made in consequence of that change. Not, of course, upon these products, but upon other products; or, in other words, what are known as consequential changes. I desire, therefore, to make it plain that the adjustment which I had in mind did not relate to these products. I may say, in order that there may be no doubt whatever about the matter, that it is not the intention of the Government to introduce any further tariff changes at this session of Parliament.

But to keep
an open mind for the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend knows that my distinguishing characteristic is an open mind.
Yes, that is so, but not always in the right way.

On motion of Hon. George E. Foster (Minister of Trade and Commerce), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair:
Resolved that it is expedient to amend the Canada Grain Act, chapter 27, of the Statutes of 1912, and to provide that advances to an amount not exceeding five hundred thousand dollars may be made to the minister out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada for the payment of freight charges and weighing and inspection fees on grain received into or shipped from elevators operated and managed by His Majesty, and that such payments shall be subject to all the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, and when the amounts so paid are refunded to His Majesty they shall be paid to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General of Canada for deposit to the credit of the said Consolidated Revenue Fund.

Before the resolution is
adopted, I am sure the Minister o.f Trade and Commerce will give the committee some information that was asked for on a previous occasion in regard to the operation of the Canadian terminal elevators, to facilitate which operation this resolution is to be be passed.

Perhaps my hon. friend
would be just as well pleased to take that up when we come to the Bill. This is simply a resolution, and the information that he requires I shall then be prepared with. If my hon. friend will kindly indicate what particular information he desires to have, I shall be ready with it when we take up the Bill, probably on Monday or Tuesday.
The information requested of the minister was as to the rates that were to be charged for services in connection with the interior elevators and the system under which business would be transacted.
I shall be prepared with any information relating to that.

We would like to have the fullest possible information in regard to how the Government intends to operate those elevators, pending their completion, and in regard to the handling of the coming crop. There may be further information required in regard to the terminal elevator at Fort William.

My hon. friend will recollect that, in Committee of Supply, we passed the Estimates referring to elevators, and I

said that when we were on the Estimates referring to steamship subsidies, any questions that had not been asked with reference to the elevators or their operation could be asked and would be answered when we took up those,Estimates. There is still an item remaining in the Estimates on which that could be brought up.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

On the motion of Hon. Martin Burrell (Minister of Agriculture), the House went into Committee on Bill No. 112, to regulate the Manufacture and iSale of Dairy Pro-' ducts, and to prohibit the Manufacture or Sale of Butter Substitutes, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 4-quality of milk to be delivered to manufacturers or shippers:

This is the same as the section in the existing Act, except that the words milk powder or casein manufactory, or to a milk or cream shipping station, or to a milk bottling establishment or other premises where milk or cream is collected for sale or shipment, axe added, in order to cover new processes introduced since the old Act was brought into force.

I do not wish to delay
the progress of the Bill, but the dairy industry is a very important industry in the part of the country I represent. While it may be that no trouble has arisen in the past, it strikes me that there is a great deal of room for trouble under .sub-section (b) which reads:
(b) Milk from which any portion of that part of the milk known as strippings has been retained;
I do not know how far the lion. Minister of Agriculture is familiar with the practical operation of dairying, but I think this is a provision that is not practical, and that under it a dairyman might be made the

subject of proceedings when such proceedings were not at all warranted. I quite agree that there should be punishment for putting in impure or diluted milk, but to say that a farmer must put all the milk he gets from each cow into the product he sends to the factory is, in my opinion, and with all due respect to former legislators, absurd.

I do not know that
there has been any trouble under the old Act which included these words. And, of course, this is one of the causes that call for only minor penalties. But as the hon. gentleman knows, because he probably, like the rest of us, has milked a good many cow, the richest part of the milk is in what is known as the strippings, and there may be a temptation to a fraudulent keeping back of that part of the milk. I do not think there would be any harm in leaving the subsection in.
If the hon. gentleman does not want to improve the legislation, all right.
I think it better to leave it in.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-butter substitutes and remanufacture of butter prohibited:
What are people to do who wish to purchase an absolutely healthy substance, labelled as what it is, and not purporting to be butter?

This matter has been discussed very thoroughly not only by the dairy associations but also in the Agricultural Committee of this House, where this clause was carefully considered. I am not disputing that oleomargarine might be made of perfectly healthy substances and be wholesome as food; but, on the other hand, this is the oldest piece of dairy legislation on our statute book, passed in 1886; and though there have been occasional criticisms, I do not think that any Government has thought it wise to change it, nor, I confess, do I. Although oleomargarine may be wholesome, yet, unfortunately, in practise, where the byproduct of carcases of animals can be made up into a product resembling butter, although it may be sold by the merchant on its merits as oleomargarine, yet, by the time it gets to the table of the second-rate hotel or restaurant, it is sold to the customer who pays for butter. In the United

States, where they have had some such provision as the hon. member would indicate, they found it almost impossible to work it out in practise, and it has given endless trouble.
I must say that in the interests of the dairymen as well as of the general public it would be very unwise to alter this section.

I cannot agree that
this legislation is in the interests of the general public. Public inspectors may well Ihe appointed, but the assertion that poor people should not have the privilege of buying a perfectly wholesome product is, on its face, untenable. I do not say for one moment that in the dairy interests this legislation is inadvisable, but it cannot be in the interests of all the public.

Of the majority of the
public.

Surely the object of
legislation is to legislate for the people.

My' hon. friend knows
that you cannot get absolute unanimity of opinion.

I maintain that that
portion of the public which is the least able to buy food and the least able to maintain its own rights should have every facility for the obtaining of food and should be allowed to purchase cheap food so long as it is good and wnoiesome. There is no denying that oleomargarine, if properly made, is good food, and to take any action to prohibit its use is to do something in the interests of the dairy people, but not in the interests of the public who would like to buy it.

The real object of this
legislation is to do away with imitations of real butter. People may eat lard and tallow if they wish to do so, but it should not be coloured and sold to the public as butter. The genuine article ought to be protected.

The hon. member for
Dundas says that if the people want to eat lard they can, but lard is not oleomargarine; it is a different thing altogether. Oleomargarine is a perfectly wholesome product, probably just as wholesome as butter. Of course, the Bill has been passed by the Agricultural Committee and, as the minister thinks that this legislation is in the interests of the country at large, I do not intend to say
anything against it, but I share in a measure the views of the hon. member for West Peterborough.

Has the minister or the
Government any information as to any infractions of the law?

I could not give my
hon. friend any specific instances. We are continually enforcing our Butter Act; so far as oleomargarine is concerned, I think the law has been pretty well lived up to, because it is known that the department will strongly attack any attempt to contravene the law. Notwithstanding what the hon. member for West Peterborough says, I have no doubt that if we eliminate this section and allow the production of butter substitutes, it would take a whole army of inspectors to prevent fraud.
Does the minister know of any oleomargerine having been sold in Canada ?
I could not answer my hon. friend on the spur of the moment; I shall be glad to get him that information.
What is the minimum amount of water permitted in butter ?
Sixteen per cent.
Is subsection (c) a new provision ?

Perhaps I can make the matter clear by reading section 299 of the old Act:
No person shail mix with butter any acid, alkali, chemical or any substance whatever, which is introduced or used for the purpose or with the effect of causing the butter to absorb water or any part of milk or cream; or manufacture, import into Canada, or offer, sell, expose or have in his possession fob sale any such mixed butter, any renovated butter or process butter.
Subsection (c) of section 5 of the present Bill makes it quite plain that we can prosecute those who undertake commercially what is known as the process of renovating butter by re-churning and adding more water.

There is a difference between grading, mixing the butter and putting it into merchantable shape, and reworking it for the purpose of introducing an extra amount of water. The big dairying establishments have out-stations at which they buy cream and butter from the farmers. The butter is made up into different forms and qualities, but is probably perfectly good butter, though not in mer-

charitable shape. It is brought to the central factory, graded, re-worked, put into merchantable shape and sold. I know that that is a legitimate part of the business of large dairy interests in Edmonton. I have never heard any objection to its being done; it always struck me as being a very proper proceeding.
They closed a factory in Winnipeg for doing the very same thing.

Possibly; but it seems to me to be a method strictly in line with the best interests of all parties concerned. It enables the farmer to get a cash price for his butter and enables the dealer to dispose of it to the satisfaction of his customers.
Re-churned?
I do not know whether it is re-churned, but it is re-worked.

I think that would be
all right. I understand what my hon. friend means. The trouble is that there has been a definite commercial process of absolute fraud in renovating butter, absolutely rechurning poor butter and adding water, the result being that it would keep for only a couple of days, while the water has been sold for the price of butter so that firms are making hundreds of dollars a day. There would be no desire to interfere with any legitimate process of re-working butter. The desire is to stop the fraud that is now being practised.

This section does not
prevent the legitimate re-working of butter? I met a gentleman from Winnipeg who told me that he had been interested in some such enterprise and he had been put out of business.

A firm in Winnipeg composed of men from my own town had a factory in which they invested $15,000. They were buying the cheaper grades of butter and re-working it. I do not know what the process was, but they were not making it out of any other substances than butter made by farmers in the surrounding district. They were put out of business by the late Minister of Agriculture and lost all the money invested. A claim was put in by Mr. D. P. Reid, of Selkirk, who had invested a lot of money, and the late Government promised to compensate him for putting him out of business because when he went into business there was no Act against it. I have always thought that the firm was treated in a very harsh manner, and that

the Government of Canada owe these people about $10,000.

The re-working of butter is permitted. A merchant goes through selections he has gathered, picks out the colour that suits best, puts it into the worker and makes up two or three tubs of the butter. The Bill does not interfere with that practice, but it does interfere with a man who melts butter and adds fresh milk and acid to give it a peculiar flavour which will last for three or four days. I have considered this Bill very carefully, and believe it cannot be improved upon in the interest of the public.
The wording of the section, I think, would prohibit that. The butter the hon. member speaks about would be a process butter, re-worked butter.
Process butter is homogenized milk.

I do not agree that
re-working butter would not come under this section.
You must consider the difference between re-working and re-churning.	,

You cannot re-churn
butter; that is a farce.

My dear man, allow me to inform you that I can take you to a factory in Canada where they have been trying to do that for two years,
4 p.m. and in some cases they have succeeded so well that they have sold two hundred pounds of water at the price of butter.

Coming from a county
largely interested in dairying, I would urge that section 5 be extended to prohibit the sale of such butter. Probably, however, section 6 would sufficiently cover that.

I would like to have a
definite statement as to whether these big dairy establishments in Edmonton are to be allowed to re-work butter in a legitimate way. I would read this section that they are not, but if the minister says it is the intention of the department to administer the law so as to permit the legitimate re-working of butter I would be satisfied with that; otherwise I would certainly have to protest against the section.

While I do not know
the circumstances of the firms to which my hon. friend refers, I do not think there will

be any attempt to stop the legitimate re-working of butter.

But might not some
private individual set in motion the machinery of the law? The enforcement of the federal law does not always come under federal authority. Things would be in a pretty mess if we would be safe in handing out reckless legislation on the country because we ourselves are so wise and prudent as not to take advantage of it. I think the minister's .suggestion does not answer the objection raised by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mt. Oliver).

I do not think my hon. friend need be alarmed about that. So far as I know, there has never been an attempt by any government to impose the slightest hardship in this regard, but it is very difficult to cover all cases in the dairying business without phraseology seeming to cover something that may be illegitimate. The Act will be interpreted by the officers of the department so as not to interfere with anybody carrying on a reasonably proper business.

Might there not be private prosecutions under this Act?
Mr. iBURRELL: It has never been done, so far as I know.

I do not think that is any answer. There might be private prosecutions, and if there were would it be any reply on the part of the accused to say that the Minister of Agriculture had said in the House of Commons that such and such was not the intention of the Act.

This Bill has been
given the most deep .and careful consideration, and is believed to be in the interests of the country as well as the dairying industry. I think its provisions will have to stand as they are. If a man is doing *something deliberately illegitimate he would certainly have to take his chances.

If the minister continues to take the stand .that he has taken up to the present and will not listen to argument, .saying that the Bill is wise legislation and will have to stand as it is, I, for one, wish to register my protest against passing legislation in that way. He might as well not bring it to the House at all.

The practice in this
House, o| course, has been to refer Bills to committees composed of members of both sides of the House, who thresh out
200	l
the details and report to the House. I have had a fairly long experience in the House, but I can only remember one instance-and that was a very extraordinary one-where the House did not accept the findings of the committee. I am not saying that the House is necessarily bound .to accept their findings, because we know it is not. In this case, a great many members from both .sides of the House gave this danse the most careful consideration in the committee and they passed it unanimously. I am only pointing that out to show that it has not been carelessly drawn up.

A fair argument, but
not final. It does not close the matter.

If the hon. member has
any objection to this Bill why does he not state it?
That finishes me.

I think the hon. member has stated his objection; but I wish to refer to a point on which I think the hon. member for Brockville can put us right. I gather from what the hon. member said a little while ago that butter that has been re-worked would not be known as process or renovated butter. If the hon. member is sure about that there is no difficulty.

You have grasped the
situation exactly.

Subsection (a) of clause 3 says that no person shall sell or offer for sale butter that is not in a certain shape, but the last sentence says:
Nothing in this paragraph shall be held to apply to butter in rolls or lumps, of indiscriminate weight, as sold by farmers.
If the farmers sells to anybody but the consumer, the person who buys from him has in turn to sell again, and it seems to me that the section as drafted can scarcely convey the intent that its framers had. There must be some way of permitting the merchant to sell the rolled butter that he has bought from the farmer without reworking it the shape that the first part of the clause calls for.

The first part of the
clause applies to creameries and other large establishments who make a practice of selling butter in certain shapes, but it is not meant to apply to the ordinary farmer who may go into a store and offer a lot of rolls weighing either half a pound, three-quarters of a pound, or a pound, which are sold by total weight. The clause is designed to give



to the public full weight from all the great butter-making establishments.

I quite agree with that.
But does not my hon. friend see that this clause is mandatory? A merchant who buys butter from a farmer must have it in a certain shape before he can sell it again. It seems to me that that clause should be amended in some way.

The clause reads:
Nothing in this paragraph shall be held to apply to butter in rolls or lumps, of indiscriminate weight, as sold by farmers.
Therefore, it is in a merchant's hands to sell any size and any shape of butter.

My hon. friend did not
read the whole sentence.
I do not think there is any danger of a merchant buying butter from a farmer without weighing it up.
I do not know about that. I have had something to do with that business myself.
I would risk you.

I know many merchants who buy round pats of butter supposed to weigh a pound, and they only count them, and the same with pound squares.
I think that many times I have seen the honest yeomanry in po-ssesion of pats and squares of butter, not as flush in weight as they might be.

This section says that no person shall sell butter, moulded or cut into prints, blocks, squares or pats, unless they are of the full weight of one-quarter of a pound, one-half pound, one pound, or two pounds, at the time they are moulded or cut. A consumer goes into a store to get a pound of butter, and finding the butter has shrunk in the meantime he takes objection, but the merchant tells him it was of the proper weight when moulded, and there is no recourse for the purchaser. It seems to me that a person who buys a pound of butter should get a pound of butter, whether it has shrunk or not. Again it says that nothing in this section shall apply to rolls or lumps, but it [DOT]seems to me that butter sold in rolls or lumps should be of a defined weight, and that everything should be sold by the pound. The consumers of Canada are being robbed by legislation of this kind. This section would enable the merchant, or the farmer if you will, to sell butter under weight, and to say it was all right when it

was moulded. I think the law should be made plain that if a man buys a one pound print of butter he must get one pound.

When a pound package of butter has stood for two or three days, the paper around it will absorb possibly one-tquarter of an ounce of the water, and most of the dairymen make allowance for that by putting in an extra ounce or three-quarters of an ounce.
Why not say, then, in this act that the butter when sold shall be of the weight it purports to be?

If a man ordered one
hundred boxes of butter in pound packages in the fall of the year, and stored it for a few months, he would have to go over every package and add one-quarter of an ounce to it to make up for the shrinkage, which would not be fair.
What about the consumer who pays for the pound of butter; is he not to be protected?

That is unavoidable
shrinkage.
It looks as if the dairymen were strong on the committee that drafted this Bill.

The objection raised
by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), as pointed out by the hon. member for Broekville (Mr. Webster), is not reasonable. You may ship one thousand pounds of butter, having ample weight when you shipped it, but when you store it the water evaporates and actually you get the same amoimt of butter, but you get a little less water. It was pointed out before the committee that certain persons in Montreal had been buying butter, rechurning it and remoulding it, and that samples were actually discovered which contained fifteen per cent of water. The object of this clause is to prevent anything like that, and I think it is perfectly clear.

That may seem fair
to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sexsmith), but is it fair to the consumers? For example, if one light-weight loaf is found in the establishment of a baker, his whole supply of bread is confiscated.	,
But bread does not get to be three months old.

Bread shrinks in
weight very rapidly, and the baker has to make allowance for that when he is making up the loaf, and quite properly so in the

interests of the consumer. If the dairyman knows that his 'butter is going to shrink, why should he not be compelled to put in the extra half ounce in the same way as the baker has to? A great necessity to-day is that we should have some proper law governing weights of commodities which are sold to the consumer. A man buys a pound of tea and he has to pay for the weight of the paper and the lead around the tea, which is absolutely unfair.

Is there anything in
the law that regulates the percentage of moisture in bread?

Every one knows that
bread shrinks in weight.
Yes, but there is nothing in the law to say that there shall only be a certain percentage of moisture in it, and the law provides for the percentage of moisture in the case of butter.

Bread and butter go together, but they are not parallel examples in this case. A baker can tell fairly well how long the bread will be on his hands, and what percentage to allow for shrinkage, but the butter-maker does not know whether the butter will be consumed in three months, or twelve months, or the day after it is made. I agree with the member for Brockville that it would be almost impossible to lay down a rule as to the allowance that should be made for shrinkage in butter. The last part of this clause reads:
Nothing in this paragraph shall be held to apply to butter in rolls or lumps, of indiscriminate weight, as sold by farmers.
I think that provision is all right, and it would Ibe very difficult to get over the necessity for it. Many farmers make their butter up in lumps of indiscriminate weight, and if we do not prevent that practice altogether we will have to leave this section as it is. I do not think we have yet reached a stage at which it would be wise to prevent farmers making their butter up in rolls or lumps.

To illustrate, I might
say that last June a gentleman in the West ordered from me 1,000 boxes of fancy June butter which was put up for him and placed in one of the best storage houses in Montreal. On the 1st of September one carload was shipped to him, find it held its weight pretty well, but when the second lot was shipped to him in January some
aooi	1
of the blocks were half an ounce light. How are you going to prevent that? The merchant bought at June prices, put the butter in storage at his own risk, and I would like any hon. gentleman to tell me how the natural shrinkage could be prevented.	-

Thu percentage of
water was reduced in it?
Yes.

It seems clear that the
hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) and myself will have to form ourselves into a consumers' union, with regard to this matter; the dairymen seem to have control of the situation.
Well, we get our bread from you.

If the contention of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) is right, with reference to the sale of butter in rolls and lumps, then the consumer has no protection at all, because, if a dealer has light-weight butter in his store, all he has to do is to say that he got it from a farmer, and he is free from any penalty. Again the unfortunate consumer gets the worst of the bargain.

I think the hon. member for Edmonton misunderstands the position. This is where there is no pretence of a discriminate weight.	The
farmers often bring to the country stores butter of indiscriminate weight.	The
farmer's wife, or whoever makes up the butter, makes it up into a lump of five pounds three ounces or five pounds five ounces or some other odd weight. The-merchant pays the farmer for the weight of butter in the roll or lump; the farmer does-not pretend to give any particular weight. It is in a different position from the other, in which there is a pretence of a certain weight, the butter being apparently in quarter-pound or half-pound or one pound prints. The butter referred to in this paragraph is not of any specified weight at all, and is weighed just as a load of wheat or a quantity of nails is weighed. As I understand it, the Bill does not pretend to guard people in such a case; it only attempts to guard where one has the right to assume that a certain article is of a certain weight. It requires that an article which pretends to be of a certain weight shall be of the weight which it pretends to be.

In many cases where a merchant purchases a roll or a lump of butter, he does not sell it en bloc; he cuts it up to suit his customers, giving one customer two pounds, another one pound, and so on. When he purchases it, he weighs it and pays the farmer for the weight that he gets.

Supposing a creamery man puts up a thousand pounds of butter in prints with fifteen per cent of water, as he is compelled to keep within the percentage of water designated in this Bill, namely sixteen per cent. He sells that butter; it is placed in cold storage for perhaps six months, and the retail merchants sell it again. The butter was in legitimate prints when it was put into cold storage; but, according to the statements of some hon. members, when the retailer-sells these prints, if the prints are under weight, say by half an ounce, the retailer should be liable. I think that is entirely wrong, because if we analysed that butter we would find a less percentage of water in it. If the retailer were to be held liable, butter could not be stored at all.

I think, after a careful consideration of this section, that the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) will be found to be right in his contention, at least to have a strong ground for it. The section is just a little hard to construe.
I appreciate the difficulty of it.

The hon. member's point appeals to me. It is unfortunate that the following words are inserted:
Nothing in this paragraph shall be held to apply to butter in rolls or lumps of indiscriminate weight, as sold by farmers.
I think the section is sufficient without these words to apply to persons selling butter in pats, prints, blocks, or squares. The section could be read in this way with the same meaning:
Nothing in this paragraph shall be held to apply to butter in roll or lumps of indiscriminate weight, as bought from farmers.
I think that would be better.

Under that wording of the section, if a man bought fifty or a hundred pounds of butter from a farmer, and put it into rolls or prints, he could say: I do not have to have the weight, because I bought it from a farmer.
IMr. L. Thomson. 1

What about butter in
tubs?

The same thing would
apply.

Why put in the words
' rolls and lumps '? Why not have it read in this way:
Nothing in this paragraph shall be held to apply to butter of indiscriminate weight, as sold by farmers.

After the careful consideration given by the committee to this Bill when last before them, I think it will be found to be very difficult to improve upon it. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) has grasped the situation as a practical man. One who has not had everyday practical experience has very little knowledge of the quantity of water sold illegally to the people of this country. I myself have bought what was called packed solid butter from a creamery and have weighed it the same night; I have set it out in a low temperature of say twenty degrees below zero, and the next day that same quantity of butter had shrunk three pounds per box. In some cases you will see the -cloths in which the farmers- have brought butter to market so wet that they will wet the paper and the basket through. That is owing to the temperature at which the butter has been worked, the butter having absorbed so much water. When the temperature is reduced the butter becomes solid and the water comes out. The hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith) says he has given the question careful consideration; I have talked it over with the butter manufacturers, both wholesale and retail, in the country, and they tell me that this Bill covers the ground as well as it can possibly be done.

The reason of these
words:
Nothing in this paragraph shall be held to apply to butter in rolls or lumps of indiscriminate weight, as sold by farmers.
-isbecausebuttereoldinthis way is weighed by the customers; but butter put up in prints by a creamery or by a farmer in the -little patent arrangement used for making a print is not weighed by the merchant when bought by a customer, if put up in a standard quarter-pound or half-pound or pound print. I would like to ask the
minister for information as to what a lump of butter really is. Supposing a man is charged with having sold butter underweight, he says: I bought this from a farmer as a lump of butter. What is a lump of butter? Every square block of butter is a lump of butter.
Not in the trade.

There is nothing in the

I agree with the suggestion of my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy), and I think my criticism of the section would be met if his suggestion were adopted. As it is, it makes the merchant who buys from the farmer subject to the final responsibility of sale to the consumer. The section should be made to read:
Nothing in this paragraph shall he held to apply to butter in rolls or lumps of indiscriminate weight, as bought from the farmer.
This would protect dealers and would not interfere with the intent of the section.

It would protect the dealer, but it would not protect the consumer. My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) was making an argument with regard to the tub of butter. But a print of butter, though sold as a pound print, may contain only fourteen or fifteen ounces. Why should not the consumer be protected? Why should the merchant be allowed to sell what purports to be a pound of butter or of anything else when he really gives only fourteen or fifteen ounces?

I think that if the section were to read as follows, we should get over the difficulty:
Nothing in this paragraph shall be held to apply to butter in rolls, blocks, tubs or other receptacles as bought from farmers.
Does not the farmer sell butter in lumps?
That would not be a happy expression as applied to my district. It has a meaning of its own.
I think I would leave in the words ' of indiscriminate weight.'

Yes, and widen the
clause so as to make it read ' bought from farmers,' instead of ' sold by farmers.'
I do not see any particular objection to that; but I do not think it would make much difference.
The hon. member is only enlarging it; I think the clause is all right-

If hon. members insist on pressing the point, I cannot see objection to the change. But really, I think the Bill covers the point and will work out all right. We threshed out these points in the preparation of the Bill.

I think that the clause is plain. We do not have to protect the public if they buy from the crock or lump, for in that case the butter is weighed, but only in the case of prints which the dealer is not supposed to weigh.

Section agreed to.
On section 10-penalties:

Section agreed to.

I have had under my own observation a case in which great expense was incurred by the withdrawal of one section from the statute regarding tuberculosis by Order in Council published only in the Canada Gazette. fMr. Nesbitt.]
any section of the statutes should be given in some wider and more public way. Surely with all the printing we do; with all the millions that are spent every year on blue books, many of which are never read by those who receive them, some means can be devised whereby notices of changes in the law can be given to the public. So far as the legal aspect of the matter is concerned, my hon. friend, being a lawyer, appreciates the difficulty of having for this purpose anything but an official gazette. On section 18-proof in deteriorated milk prosecutions:

Section agreed to.
On section 19-evidence:

Is there anything in the meaning given to pure milk represented by a standard or percentage of butter fat? I have seen many prosecutions against men who I think were honest. They would be sending in milk to a factory from a cow that would give a percentage of butter fat of perhaps only two per cent. Thus their dealings were honest but suspicious. I wondered if the standard was fixed under the Act.
That point was not raised in the committee.
What is the standard?
A standard is fixed in the Inland Eevenue Department for another purpose.
Would it not be wise to define pure milk in the interpretation clause?

The percentage of
butter fat of course varies with the season of the year. The percentage is not nearly so high in April as in September and that would cause difficulty with a rigid standard. Then too some breeds of cows give a small quantity of milk with a high percentage of butter fat and others give a large quantity of milk with a small percentage of butter fat. Either one of these would be a quality of pure milk.

What would be classed
as 'inferior to pure milk?'

The difficulty is to define what is pure milk. The hon. member for Brockville says that pure milk in the fall is of a higher standard than in the spring and therefore a man might be convicted of an offence who was supplying pure milk of a standard up to the spring standard but less than the fall standard.
He would be judged by a comparison of the milk supplied with milk taken from a cow at the particular time of the year.

Looking at the matter
from the standpoint of the liberty of the subject, it seems that with a sliding scale like that the producer of milk does not stand much chance.
Would the milk from the Jersey and Holstein be qualified as inferior under this section?
Not at all. The criterion of whether it was pure milk or not would be a comparison with the milk as it comes from the cow.

The difficulty in defining pure milk in Ontario has been that a lot of milk is collected on the pooling system. Some factories buy by the Babcock test. Some cows of one breed 5 p.m. might produce milk with not more than two and one-half per cent of butter fat and others might run up to five or six per cent. If you set a certain standard it will make it very difficult to continue that system.
As I understand it, the penalty would not be inflicted unless a person had mixed something with milk.
Or skimmed it.

How is the test
applied? I do not pretend to be an expert, and I would like to know how you can tell whether anything has been mixed with the milk or not. For instance, take the milk of a cow that tests at 3J, and suppose sufficient water was put in to make it test at only 3, is it possible to tell that it is not pure milk?
Absolutely.
Section agreed to.
It would seem from the last few sentences of this Act that the only way for a man to preserve his liberty is to sell his cows.

I would like to ask the minister, or the Chairman of the Agricultural Committee, why, in the interpretation clause, a dairy is described as a place where the milk or cream of less than fifty cows is manufactured into butter. Why do they not call a dairyman a man who manufactures into butter the milk of his own cows only, and the place where he manufactures it a dairy? Why should a man with seventy or a hundred cows not be allowed to call his place a dairy, providing he does not take in outside milk? With us there a great many men with more than fifty cows, but their establishments are dairies, not creameries, as they manufacture no milk but what their own cows produce. My idea of a creamery is where they manufacture milk outside of their own production. I would like to know why the definition of a dairy stiplates for less than fifty cows, and why it was not on the basis I have suggested.

It is rather arbitrary, but it is difficult to define the difference between a dairy and a creamery, You have to draw the line somewhere. New Zealand has placed it exactly at fifty, I understand.
I do not think there is any great object in having the definition altered.

I am not asking for that. Our farmers call their places dairies so long as they manufacture the milk from their own cows only; and call places that take in outside milk creameries. My hon. friend from Brockville is an experienced man, and I will ask him why a man should not be allowed to call his place a dairy so

long as he manufactures his own milk only?

I think that if a farmer had the requisite number of cows to bring his place under the heading of a creamery, he would be very glad to do it. He would prefer to have it called a creamery because, as you will have noticed in the papers, creamery butter is dearer than dairy butter. In the committee, I took the ground that it was unfair to the farmer that we should designate a certain class of butter, dairy butter; and another class, creamery butter; so we decided on the fifty cows. There are a great many people making butter with less than fifty cows, w'hose product is as good as or better than the creamery product. We could not come to any other solution of the difficulty of distinguishing the two.

Would you mind my
saying that with our farmers the old policy of putting ' creamery ' on their wrappers is rapidly passing away, if it has not already passed. The idea in the public mind is that a creamery is more of a wholesale factory, taking in milk from various people. The word ' dairy ' with us carries more weight than the word ' creamery ' for the simple reason that if a man running his own dairy has cleanly habits his butter is likely to be more valuable than creamery butter made from milk from different farms, which may not be cleanly.

I was present when this Bill was before the committee, and we discussed each of the clauses thoroughly. On the majority of farms in Ontario you will find less than fifty cows to a dairy, and for that reason we thought it right and just to say fifty in the Bill. A man with only fifty cows is very often not able to work up the milk on his own farm and has to send it to a creamery. There is a good deal of difference between creamery and dairy butter. One is the product of separated milk, and the other is not. My hon. friend would intimate that dairy butter is superior to creamery. From my own personal experience I can say that during what little time the Lord will allow me to live I want to eat creamery butter.
With us, any farmer with six or ten cows uses a separator.
Not necessarily.

They are not forced to,
but as a matter of practice they do. I do

not know of anybody with more than six cows who does not use a separator in his dairy.

I know some farmers
following the deep water setting system.

I am glad to say that is not the case with us; we have advanced in the art. I know, as my hon. friend says, that the great majority of farmers have less than fifty cows There are a great many who want to call their butter ' dairy butter.'
With us, they all want to call it ' creamery butter.'

The manufacture of
butter in the old way is gradually diminishing. In my district a farmer who has only three or four cows uses a separator. I am surprised at the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) saying they want to call it dairy butter, because all over the Dominion the creamery butter is selling at a higher price.

There are dairymen in
my riding who sell their butter at a higher price than any. creamery ibutter will fetch. They sell it all the year around and they call it dairy butter, and any one who visits their dairies and sees how they conduct their business would pay more for their butter than for any creamery butter made from the milk of cows from the public.

What proportion of this
vote would be for service, and what proportion for compensation for animals slaughtered?

The heaviest expense is for
the inspectors, of whom we have about 131, counting the riders in the mange district and including their assistants.
Is the mange decreasing?

There are some areas
that have been relieved in Alberta, and we have wiped out the whole of the mange district in British Columbia. In the mange districts we have certain herds which are quarantined and under special inspection. From the whole of the mange area animals are not allowed to be moved outside of the area unless they are ^dipped, but those not quarantined can be moved within the area. The only execeptions are animals consigned for slaughter to the abattoirs, in which case some are inspected at Winnipeg and some go straight to the abattoirs on the Pacific coast, or to places in the mountain districts where there are no agricultural areas. The outlook is more hopeful.

Does dipping mean
two immersions?
Yes.
What is the situation in regard to hog cholera ?

We have this year paid out more for hog cholera than we did last year. I will give my hon. friend the comparative figures. In 1911-12 we paid out $23,446; in 1912-13, $52,785, and in 1913-14, for ten months, $46,860. There has been some increase in that, noticeably in parts of Saskatchewan and Ontario, but on the whole nothing like what we had to contend with during the first year or two after the Act came into force. Although it is costing a good deal, I do not think we can adopt any other method than the one we are following now. In the United States they have an entirely different system, whereby they immunize the hogs from cholera. It has been found, however, that a particular hog may be immunized and still be a carrier of the disease. Their system costs them millions of dollars as compared with our thousands. We passed a regulation prohibiting the introduction of virus for this particular form of inoculation. We think the best system we can adopt is the system we are carrying out at the present time.
There is no doubt that many cases of hog cholera have been spread from points where uncooked garbage containing infected meat has been brought in from the other side, or even from hogs on this side. In regard to that, not only are we urging better sanitary precautions on the part of the local municipalities who should ob-

serve them, but we have passed an Order in Council stating positively that the Government will not undertake to pay compensation to people who deliberately feed uncooked garbage to their hogs. I think that is in the public interest.
Under what circumstances have the outbreaks of hog cholera taken place recently ? Have most of them been owing to garbage-fed hogs, or have they occurred outside of such conditions ?

I think most of the cases have occurred as my hon. friend has stated. We think we have been able to trace them to garbage-fed hogs. In some cases the disease has been brought in from the other side, although our regulations are pretty strict. This year we contemplate putting two or three special men to do educational work in regard to cleaning up garbage and seeing that it is properly cooked, especially wherever hog cholera has already been prevalent, so as to drive into the public mind the great importance of feeding properly cooked garbage.

There was hog cholera
last year amongst my hogs, although they never saw garbage of any kind. They were all fed on good, clean, second-grade flour, and shorts and oil cakes. They ran in pens that were what we call gravel-loam soil, and the inside pen was just as clean as this chamber. Every condition that was possible to surround them with was perfect, even with regard to running water. I think the Lord sent the cholera. I do not know where they got it.

As my hon. friend the
minister knows, I am asking for definite information for very definite reasons. How far can the department go in the matter of preventing this disease, having regard to the conditions surrounding the keeping and feeding of hogs?

I would not like to
answer that question offhand, because it is in the nature of a legal question. I suppose we can go pretty far, but I imagine there will be still ample power in the municipal and provincial authorities to deal with some phases of the matter. I do not know how far we can interfere locally with sanitary questions such as my hon. friend has mentioned. We could plainly say that if they do not live up to certain conditions, we shall refuse to pay any compensation in that district. I would not, however, like to express any opinion offhand.

What is the action that
the department is permitted to take and, as a matter of fact, does take, as regards the measure of responsibility assumed by the Government under the law as it stands at present, in case of an outbreak of cholera?

Directly we are informed of an outbreak or discover it in any place, we send an inspector there. The place is immediately quarantined and the hogs are slaughtered. In some cases, where there is a holding of a large number of hogs and where there has been very slight contact, it may possibly be necessary to slaughter all the hogs; but we are coming very fast to the conclusion that it is dangerous to exempt any, and that it is better to slaughter all the hogs that have come in contact with hogs infected with the disease. I think we ought, before another session, to consider the raising of the valuation of hogs, because they have increased very much in price during the last two years. Last year we took up the increased valuation of horses, and I am not sure that we should not go into the question with regard to hogs. Some people will argue that you should not pay compensation for any of these things, because it is in the owner's interest and in the public interest to stamp out these diseases; but if you do not compensate, you will have people concealing these diseases, and you will never be able to stamp them out.
Where a man owns an animal and another man has a lien note or a chattel mortgage on it and the animal is killed, to whom does the Government pay the money?
My hon. friend is better able to answer that question than I am, because he is a lawyer. I think the owner of the animal would get the money.
I have seen the point come up, and it is very embarrassing.
I am afraid I cannot speak offhand in regard to it.

I would like an answer in regard to it, because I understand that the ruling of the department is that they will not give anything to the lien holder. That works an injustice, because if a man of straw owns a pig and another man has a lien on it, the luckiest thing the owner can do is to give the pig hog cholera.
I will make a note of the matter.

There has been a substantial increase in the valuation of hogs in recent years, so that the valuation that was perfectly good a few years ago is not so now. Therefore I think there should be a measurable increase in the valuation.
I agree with my hon. friend. We shall have to deal with that matter before long.

We do not have such things as local inspectors. Our inspectors are liable to be transferred to any point throughout the country. Some of them, of course, have a very wide range 'of territory. How many inspectors are there for the province of Quebec?

I have forgotten. The
chief inspector is Dr. Couture, at Quebec.

In the case of a district
many miles removed from the residence of an inspector, when an inspector is sent for sometimes he comes, and sometimes he does not. I think a certain route should be marked out and periodical visits made.

We do not undertake to do the local work. We do the work at boundary points. We do not undertake to have local inspectors at all points throughout the country, but we try to cover the ground we are supposed to occupy.
How about a case where an animal is diseased?
That is a private business, and the owner calls in a local veterinarian.

But how about the case
of a contagious disease?
Mr. BURRELL. Of course, if it is one of the diseases scheduled by the Act, that is different. But there are very few such diseases-hog cholera, glanders and dourine are the only ones at present.

Is there any glanders in
Quebec?
Very slight. Our greatest trouble is in Saskatchewan.

Is the minister not yet
able to enlarge his field to cover tuberculosis in cattle?

We have that under consideration, and in fact, the increase in the Estimate for this year was partly made in order that, if we decided to take a step in that direction, we could do so. I am sorry I am not in .a position to make a definite statement on the subject. I hope to be able to make a start in the matter, though, as the hon. gentleman knows it is a very difficult question, and the more it is looked into the more difficult it becomes.

Does the
minister intend to take steps to eradicate the weed which, as he knows, produces what is known as 'cattle disease'? The minister reached the conclusion that it wa3 not a contagious disease, and therefore no compensation was allowed for losses. But as the Government has undertaken to act in co-operation with the local governments, I think it should take steps to prevent the spread of the disease, and to that end to destroy this weed which, by causing this disease, has led to the loss of hundreds of thousands of dollars in the eastern part of the province of Nova Scotia.

We reached the definite conclusion that the disease was due to the weed in question and that it is not contagious. So far as cleaning up the area infested by that weed is concerned, that is a matter for the local authorities. Anything that we cam do to co-operate with them, of course, we shall be glad to do.

But the minister has
not decided to act in co-operation with the local government to eradicate the cause of the disease!

I cannot say that we
have entered into any arrangement with a [DOT]local government as to the eradication of weeds in their district. I cannot tell at this moment what may have taken place lately as between the local authorities and the officials of the department.

I lately received a
letter from a clergyman in the eastern part

of my county, which adjoins that of my hon. friend. This -clergyman sent me statistics that were absolutely astonishing as to the losses going on, through this disease. It is extending eastward and in some cases to the Island of Cape Breton. It seems to me that some investigation ought to be made with the view to ascertaining whether some cure could not be effected. A careful diagnosis of the symptoms might lead to such a result. Apparently, when a veterinary is called in to attend a sick animal, if he diagnoses it as a case of ' cattle disease 5 that is the end of it-he seems to regard it as a hopeless case. It seems to me that the finding of a remedy is a subject to which the department might well direct its energies. difficulty is this:	The farmers interested

New South Wales.

This is a great hardship, because the butcher does not want cattle that have been knocked about and bruised by dipping almost immediately before they are slaughtered. One of the large companies that violated the mange regulation is greatly benefited by the regulations now in force. They are permitted to ship their cattle to Vancouver and other points on the coast for slaughter, while the small man who ships to Nelson, Fernie, or other points iin the iQrowsnest Pass must dip his cattle once before shipment. The consequence is that, because of the dipping regulation, the butchers along the Crowsnest Pass would rather buy from the large packers in Calgary or Edmonton than buy live cattle in southern Alberta.

I will look into the
matter and see what can be done.
I understand that if a portion of a herd of hogs is found diseased, the whole herd is destroyed. Is compensation paid for those that are slaughtered, but are not found to be diseased?

Yes, compensation is
paid for all.
Is it permitted to dispose of the carcases of those animals which are slaughtered but not found to be diseased?

Under the regulations, the whole herd may be killed and no use permitted of any of the animals destroyed. In some cases in the past animals which have been in contact with the diseased herd, but which have not shown symptoms of the disease, have been used for food. But the difficulty is that while no lesion^ might be apparent, on account of the disease being in its early stages, the virus might nevertheless be there, and if the meat were left around uncooked it could actually transfer hog cholera to another district. On account of this danger the regulations provide for our dealing with the matter in a most drastic way, and paying compensation accordingly.
Has compensation been paid in the case of the outbreak of hog cholera at Edmonton ?
I think so.
There was a question as to whether the garbage was cooked or not; some think it was not cooked.

Before the Order in Council to which I have referred was passed, the people were informed that if they did this unknowingly or unwittingly they would be compensated, but if a man, after being warned, deliberately fed uncooked garbage to the animals with the result that hog cholera was contracted, he would not be entitled to compensation. Although some discretion has been used-in the enforcement of the Order in Councils I think we shall have to educate the public to understand that if they feed uncooked garbage to the animals and hog cholera results, they will not be entitled to compensation.
Has the minister been made aware of the development of the horse meat industry in the county of Chambly ?

The matter has come to the attention of the department. This horse flesh is being supplied, I believe, to the city of Montreal. We were asked to appoint an inspector to see that the meat was not diseased, but we did not feel that it came under our department. I must say that we have taken no steps to encourage that particular industry.
Does it not come under the Department of Agriculture ?
No.
What about the inspection of the meat ?

We inspect only those shipments which are concerned with inter-provimcial trade. I understand that this industry is confined to the province of Quebec, Montreal being the only city in which horse flesh is being eaten at the present time.
The newspapers have announced that a laffge portion of this product is sent to Sweden. Would not shipments in. that case come under the control of the minister?
I have not the Act before me, but I think that its provisions would not permit us to deal with horse flesh.
For export?
I do not think the Act covers the inspection of horse meat..
As this is. a rather important question foe the city of Montreal, perhaps the minister would look into it.

I will give it careful
consideration.
Has the minister any information with regard to a serious outbreak of dourine at Raymond, Alberta?

We are paying a very heavy compensation there, and hope to get the situation under hand before very long. As my hon. friend may know, through the excellent work of Dr. Watson at Lethbridge we have adopted the complement fixation test which enables us to detect almost without any doubt the existence of dourine. We have tested several hundreds of these horses and the chances are that before we are through it will cost us $40,000, or more but we hope to wipe out the disease.
I understand that some of these animals were recently imported.

I think so; I know that some of them were pure bred. The area is a comparatively restricted one. We are not having half as much trouble as they have in the United States, where it is cost. ing a great deal more, and I think by going after it in this drastic way we shall be able to control it.	.

The United States
authorities told us for many years that we were wrong and that they did not have it, but the chief inspector told me not long ago that they had some eight or ten thousand cases.

Has the
minister received a copy of a resolution passed by the Antigonish Board of Trade, asking the department to make a survey of a railway line, starting at or near Antigonish and running through South River valley to Country Harbour? If the minister has received such resolution, what does he purpose about it?

I cannot remember just now; although I think there was such a resolution received. I shall be able to give the hon. gentleman full information later.
Mr.WILLIAM CHISHOLM (Antigonish): I appreciate, that the hon. gentleman being only acting Minister of Railways, it would hardly be fair to ask him to make a statement on a matter of this kind, but I desire to take advantage of this opportunity to put on record, for the guidance of the Minister of Railways when he returns, the importance of complying with the request of the petition of the Board of Trade of Antigonish. On March 27, 1912, I had occasion to bring the question of this line from Antigonish to Country Harbour to the attention of the House, and I then set out the importance of the road and the desirability of constructing it. The Minister of Railways seemed to realize then that that line was shorter than any of the proposed lines to connect Guysborough county with the main line of the Intercolonial railway. The remarks I made will be found at page 6227 ' Hansard,' March 27, 1912. I asked the minister if he had in contemplation making a survey of that route with the view of building such a railway, and he replied that he would take occasion to investigate the different routes during his tour of inspection and decide which would be the best. Later, on January 30, 1913, I brought the matter up again and put this question (page 2416 ' Hansard,' 1913):
Has a survey been made lor for the proposed railway route between Country Harbour through the South River valley, connecting with the Intercolonial. If so, has a report been made?
Mr. Cochrane:	The department has no
knowledge of any such survey having been made.
This was rather an extraordinary statement for the minister to make, on the 30th of January, 1913, in view of the solemn promise he had given on the 27th of March, 1912, that he would have a
survey made. I was particularly surprised to see such an answer, because there was a by-election in Antigonish for the local Legislature in January, 1913, and during that by-election what purported to be copies of correspondence with the Minister of Railways were exhibited, and it was stated throughout the length and breadth of the district that that part of the country was to be afforded the railway communication asked for. On April 13, 1913, some months after that by-election, I brought the matter up again, and to my great surprise I found the Minister of Railways repudiating the statements made in the county, regarding the construction of this road, by men of responsible position, one of whom was seeking to be a member of the local Legislature, and another was an honourable senator. There were also read letters which purported to have come from the Minister of Railways, but which were afterwards repudiated by the minister of Railways on April 30, 1913. I pressed the minister for an answer to the question why the survey had not been made and what the intention of the Government was in respect to that. As the Minister of Railway was stolid, implacable and impervious to anv appeals for information I made on that occasion, I was obliged, in order to place myself right, to make some further extended remarks with respect to the necessity of building that road. Those remarks will be found, under date of April 30, 1913, at pages 8873 and 8875 of volume 5 of 1 Hansard,' 191213. Therefore, I do not propose to enter into the argument into which I entered on that occasion. Those references will be sufficient to show my position in the matter, and to call the attention of the Minister of Railways, when he returns-which I hope will be in a very short time-to resume the duties of his office, to the reasons why I urge that that road should be built.
I have just one more observation to make. I moved for a return for the correspondence on file with reference to the suggested survey and construction of a line of railway from Country Harbour to Antigonish to connect with the Intercolonial railway. A return was brought down on the 22nd day of January, 1914, but I cannot find in it any reference, or petition, or request from those persons who claimed to be doing so much for the good of the road, and to be endeavouring to secure the accommodation so much desired in that vicinity; nor can I find any suggestion of

any kind urging the building of a line of railway through that section, except letters from myself, which are dated May 14, 1913, March 3, 1910, and January 13, 1911, also a letter from the secretary, Mr. Jones, under date of March 18, 1912, and a letter from Mr. W. C. Milner, under date of January 22, 1912. Mr. Milner was asking for a subsidy for a line of railway in that locality and I was endorsing his application with my humble support. My conduct has been subjected to more or less criticism, by my political opponents, it being alleged that I have not been friendly to this proposition, and that is why I take this opportunity of putting myself on record.
I can only say, in conclusion, that I hope the minister, when he returns, will see that a survey is made, and I would call his attention to the facts expressed by myself to the House on the occasions to which I have referred, particularly on the 27th of March, 1912, and again on the 30th April, 1913. I would urge upon the minister to see that the survey is made as soon as possible.
Let us have something more tangible than pre-election promises by men whose assurances are now very properly discounted in that part of the country, for it is now clear to every one that these pretending friends of the road were after votes, when they needed them, and not the railway. But the people there want the road, and are entitled to it, and it should no longer be denied or delayed to them.

I will certainly look into
the matter myself and see if I can get any further information, which I will give to the hon. member. I will also draw the remarks made by the hon. member to the attention of the hon. minister on his return, which I hope will .be at a not very distant date.

Will the hon. minister be
good enough to .say whether or not any move has been made with a view to taking over the branch line owned by the Cape Breton railway between St. Peters and Sydney?

yet.

I do not know. ' An engineer may have been sent by the general manager of the Intercolonial, but I know nothing about it.
