When I was at St. Peter's a few weeks ago, I was informed that Dr. Martin Murphy, formerly provincial engineer for the province of Nova Scotia, was to be sent down by the Department of Railways and Canals in a few days for the purpose of making am investigation as to the physical condition of the road, and making a report to the department. I understand from the remarks of the hon. minister that neither Dr. Murphy nor any other engineer has gone over the road for that purpose.

I do not know. Several
gentlemen have suggested to me that there should be .some scheme for developing the Bras d'Or lakes, and that there .should be some hotel system there in connection with the Intercolonial railway. I suggested that perhaps it would be well for the general manager to send an engineer or some -one down to look over the situation and advise me.

What does an
engineer know about hotels?

It would be necessary to
look over the road. It may be for that reason that .an engineer has been sent down. I do not know whether or not there is anything in it.
No action has been taken by the department to make a survey of the proposed route between St. Peter's and Sydney with a view to extending the 'line in that direction?
No.

Mr. Gutelius has
been doing things that the minister does not know anything about. Did not Mr. Gutelius have an interview within the last two weeks at Halifax with certain gentlemen in (regard to taking over the line between New Glasgow and Thorburn?
I did not see it in the newspapers.

Neither did I, but
did not Mr. Gutelius have an interview with certain gentlemen interested' in the taking over of the line belonging to the Acadia Coal company from New Glasgow to Thorbum?
I do not know whether he met them or not.

Did the minister
authorize him to meet them?
No, I did not.

Speaking of branch lines, I wish to say a word in favour of the Gaspe railway. My hon. friend knows that what is known as the Gaspe railway is made up of two lines: One extending from Matapedia on the Intercolonial railway to New Carlisle, and the other from' New Carlisle up to Gaspe basin in the county of Gaspe. The first section was built thirty or thirty-five years ago and cost the country a very large sum of money. It serves .a, vary rich section of the country, which might be very prosperous if the line were in good order. The first twenty miles of the section, called the Atlantic and lake Superior, was built originally by the Government. It had been intended at first to build it from Matapedia to Gaspe basin, as a branch of the Intercolonial. This decision had been arrived at when Sir Chas. Tupper, I believe, was Minister of Railways and Canals. For some reason or other that idea was abandoned and the road was taken over by Mr. C.	N. Armstrong, a gentleman well known in the railway world; and, by subsidies from the Dominion Government and from the Provincial Government, he succeeded in building the first hundred miles, that is to say, from Matapedia to New Carlisle. It is a beautiful section of country represented by my hon. friend the member for Bona-venture (Mr. Ma/rcil). Unfortunately it seemed that the large fishing establishment known as Robin and Company, later on merged into the Robin-Colas Company, a Jersey firm, was opposed to any railway construction in that country because, forsooth, the railway might induce the fishermen to migrate into other sections of the country, and the fishing establishment would be deprived of the valuable services of that population of fishermen. After many years that first section was finally completed, but it is to-day, as it has been for a long time, in very poor condition indeed. If the hon. member for Bonaven-201
ture were in his seat, he could describe to the committee the very dangerous condition of that road. When I was elected member for the county of Gaspe in 1896 I took up the question of building the second section of the road, extending from New Carlisle to Gaspe Basin. A company was formed, subsidies were voted by this Parliament, a land grant was voted by the legislature of Quebec and the second section of the line was completed in 1910. There is quite a difference between the two lines. The first, >as I have said, is in very poor condition; the second is a really well-built road, upon which trains run regularly from New Carlisle to Gaspe Basin. But in order to connect the Gaspe end with the other parts of the country, the trains have to run on the first section, which is not in tgood condition, and the result is that one* section of the line is in good order and the other is not. As has very often been said, it is an extraordinary thing that the original intention of the present Government has not been carried out; that is to say, that this section of the country has not been connected with branch railway lines as part of the Intercolonial system. To-day, on account of this mishap to the first section of the road, the company cannot prosper. It is true that trains are run both ways, but they are run without profit. If the Government were to make the necessary arrangements with the company and obtain the road upon fair terms, I am sure that they would be really doing something for that most interesting section of the country. For almost half a century that section of the country was deprived of railway communication; yet it is the oldest county in the whole of this Dominion. It is well known that when Jacques Cartier came to Canada in the sixteenth century, he first landed on the shores of the bay of Gaspe. I understand that the Government cannot acquire the road without introducing special legislation to that effect. In order to facilitate the acquiring of tho;e lines, why should not the minister and the department feel their way by approaching the various companies and establishing to their satisfaction, as well as to the satisfaction of Parliament, what would be the cost of taking over those branch lines? It seems to me that this would be putting the oxen before the cart. I believe that if last year Parliament had been made aware of the cost of the various branch lines, the legislation which was introduced could have been passed and the amendment introduced by the Senate would probably not have been made. During the time that I was member



for Gaspe, a period of 16 years, I received many communications on this subject. Although their end of the road is in perfect order, my former electors in the county of Gaspe are anxious, in order to ameliorate the conditions, that this road should be taken over as a branch line from Matapedia to Gaspe Basin.

I would suggest that
during the holidays the minister should do his best to meet the representatives of the various companies and ascertain in some of the cases what would be the cost of acquiring the lines. This would pave the way to enabling legislation empowering the minister to purchase a certain number of railways. If beforehand he could say to Parliament that it would cost so much for this or that line, Parliament would feel better able to deal with it.
That is a very good suggestion, and I will draw the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals to it, or, if he should not be there, I shall be glad to follow it up.

Can the minister tell us what is proposed this year in branch line construction? Some of us on this side were much encouraged by the Government accepting a resolution moved by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) favouring the construction of certain new branch lines in Nova Scotia in counties not now provided with railway facilities. Will the minister say whether any provision will be made in the Supplementary Estimates for the construction of any of these branch lines in Nova Scotia?

There is no vote for new
branch lines; there is a vote for surveys to be made, and I think that the staff are at work, or are about starting at work, on the surveys along the Intercolonial railway.
There is no vote in the Main Estimates but we would like to know whether there will be a provision in the Supplementaries.

I could hardly state that until the Supplementaries are passed by Council. In the Main Estimates is a vote for $50,000 for surveys and inspection. I do not think the hon. gentleman would expect me to make an announcement as to the other.

I think the acting minister should be prepared to state the policy of the Government with regard to the branch lines, so that the committee might know whether the department intend to go forward this year or not. That would be a proper thing for the minister to deal with when he is bringing in his railway Budget. I am not asking him to reveal secrets or to say how much he is going to spend'. But will he spend any?
The Supplementary Estimates will have to be discussed in Council before I can make any announcement.

While I am in hearty accord with the policy of the Government in taking over the branch lines, I would suggest to the acting minister that he must be just before he is generous. On a former occasion I brought up the question of the refund of damages paid by the municipalities of Pictou, Antigonish and Guysborough for the right of way for that portion of the Intercolonial railway running between New Glasgow and the strait of Canso. The subject was discussed on that occasion, but not at great length. The Prime Minister'discussed the matter shortly, and the hon. member for Cape Breton, the hon. member for Guysborough, and I think the hon. member for Pictou made some observations regarding the injustice of this claim. But the minister of Railways on that occasion stated that he did not know anything about this claim until it had been discussed that night. He, however, gave an assurance that he would look into the question so that he could discuss it at a future date. His remarks will be found in volume VI of ' Hansard,' 1912-13. The occasion for the discussion of the matter was the proposal for a subsidy to the Ontario Government of $2,000,000 in connection with the building of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway. It was pointed out by myself, and urged by others, that in view of the precedent thus established there was no reason for further delay in paying to the municipalities the sums they had expended in that portion of the Intercolonial railway to which I have referred. The whole of the 2011
Intercolonial railway from Sydney to Montreal has been paid for by this Government -by the people of Canada. But as I was explaining, and as I am sure it will surprise the acting minister to know, the municipalities of these three counties have had to bear the cost of the right of way of that portion of the Intercolonial railway and the money was never refunded. There are other parts of the Intercolonial railway that were taken over from time to time in connection with the general scheme of building, but the provinces that had put their money into these lines were recouped. I do not think I can lay the case before the committee better than by giving somewhat in detail what was urged for and against the claim made by the Province of Nova Scotia in this connection, so that the minister may have all the facts when he returns; and I propose to give both sides of the case. This is an old question, dating back as far as 1891. There is a history to it, and I think it right that both sides of the case should be presented. Therefore, at the risk of wearying the committee, I propo.se to put on the pages of * Hansard ' the pros and cons.

The hon. gentleman stated
that this dates back to 1891?
The history of it goes back to 1891.

Yes, but did the claim
originate then on the building of the Intercolonial railway?

It originated before
that portion of the road known as the Eastern extension, running from New Glasgow to the strait of Canso, was taken over by the Dominion Government. That railway was built by a company subsidized by the province, and the municipalities paid for the right of way. Later, the Dominion Government took it over and repaid the province what it had put into the road, but never repaid the municipalities the amount they had paid for the right of way. My point is that for every other part of the Intercolonial from Sydney to Montreal the municipalities have been held free from any portion of the cost. The Government paid the whole cost of the road. The matter will be explained better than I, can explain it if I place on 'Hansard' the resolutions that were passed as far back as 1891. On the 15th day of May, 1891, the legislature of Nova Scotia passed, and afterwards presented in due course to His Excellency the Governor General, an address which sets forth the facts as follows:

on the people of the municipalities mentioned, the said municipalities voluntarily offered and agreed to pay the amounts involved in the purchase of the right of way of the said line. Such were contributed in consideration of the advantages to be derived from the construction of the line, and were not intended to form any lien upon the railway so constructed, nor were they paid under any expectation of reimbursement. That since the railway had been operated by the Dominion Government, its efficiency has been increased far in excess of what could have been reasonably anticipated by the residents of the above mentioned municipalities when making the grant which they did in aid of the construction of the line.
That the mere fact that some other counties did not make a like contribution to railways which were constructed through them does not seem to afford substantial reason for the present claim.
What date was that?

About 1893. The matter stood thus for some years until happily for the province of Nova Scotia a Liberal Administration came into power at Ottawa in 1896. So impressed with the justice of the claims made was the Government of Nova Scotia that, notwithstanding their previous refusal, they again submitted their claim to a Government which was naturally supposed to be more sympathetic, and in which they believed they had an especial friend at court in the person of the then Minister of Finance, the Hon. Mr. Fielding. On the 15th of October, 1897, the claim was again presented to the Laurier Government. Inas-. much as I have read to you the position taken by the previous Conservative Administration here, as disclosed in the report of the Privy 'Council of the 28th of October, 1893, from which I have quoted, it is fitting that the rejoinder thereto should be placed on ' Hansard.' The House will pardon me for taking up its time, but I want all the facts laid before it so that the Minister of Railways, who is unfortunately absent, may grasp all the facts of the case, about which there seemed a great deal of misapprehension in certain quarters. Therefore, I propose to lay on * Hansard ' the further argument of the Government of Nova Scotia as contained in the documents presented to the late Laurier Government in 1897. I quote the following:
Eastern Extension Railway.
The terms of Confederation imposed upon the federal Government the responsibility of constructing the Intercolonial railway as a Government work, and, while the actual terms of the British North America Act only required that the railway should connect the river St.

Lawrence with the city of Halifax in Nova Scotia, the Government has seen fit, as a matter of public policy, to extend this road on the one side from Riviere du Loup to Lfrvis, and still later to the city of Montreal, and on the other to Sydney Harbour, in the county of Cape Breton. Every portion of this railway has been constructed and paid for out of the consolidated revenues of Canada, and the right of way for the whole work has been paid for out of the consolidated revenues of Canada except one portion between New Glasgow and the strait of Canso. That portion was built by the Halifax and Cape Breton Railway and Coal Company, by aid of a Liberal subvention from the Government of Nova Scotia. It was undertaken upon condition that on its completion it should be further aided by being handed over the line of railway then belonging to the Dominion between Truro and Pictou, which was then and still is a very profitable piece of road. Believing that it was in the public interest that this Eastern railway system should be in the hands of the provincial Government rather than in the hands of a company, the Government of Nova Scotia, in the session of 1883, took steps to acquire the Eastern Extension railway which carried with it the right of possession and ownership of the Pictou branch. A clause had been inserted in the contract with the Halifax and Cape Breton Railway and Coal Company enabling the Government, after the completion of the line, to take it over by paying the amount of the actual outlay of the company over and above the amount of subsidy it had received from the Government. The power of acquiring was exercised, and the Eastern Extension railway came into the hands of the Government during the year 1883, and was operated by the Commissioner of Public Works. On applying to the Dominion Government for the handing over of the Pictou branch, under the terms of the agreement and Act of Parliament, the federal Government imposed such conditions in respect of the transfer as made it impossible for the Government of Nova Scotia to carry out its policy of acquiring and managing the Eastern railway system, with its contemplated extension through the island of Cape Breton, without incurring flnanical responsibility far beyond its resources. The terms which the Dominion Government imposed as the conditions of handing over the Pictou branch were so unreasonable and so exacting as to raise a very strong presumption that they were imposed in furtherance of the well devised policy of the Government to themselves make this Eastern Extension a part of the Intercolonial and extend the same to Sydney Harbour. The result was that the Government of Nova Scotia was compelled reluctantly to abandon its own policy, and to hand over the Eastern Extension railway to the Dominion Government as a part of the Intercolonial railway system upon being refunded the amount that they had actually paid to the Halifax and Cape Breton Railway and Coal Company. At the time of this transfer, as will be found in the Journals of the House of Assembly, 1884, the Hon. Messrs. Pipes and Fielding, who were the delegates representing the Government of Nova Scotia, urged on behalf of the Government of Nova Scotia that the Dominion Government on taking over the Eastern Extension railway, should not only pay its costs to the provincial Government, but the provincial sub-

sidy as well; and no doubt this would have been insisted upon if it had not been that the action of the Dominion Government in refusing to hand over the Plctou branch, except upon terms which were quite unreasonable and quite impossible of fulfilment, compelled the provincial Government, in self-defence, to give up the road upon being recouped the actual amount which had been paid out to the company.
The fact remains that from Lfrvis to Sydney Harbour every single mile of the Intercolonial railway now running, has been paid out of the consolidated revenues of Canada, including the right of way with the exception of the short piece between New Glasgow and the strait of Canso, and this part of the national highway has been partially paid for out of the revenues of the province of Nova Scotia, and the right of way has been paid for by the ratepayers of the municipalities of Pictou, Antigonish, St. Mary's and Guysborough. The Government of Nova Scotia simply asked that this portion of the Intercolonial railway be placed in precisely the same condition as ail the other parts of the Intercolonial railway ; that the sum of six hundred and seventy-one thousand eight hundred and thirty-six dollars ($671,836), which the province of Nova Scotia, out of its limited resources, has paid as a subsidy to this part of the Intercolonial railway, be refunded to the province, inasmuch as if the Intercolonial railway had been extended by the Dominion Government eastward?

as it actually has been in accordance with its well defined policy-it would have been necessary to have paid for the construction of the portion between New Glasgow and the strait of Canso as rhuch as the amount which had actually been paid for it, plus the subsidy which has been paid out of the revenue of the province of Nova Scotia ; also the cost of the right of way. The piece of road between the strait of Canso and Sydney Harbour stands in precisely the same position as a part of the whole national work. Every dollar of the cost of construction has been paid for by the Dominion Government, and it will be difficult to devise means of pointing out any distinction which exists between the case of that portion of the Intercolonial railway, and the portion between New Glasgow and the strait of Canso, towards which the province of Nova Scotia has actually contributed the sum of six hundred and seventy-one thousand eight hundred and thirty-six dollars ($671,836).
It is scarcely necessary to remind you of the action of the Government of Canada in relation to the province of Quebec in respect of a case so very similar to this, only, perhaps, not as strong. In that case the Dominion Government undertook to refund to the province of Quebec their subsidies paid for the Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa and Occidental, because it seemed to be a part of the general railway system of the country. The case is surely not as strong as in a case where the road "itself becomes the property of the Federal Government, and is being operated now as a national Government railway.	'
The claim, therefore, of the province of Nova Scotia is that this sum should be refunded with interest and that the amount paid by the municipalities of Pictou, Antigonish, St. Mary's and Guysborough for a right of way should likewise be refunded to those municipalities.
Now, Sir, I have laid before the House both sides of the case. The temptation, to
discuss the arguments pro and con is very strong; but that would be inexcusable as we have a quasi judicial pronouncement on the facts.
The Laurier Government showed its sympathy with the claimants by directing that the whole matter so far as these claims are concerned should be left to arbitration. The arbitrators appointed under an Order in Council dated July 19, 1900 were: Sir George Burton, an ex-Chief Justice of the province of Ontario; F. B. Wade, a leading lawyer of the city of Halifax; and Edmund J. Barbeau, a prominent banker of the city of Montreal. The case of the province was presented by the Attorney General of Nova Scotia, and the present member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and part of the time by the late Christopher Bobinson, K.C., of Toronto, while Mr. Lafleur, K.C., of Montreal, represented the Dominion Government. The decision of the arbitrators will be found in the sessional papers for 1901, Vol. xxxv, No. 13, as Sessional Paper No. 73. It is a complete vindication of the position taken by the Fielding Government, and afterwards by the Murray Government of Nova Scotia. It finds that the claim of the province was a just one. To quote the language of the board:
We are forced to the conclusion that the claim of the province is a just one and we respectfully recommend that they should he paid the sum of $671,836, the amount of the bonus.
The findings of the arbitrators must be regarded as binding in law and fact, and conclusive as to the matters in dispute between the two governments-just as binding as a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada or the Privy Council in a matter that properly comes before them. The personell of the arbitrators, their high standing, and the professional standing of the counsel employed on either side renders the decision of the board such as makes it acceptable to all parties. The argument was made on behalf of the Government that the province voluntarily transferred the eastern extension for a certain fixed amount, namely the amount paid by the provincial government to the company for a transfer of the Toad by the company including their rights 'and interest in the Truro branch under the tripartite agreement, so called, and all parties were bound by that bargain. The amount was as stated $1,284,311.97. This amount, it will be observed, did not include the subsidies that had been given by the province during the construction of the road, amounting to

$671,836, nor what was paid by the municipalities for the right of way, which with interest to date would in round numbers approximate:

It will be noted that the refund to the municipalities for the amount paid to them for the right of way was on all occasions as strongly urged as was the claim for the refund of the provincial subsidies paid the company. It would seem manifestly unfair that the Dominion Government, representing the whole of Canada, should take over that railway as a part of the Intercolonial railway belonging to the whole of Canada and constructed and operated for the whole of Canada, and not for the convenience or accommodation of any particular section of it, without paying for it every cent that it actually cost. Whilst individuals or corporations may well be justified in driving the best bargain they can, and may well insist on enjoying any legitimate advantage the one obtains over the other in a bargain made, I submit that rule should not be invoked by the Government of the country dealing for the whole country. It should not deal in a huckstering spirit, but should have regard to what is fair and equitable and just in foro con-scientiae, without seeking to take advantage of any technical objections available, or of anything strictly legal, in contradistinction to equitable, defences. From a reading of the arbitrators' report it appears this view seemed to have properly influenced them. They found this Government should repay the subsidies advanced by the province in the building of that part of the Canadian road. Can any one doubt that if the claim of the municipalities had been dealt with by these same arbitrators they would have been allowed? If it was right and proper, if fairplay and justice demanded, that the province should get back the money that it expended in that part of the national road, equally just and equitable is it that the municipalities should be refunded their contributions. It does not seem fair that Canada as a whole should pay for the right of way of every other portion, of the people's road except that' portion from New Glasgow to Mulgrave. It does not seem fair, and there is no principle of justice or equity on which you can contend, that these municipalities of Anti-gonish, Pictou, Guysborough and St. 
Marys should alone, of all the municipalities from Cape Breton to Montreal contribute directly or indirectly to building or extending the national railway required to be provided by Canada as a whole under the terms of Confederation ? The late Conservative Government took the position that in view of ' the facilities and accommodation which the construction of the said railway would confer on the people of the municipalities mentioned, the said municipalities voluntarily offered and agreed to pay the amounts involved in the purchase of the right of way of the said line,' and that ' such were contributed in consideration of the advantages to be derived from the construction of the line.' As a matter of fact, they did not do so voluntarily. But do not the very same advantages, facilities and accommodations extend to every other municipality from Montreal to Sydney ? Why, therefore, should we be saddled with burdens which the others have not had to bear ? When the Intercolonial railway was extended from Mulgrave to Sydney did the municipalities through which it ran have to bear the cost of the right of way in view of and in consideration of the advantages, facilities and accommodation such extension would give ? Not at all. I submit therefore, that the position taken by the Minister of Railways in 1893 is not tenable, and his conclusion ' that the mere fact that some other counties did not make a like contribution to railways which were constructed through them, does not seem to afford substantial reason for the present claim,' is alike illogical, unjustifiable and unfair.
Now, Mr. Speaker, you may ask, why was not the claim of the municipalities which on its face seems much stronger than that of the province submitted to the board of reference. It is unfortunate under the circumstances that it was not, for unquestionably it would have received favourable consideration. You have observed these claims were urged in the various memorials presented. These memorials were passed in 1886, 1889, 1891, 1894 and 1898 respectively. In the report of the arbitrators I find a reference to the municipalities' claims as follows:
A claim was made at the opening of the case by several municipalities who had assisted the railway by grants of money, to be heard by this board; but it was determined that such claims did not come within the scope of the reference, and we adhere to that position.
My information is that when it came to the submission to arbitration, the claims

of the municipalities were intentionally omitted in the order of reference. It was thought advisable not to confuse or complicate the issue by submitting more than one claim. The claim of the municipalities being considered much the stronger, the claim of the province was first submitted alone, it being assumed that if a favourable award were obtained in this case, there would be no question about the right of the municipalities to recover later. On the other hand, in the event of an adverse decision by the board, so far as the claim of the province went, the claim of the municipalities might be jeopardized by being linked up with the weaker claim. At any rate, the board did not adjudicate these claims, and they now come before this Government for settlement.
After the award was made in favour of the province and the amount thereof nearly three-quarters of a million dollars was paid, the municipalities claimed the province should recoup the amounts expended by them. The contention was made amongst others, that the local Government at the time had unjustly imposed and reimposed the obligation of paying for the right of way upon these municipalities against their will; that the province in undertaking to deal with the road and to transfer it to the Dominion Government was bound in fairness to pay them itself, or as a result of their dealing with it, to obtain payment for them; and that under these circumstances it was the duty of the local Government to see that the claims of the municipalities were included at the time of the arbitration held in 1901, as a part of the claim to which the province was entitled, and which the province should refund to the municipalities inasmuch as the province had improperly, it was urged, fastened this burden upon them when the construction of the road was undertaken. I am not going into details regarding this phase of the matter. I may say, however, that under chapter 3 of the Nova Scotia Acts of 1905, and chapter 50 of the Act of 1907, which extended the scope of the inquiry, a commission was appointed by the local Legislature to report on and adjudicate the claims of the municipalities, as made against that Legislature. There was some delay on the part of the municipalities in availing themselves of the machinery to adjudicate their claims; and it was not until the 24th of June, 1912, that the commission, consisting of Chief Justice Fitzpatrick of the Supreme Court of Canada, Chief Justice Townsend and Judge Drys-dale, of the Nova Scotia Supreme Court,
gave their decision, finding that there was no claim against the Government of the province in connection with the matter referred to them. The question they decided was the liability of the province to recoup the counties. The right of the municipalities to be recouped by somebody was evidently assumed. The commission decided that the province was under no legal or moral duty to do so. The inference is obvious. ' Disappointing as this decision may be to the municipalities, it is, and must be, accepted. This was not a commission composed of party friends of the local Government, who would in advance take instructions as to the goal desired, the decision to be reached; but it was composed of men who know not politics since their elevation to the Bench, and who, before their appointment to the positions they now adorn, although they had their party affiliations, two of them Liberals and one Conservative, could always rise above and beyond the level of the partisan to the higher plane of professional duty, and always had and retained the confidence of the public generally. Their investigations were not ex parte, or conducted in secret; but on the contrary, in open court and in the presence of counsel for all parties interested. I make these observations in passing, because I know it to have been stated by men prominent in politics, some of whom occupy positions in public life that would at least lead you to expect more honesty from them, that the Murray Government at Halifax referred the matter of the claims to this commission in order to secure the dismissal of the claims as against them. Such an assertion is as false as it is malicious.
It is very easy to be wise after the act. Men's hindsight is greater than their foresight. It is perhaps for that reason I could never see why the claim of the municipalities was not made, in the first instance, against the federal Government, instead of against the local Government. The local Government, under the Burton award, only received the amount of provincial subventions which went into the building of the Eastern extension. Had that board dealt generally with the cost of the Eastern Extension railway and the amount which, as a matter of equity, the Dominion Government should have paid for that portion of the Intercolonial, when it was taken over, and an award had been made accordingly, then I could understand the municipalities properly claiming to be recouped by the provincial Government. But as it dealt specifically with the subventions from the

provincial treasury alone, and it was distinctly stated in the award the claim of the municipalities could not then be considered by them under their order of reference, it is obvious, to me at any rate, that the further claims should have been made later against this Government, and not against the local Government. I have no doubt that, had the municipalities promptly pressed their claims against the Dominion Government, they would, in the face of that Burton award, have been settled long before now. But as I have already stated, it is easy to be wise after the act. The municipalities, doubtless, thought the claims could be more expeditiously, and with less expense, recovered from the province; and the province could then claim from this Government. The principle on which the municipalities rest their claims against this Government is found not only in the Burton award, and in that case where the Dominion Government refunded the province of Quebec their subsidies paid for the Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa and Occidental railway, mentioned in the memorial dated October 15, 1897, but also in a more recent case, which I happened to come across, that of the claim of New Brunswick in re the eastern extension. In that case, the facts, which are almost on all fours with the claims made by Nova Scotia, were as follows:	In 1869
the Dominion Government took over and adopted as a part of the Intercolonial railway that part of the road formerly known as the Eastern Extension railway, and extending from Painsec Junction eastwardly to the boundary line between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, a distance of 37$ m.les. The Dominion Government paid $894,000 for it, of which $644,000 was paid by them to the contractors who built the road, and the balance of $250,000 was paid to the New Brunswick Government, by being passed to the credit.of the province on debt account. The province had up to that time paid for the construction of the road $400,000, and there was, therefore, a balance of $150,000 of the total expenditure by the province in the road. In 1834 the Dominion Government voted $150,000 to reimburse the Government of New Brunswick for money expended by them in the construction of this section of the railway, and this was, on July 1, 1884, passed to the credit of the province on debt account. The province up to that time had not only claimed this balance of $150,000, but in addition, [Mr. W. Chisholm.!
interest on that amount from 1869, when it was claimed this balance should have been placed to the credit of the province. The Dominion Government, on the other hand claimed that the payment of $150,0C0 was in full of all claims by the province in connection with that road. On the 16th February, 1900, an arbitration board was created to inquire into the claim made by the province and adjust same. The arbitrators were Judge Barker, of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick, Judge LangeJier, of the Supreme Court of Quebec, and Mr. Duncan Coulson, general manager of the Bank of Toronto. On the 1st April, 1901, they made their award, allowing the province the interest claimed, compounded, which amounted to $145,218.75. This report is found in the sessional papers for 1901, Volume xxxv No. 13, and in sessional papers is No. 73b. Not only was it considered equitable that the amount certified by the engineer to have gone into the construction of this section of the road should be paid, but the interest on it, from the time it should have been paid, must also be allowed. The actual expenditure by the provincial government should be recouped. It was thought but fair that the Dominion Government should pay every cent that portion of the Intercolonial railway cost.
Now I ask you, Mr. Speaker, are not the claims of the municipalities which I am endeavouring to present not Only just, fair and reasonable in themselves, but their uayment by this Government justified to the hilt by precedent? For very many years, this has been a source of rankling and complaint with the people of these municipalities. They have considered, and very justly so, that justice has been denied them by the late Conservative Government and .delayed to them by the late Liberal Administration. From the view point of the late Conservative Government, they saw no legal duty on them to pay these demands although clearly, as indicated by the decisions and awards which 1 have read, the moral and equitable obligation was there. And so far as the late Liberal Administration went, they virtually admitted their liability, when they recognized their obligation in the similar cases, to which I have referred. It is hoped, therefore, that the grievance which has rankled in the minds of the people of these counties will be speedily removed.
Before leaving this point, let me give some

brief quotations expressive of the opinion of the leader of the Opposition in the province of Nova Scotia on this subject. In the debates of 1912 at page 304. Mr. Tanner is reported thus:
He had always held that the federal Government should pay the claim. He had said so in 1905, and he had never hidden his opinion.
Again:
He would repeat now what he said then, if the federal Government would now pay the claim, the provincial Government should do so.
Also:
He would say that in his opinion the provincial claim was a very weak one, and that the municipal claim is stronger than the provincial one.
These observations were made before the board of arbitrators was appointed to deal with the liability of the province in respect to these municipalities' claims. Mr. Tanner had no doubt the federal Government should pay these claims, and he apparently took the position, which it turned out was the correct one, that it was to the federal Government the municipalities should look rather than to the provincial; but so impressed was he with the justice of the municipalities' claim that he went so far as to say that if the federal Government did not pay the claims, the local Government should.
In conclusion, and here I again apologize for taking up so much time-let me summarize the grounds why these claims should be paid, by quoting from the statement of claim oh behalf of the municipality of the county of Pictou, found in the return brought dowu lately, and invoking these grounds on behalf of the county of Anti-gonish which I have the honour to represent :

Because the Government of Canada are now the owners of the piece of railway between New Glasgow and the strait of Canso and have never paid to any one the cost of the right of way and land on which said railway is built, and should for equitable reasons pay to the county of Pictou the amount they were compelled to pay to the original proprietors over whose lands the railway was built.
2.	The road from New Glasgow to the strait of Canso forms part of. the Intercolonial railway, extending from Montreal to North Sydney, which road by the provisions of the section 145 of the British North America Act was to be a national work, and constructed as it has been at the expense of the federal authorities. Being a national work, it cannot be expected that a municipality should be compelled against its will, to bear the expense ol the right of way or any part of it.
3.	By the extension of the Intercolonial railway to North Sydney as one of its Atlantic
termini and making it the commercial highway through the last named point with the colony of Newfoundland, the Parliament Of Canada has made and declared that part of it from New Glasgow to the strait of Canso within the meaning and intent of section 92 sub-section 10	(c) of the British North

I wish to supplement the argument made by the hon. member of Antigonish with regard to the line of railway in the counties referred to. The cost of the right of way was paid by the municipalities mentioned, not voluntarily, but under an Act of the province of Nova Scotia which imposed the liability upon them. The legislature of Nova Scotia, after the transfer of 1884, always asserted that the province should pay back to the municipalities the sum of $671,000 which, they alleged, had been wrongfully withheld from them by way of duress, and that the amount paid for the right of way should also be refunded to the municipalities. A reference was made, and the municipalities were under the impression that the order of reference to Chief Justice Burton covered the claim of the municipalities. When the case came before the tribunal Chief Justice Burton ruled that the terms of the reference were not sufficiently wide to enable (him to adjudicate upon the matter, consequently the question has since been left undetermined. The municipalities urged the local Government to pay them out of the money they had received. The . reference my hon. friend made to Mr. Fielding has really no application to the case, because previous to his 
being minister he urged, not on behalf of the province, but on behalf of the municipalities, through the legislature, the justness of the claim. The intention of the parties at the time the order for reference was made was that the claim should be adjudicated upon by Chief Justice Burton, but on account of his having ruled that the terms of the reference were not sufficiently wide, no supplementary reference having since been made, the matter remain unsettled. I hope the minister of Railways will look into the matter very carefully; the facts will warrant his taking some action with regard to it.
With regard to the coal contracts, I would be obliged to the minister if, before he takes up his Estimates again, he will get fuller information with regard to the delay in the settlement of one of these contracts, which happens to be in connection with a company in my county. As a consequence the spring operations have not been resumed, and in some cases real hardship exists among the miners on account of failure to get work. With the settlement of this contract they may go on with some reasonable degree of certainty.

The local Government and the Dominion Government between them have acquired the road which is now part of the Intercolonial railway. The other municipalities along the line of the Intercolonial have all been paid for the right of way but the four municipalities mentioned by my hon. friend have not been paid. Eighty miles of right of way has not been paid foT by any one, and that stretch is one of the most profitable portions of the Intercolonial. The municipalities certainly have a moral claim against this Government, if not a legal one. I have given these facts to account for the delay in bringing this claim forward. I think it was only two years ago that the decision was given that the local Government Was not liable, and the municipalities are now claiming against this Government on the principle that there must be a remedy somewhere, and if it is not in Nova Scotia they think it is here. I am not going to argue the claim to-night, hut I wish to say that it is a matter too important to be brushed aside, and one that should receive the serious consideration of the minister. I would also like to get some information in regard to proposed improvements of the grade of the Intercolonial between Halifax and Moncton. Several schemes were proposed. This matter was discussed last year, and I have no doubt the minister has the information at hand that he may lay before the House before the Intercolonial discussion is concluded. There were two or three proposals: one was that a line should be built by Parrsboro; another for a line across the mountains, and a third proposal was that a northern direction should he taken around by New Glasgow. A good deal of money has been spent .in surveys and investigations, but the country has not yet got information as to the policy of the Government in regard to this matter or as to thei *result of the investigations. If the minister, before Tuesday, when I understand the Railway Estimates are coming up again, would furnish the House with any reports he has on that question, and give us some idea as to the policy of the Government in this matter I should be very glad because a great deal of interest is felt in this question in the province of Nova Scotia and the people are waiting for some statement by
the acting minister as to the Government's intentions.

I remember discussing this
matter with the minister when going down to Halifax to see him off. I remember the place too where there is a very heavy grade. The minister had a discussion with Mr. Gutelius at that time, and I know they had in view the reducing of the grade at that place. Mr. Gutelius said they were making surveys with a view to trying to get around it in some way. I will see if they have any information in the department. Of course, the Minister of Railways, if he were here, could explain the whole s:tuation, as he understands it thoroughly. If I have not any information in the department, I will write the minister or telegraph the general manager for information, which will, no doubt, reach us before the end of the session. We will leave some of the Intercolonial items on which to dis-euss any question in connection with the Intercolonial railway.
If the minister has the engineer's reports, I would like to see them.

If there is anything in the
department I will bring it down on Tuesday; but if I have to communicate with Moncton, the hon. gentleman will understand that it will take a week or two to get the information.

I understand from the observations made by the hon. member for Pictou and the answers given by the minister, that general improvements in connection with the Intercolonial in Nova Scotia are in contemplation. In the island of Cape Breton, from which I come, it is particularly important that any general improvements contemplated should have reference to the facilities at the strait of Canso. The enormous traffic between the Dominion of Canada and Newfoundland landed at Sydney comes, of course, by the strait of Canso. Unless better faeilities are provided there, I would submit to the minister that whatever improvements he makes in the rest of the road will not give him the results that he might expect. We have only one steamer on the st:a't of Canso, the Scotia. She is good enough for her size, but she is only one steamer.
I think another steamer has been purchased.
I am very glad to hear that.
The contract has been let for a new steamer.

That is not so good as the first statement of the minister, but it is well to know the contract has been let. I presume the new steamer will be of equal capacity with the Scotia, which is a very good boat.
She is much larger.

That is still better. When you are building for the strait of Canso you are building for Newfoundland, because although possibly there is no obligation on us to build for Newfoundland, yet for the purpose of bringing traffic to the Intercolonial railway it is just as well to do so. It has been said that a bridge over the strait of Canso is quite feasible, and if my hon. friend should continue to be Minister of Railways
I hope not.
If he should continue to be Minister of Railways a monument to his memory would be a bridge over the strait of Canso.
If I should continue to be Minister of Railways I would have a monument sooner than that.

The bridge over the Grand Narrows is a monument to the memory of the late Sir John Macdonald. At one time it was thought that Cape Breton would forever be handicapped with a ferry across the Grand Narrows, but in 1888 we had the honour of a visit from Sir John Macdonald, then Prime Minister, who having seen the situation there, decided to bridge the Grand Narrows, which has been a vast advantage to the Intercolonial and to all that part of Canada.	Some years	ago	an
Act was passed by this Parliament constituting a private company to bridge the strait of Canso, and a very eminent engineer who was in the service of that company pronounced that it was quite feasible to do so. If it was feasible for a private company, much more would it be for the Government of Canada. It would certainly be a great thing for the island of Cape Breton and for the whole of Canada.
I wish that the minister, when he is looking to betterment of the conditions of the Intercolonial railway, would make inquiry as to whether a bridge should not be built across the strait of Can30.

There is another matter to which I wish to call the attention of the minister. The hon. gentleman pointed out to the member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) that he is possibly too late now in making a claim for a refund to these municipalities on account of the right-of-way, and so I want to guard against being too late by now making a claim somewhat akin to that which the hon. member for Antigonish has made. There is a diversion of the Intercolonial in the island of Cape Breton, known as the Georges river, Little Bras D'Or, Sydney Mines and North Sydney diversion. I congratulate the Government on putting the road now where it should have been put thirty-five years ago when it was first built, but by this diversion they are abandoning about five miles of the present road between North Sydney Junction and the town of North Sydney, and for which five miles the right-of-way was paid for by the town of North Sydney when the road was built in 1888. Now that the Government is abandoning that five miles of road, and that it is not to be put to the use for which the town of North Sydney bought the right-of-way, the municipality should be put in the position in which it was before, and the money it paid for the right-of-way refunded to it. That diversion is not yet completed, and this five miles is still in operation, so that the contention cannot be raised that the claim was made too late. I give notice to the minister now that when the five miles is abandoned the town of Sydney will expect to be recouped for their investment in that right of way.

The diversion is not yer, constructed and the five miles will have to be operated for some time yet, so that the question could not come up during the present session. I will draw the attention of the Minister of Railways to the statement of my hon. friend.

subtopic: PRIVATE BILLS. ' TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

speechtext: The House again in Committee on Bill No. 59, respecting the Toronto, Niagara and Western Railway Company.-Mr. Currie. Mr. Blain in the Chair.
On section 1-short title:

subtopic: PRIVATE BILLS. ' TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
With regard to this Bill, I think an explanation is due the committee. This is an ordinary extension of time for the construction of a railway which has made considerable progress with its work and has spent a good deal of money. In the Railway Committee several sections were added. One of these sections,
I regret to say, I shall feel it my duty to ask the House to strike out, notwithstanding that it was inserted by the committee. The Bill was reprinted as reported by the committee, and the section whose excision I shall move is section 7 of reprint. Let me briefly explain the sections. Section 1 is the ordinary section. In section 2, we made an amendment to rectify an incorrect description of the authority controlling Burlington Beach. The section provided that railway should not be built along the beach without the consent of the corporation of the township of Saltfleet. But Burlington Beach is not under the control of the township of Saltfleet but under the control of the Burlington Beach Commission, that commission receiving its authority from the Provincial Legislature of Ontario. Section 3 enacts the ordinary limitations- two years to commence and three-years ' to complete the unfinished portions. Section 4 of the reprint has been added by the committee. This was done at my instance and was carried unanimously. The effect is to repeal section 10 of the statute of 1903. That section permitted a part of this railway to remain under the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature, notwithstanding that we were declaring the whole work to be for the general advantage of Canada. It struck me, and the committee agreed with me unanimously, that to expect the Dominion Railway Commission to control a railway, a portion of which was outside of their control and under the control of a provincial legislature, was incongruous. Sections 5, 6, and 7 were inserted at the instance of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell). It is with regard to one of these sections that I intend to move. But I ask the committee not to dispose of my motion at this time. 1 am informed that the hon. member for South Toronto has telegraphed that it is impossible for him to be here to-day, and as it is a section inserted at his instance that I am moving to strike out, in fairness to him I think this committee should hear what he has to say before acting upon my motion. I will pre-
sent my explanation of the case now, because, reluctantly, and much against my will-but I am bound to obey- my doctor's advice-I am unable to be here to-morrow. The condition of my health compels me to get away and not annoy you gentlemen longer, much as I should like to continue.
As to these three sections, I must admit to this House that I do not think I am entirely without blame for the mistake as I believe it to have been-that the committee made in regard to one of these sections. I have always found this House quite unduly inclined, as I think, to have respect for what I do as Chairman of the Railway Committee. So I am not going to leave here without stating frankly the position with regard to this section. The hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) moved three sections in one paper. Where I am to blame, I think, is in not having insisted that these sections should be separated and put before the committee one by one. I am satisfied that had this been done, the one to which I shall raise objection would not have carried-that	is
only my opinion, of course, and I have no right to say more than enough to make myself clear. These three sections are aimed at protecting the rights of the city of Toronto in regard to street railway franchise.
They are aimed at preventing any railway from coming into Toronto and interfering with the valuable street railway franchises of that city. Sections 5 and 6 are, in my opinion, quite proper for that purpose. I think section 5 as reprinted is waste paper, because, as I understand the Railway Act, the Railway Commission has exactly the same power as section 5 provides that they shall exercise with regard to preventing any railway from interfering with the street railway franchises of the city of Toronto. Section 6, however, is of some use to the city of Toronto, and I am in favour of it in so far as- it provides for the protection of urban rights by preventing a railway from coming into the city under the guise of being a work for the general advantage of Canada, but having in view only the object of doing a purely street railway business. Section 6 of the reprinted Bill is as follows:
Neither the company nor any other company that may acquire or have the right to run over the line of the company within the city of Toronto shall receive, carry or discharge passengers from any point within the limits of the said city to any other point within the limits of the said city; but the powers for the carriage of passenger traffic that may he exercised

by the company or by any other company over the line of the company within the limits of the said city, shall only extend to and include the receiving, forwarding and delivering of through passenger traffic originating outside the limits of the said city for delivery within the limits of the said city, or originating within the limits of the said city for delivery outside the limits of the said city.
iSection 7 of the reprint is a peculiarly worded section. The only argument used in the Eailway Committee in support of that section was that .similar sections were inserted in three other Bills three or four years ago by this House. These were new companies seeking incorporation; they were companies that had done nothing; had no vested rights, had built no part of their right of way and had spent no money. The Hamilton, Waterloo and Guelph Railway Act is chapter 108 of the Statutes of 1910; the Western Central is chapter 150 of the Statutes of 1911, and the Toronto and Eastern railway is chapter 167 of the Statutes of 1910. Two of these railways were taken over from the province without anything having been done and one was granted a charter by original Act of this House. Nothing had been done when those clauses were inserted; they were given their franchise upon the express condition set forth in those clauses, .and upon no other. I do not think it makes any difference in the year 1914 what my opinion was in the year 1910 or 1911, but at that time I was of the opinion that this very section which I am attacking was not a provision which should go into a Dominion railway corporation Act, because we have a tribunal -to which we have given ample jurisdiction and to which we keep adding every jurisdiction that may possibly be necessary -in the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada, which properly and successfully deals with the question of railway crossings. The difference, however, between those three Acts and the one under consideration 

this, I think, is where the Railway Committee made a mistake; and I take my share of the blame for not having emphasized the point by putting these three sections separately instead of in one, as I did in the Railway Committee upon the motion of the hon. member for South Toronto-the difference is that vested rights do exist in regard to this railway company, but this section puts upon them an embargo in regard to their entering the city of Toronto. What is it that 1 call the embargo? It is that the mayor and aider-men of the city of Toronto, and they alone, can decide that this railway may cross upon
the level of any of the highways in the city of Toronto, notwithstanding that the Board of Railway Commissioners might decide that this railway and others should cross upon the level in one place until a viaduct or underground passage should be constructed. Notwithstanding what the Railway Commission might do in regard to any other railway, the mayor and aldermen of the city of Toronto can permit this railway to run across the streets of the city, upon the highway level. This simply means that any dispute between the railway and the city of Toronto will be decided by the mayor and aldermen of that city. On first principles it would strike me that this provision is absolutely wrong. It is classed as a safeguard for the city of Toronto. It certainly is a safeguard for the city of Toronto, but the trouble is that it is much more than a safeguard. It is somewhat the sort of safeguard which would exist if the provincial Government would pass an Act providing that no lawyer should practise in the city of St. Catharines without my consent. That is a safeguard to me; it protects me wonderfully well, and gives me great power, I dare say, in the city of St. Catharines, but is it the sort of safeguard that I should have? Having regard to a provincially chartered railway coming in contact at the outskirts of the city with a railway which is chartered by Dominion legislation, should the city of Toronto decide whether that Dominion railway should or should not cross its streets? Hon. gentlemen should bear in mind the fact that this Bill, like all other Bills that pass the Railway Committee, contains a full protection to the city of Toronto in that its streets cannot be used for any right of way; that railways cannot be built along or upon any highway level. But authority for these railways to cross must be given by the absolute power and plenary jurisdiction of the Dominion Parliament, else we cannot be sure that any railway can build from one part of Canada to another. There must be authority here to decide, in the interests of Canada, upon what terms those railways shall cross highway levels, whether the city concerned be Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg, Calgary, Montreal or any other, because they must cross in order to get from one place to another. The power absolutely to prevent building upon and across highways for right of way purposes is, of course, a very different thing.
I said that this railway had vested rights; let me point out what they are. As I say,

the companies, in the legislation respecting which these provisions were put in, in 1910 and 1911, had done nothing. They have attempted to do nothing; and they tell me they will not attempt to do anything because of the embargo which the city of Toronto has against them whereby they cannot possibly enter that city without the consent of the mayor and aldermen. From these facts hon. gentlemen can draw their own inferences: during the course of three years these three railway companies have attempted to do nothing under their franchises. But the history of this particular Bill is very different. In 1903 the company was incorporated under the name of the Toronto and Hamilton Kailway Company. It was then a line from Toronto to Hamilton and the company were authorized to acquire by purchase, lease or otherwise all the rights, powers, stocks and everything else of certain other railways, including the Toronto and Suburban Kailway Company, not under the ordinary provisions allowing amalgamation, as provided by sections 361, et sequentia, of the Kailway Act, but under special provision to buy up the stock and acquire the franchises of these three railways, including the Toronto Suburban. They went ahead and did so. In 1904 an extension was authorized and in 1906 its name was changed to the Toronto, Niagara and Western Railway, which is its present name. The company were authorized to extend their lines to. other places, which I need not mention, to increase their capital stock to $6,000,000 and to buy up holus bolus, as I have said, and acquire absolutely these other companies.
The railway then) proceeded. They went first to the Minister of Railways and got their route map approved. Then they went to the Board of Railway Commissioners, and as soon as the matter came before the Railway Committee, realizing its importance, I obtained from the board the record of what took place. I should tell the committee that in 1909 we recognized that the ^railway had partially constructed their road and obtained permission to complete within five years. It was admitted by Parliament that they had commenced their construction and had spent more than 15 per cent and all they required was not time to commence but time to complete. We gave an extension of five years from 1909 which will run out this year. The next year they *went to the Railway Commission and applied for permission to cross these twenty-[Mr. Lancaster.}
five different streets in the outskirts of the city of Toronto, where the Canadian Pacific railway and other railways are crossing the streets upon the level of the highway ; and for the convenience of the public, and I suppose for the purpose of getting the ear and sympathy of the commission, they built their track right alongside the Canadian Pacific railway, so that in making their crossing upon the highways at grade level they crossed at exactly the same places as the Canadian Pacific railway had crossed focr some years and is still crossing. The board heard the matter, and I shall read briefly from the proceedings on the 28th of January, 1910. Mr. Johnston, city solicitor of the city of Toronto, said:
If the board thinks that the entrance should be allowed, then it should be on conditions, that they should provide protection if required, or there should be a condition in the order that if the Canadian Pacific Railway tracks are elevated further west, they should go up on the elevation also. I think with that perhaps the city would be satisfied.
Hon. Mr. Mabee: Is that agreeable?
Mr. Royce, counsel for the railway made some remarks upon the point, I suppose not wanting to give in too easily, and then the ordar was pronounced by the chairman in these words:
One order may go in these twenty-five applications. I think one order will cover the whole of them. They may all be consolidated and one order issued in these terms. Authority given to applicants to construct across the streets mentioned, subject to the following conditions:
1.	That if the tracks of the Canadian Pacific railway are at any future time elevated, then the tracks of the applicants shall be likewise elevated along the course of the line where the right of way lie adjacent to each other, upon such terms as the board may direct.
2.	Protection to be provided at such crossings as the chief engineer of the board may require before the road is opened for traffic, and if protection is recommended at crossings that any other road is interested in, then the apportionment of the cost of such protection is reserved.
Hon. gentlemen who are familiar with the Railway Act and the way we have struggled for the last fourteen years in this House I speak only of the time during which I have been a member-will see the practical result of legislation that was passed here in 1999 for the very purpose of causing the least injury to be done to the fewest possible number of people and the greatest good to be done to the general public by allowing railways to enter into every city and town at the least possible inconvenience and risk of life and property. Here the board, in its jurisdiction,

mak-es the sensible order that as the Canadian Pacific railway is now crossing these streets on the level, the Toronto, Niagara and Western railway may rnn beside it, but that when the Canadian Pacific railway is compelled to raise its tracks, the Toronto, Niagara and Western railway must not use the permission granted to them as a ground for claiming that its tracks should not be elevated. We know that the Railway Act gives ample power to the Board of Railway Commissioners to adjust in a fair and equitable way the cost of such elevations. Under the Act, as this railway was' not constructed before 1909, the whole cost of the elevation must fall on the railway itself. That is the amendment of 1909, that a railway not then constructed, when required by the Board of Railway Commissioners to get off the level, must bear the whole cost; whereas vested rights were recognized in railways already constructed by apportioning the cost oi abolishing the level crossing between the grade crossing fund, the municipality and the railway. So Toronto is quite clear from any responsibility for the cost of elevation, and the Board of Railway Commissioners have done what I would expect them to do, they have looked ahead and made the most wise order they could. They have said to the Toronto, Niagara and Western, you may run on this highway as long as the Canadian Pacific Railway is doing so, you are right alongside the Canadian Pacific railway and are creating no additional danger; but the permission that is now granted you is not to be used in future as a ground for claiming a right to continue to run on the level, and you must -elevate your tracks at your own expense, under the statute of 1909, as soon as we require the Canadian Pacific railway tracks to he elevated. Under a former order of the hoard of December 17, 1909, the railway had acquired the right of entry into the city of Toronto, a distance of two and' a half miles. They asserted, and hon. gentlemen from Toronto did not dispute, that they bought every inch of that right of way for two and a half miles under that order. They have paid soone money for right of way to the city of Toronto itself. We are now asked to drastically interfere with them after they have bought that right of way and expended $1,500,000 in buying the right of way into the city of Toronto and in building towards the city -of Guelph. They asserted, and gentlemen from that locality agreed, that they had
acquired the right of way and had graded it almost the whole of the distance from Toronto to Guelph. I was accused by a former Minister of Railways, who many years since went to his last rest, that I was a socialist and radical because I wanted to amend the Railway Act against the vested interests of the railway companies. With what little common sense I have left I must press upon the House that there are vested rights in this case; the railway company have spent one and a quarter millions of dollars in acquiring a right of way, have graded it and prepared it for the rails, -and it does seem to me that, where they are simply asking for an extension of five years in which to complete construction, it would ;be bad legislation to refuse their request. We are incorporating railways for the advantage of Canada. That means that w-e must give them some power to ^xercise properly, and, under proper authority, to proceed into or through -any city or town, from Halifax to . Vancouver, or else our charters are waste paper. If the city of Toronto has sections of this kind put in with regard to a railw-ay which we take care to say by the other clauses of the Bill shall not do a street railway business, any ordinary Dominion railway can be held up-if you wish to use that term- by the city of Toronto, and we should have the Board of Railway Commissioners dethroned as to their power to decide whether, under any circumstances, a railway should go in on the level of the highway. If we do that with Toronto we -shall soon have to do it with Winnipeg, Hamilton, Montreal and every other city. We can not say that the city of Toronto is to have certain powers in regard to railways going into that city and at the same time allow the rest of the cities ot the Dominion to be at the mercy-if you want to use thait word, but I would prefer the word ' justice '-of the Board of Railway Commissioners. With that statement I leave the matter with the House. There are a lot of elaborations that could be made, but I shall not deal with them now, but, as I leave to-morrow, I do not want to go. aw ay without expressing my opinion on this matter for what it is worth. The House, with undue kindness, as I said at the outset, pays too much respect to my work as Chairman of the Railway Committee. Feeling as I do that my physical condition will not allow me to stand on my feet any longer, I will ask the House to be contented with the statement I have made, although I may he able to

answer some questions from my seat. I move to strike out section 7- of the Bill as reprinted.

subtopic: FREDERICTON AND GRAND LAKE COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: This Bill has been entirely recast. It was introduced apparently with an entirely wrong conception of the legislation that was required for the purpose desired. They introduced a Bill asking us to declare a certain provincial railway in New Brunswick to be a work for the general advantage of Canada and then to allow them to amalgamate with another railway under section 361 of the Railway Act. It struck me at once that there must be some reason why we should take away a franchise from the province of New Brunswick, and a most peculiar franchise it is, too, and make Dominion legislation of a private Act of the New Brunswick Legislature, the like of which I never saw, in a great many respects, in any Dominion legislation. I said to the promoters of the Bill: You must either try to make the Bill contain such a power as we would want you to have, or tell me frankly what you want. It seems that all they wanted to do was to make an amalgamation of the lines under section 361 and the following sections of the Railway Act; so I had the Bill recast. On motion of Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blain in the Chair:
[Mr. Kyte.l
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Governor in Council, may under regulations made for the purpose, allow, on the exportation of goods manufactured in Canada and into the manufacture of which pig-iron imported into Canada mixed with pig-iron made in Canada has entered, a drawback, equal to the duty paid, less such deductions therefrom as is provided in such regulations, on all pig-iron imported and used by the manufacturer of such goods in manufacturing the goods exported and other goods, and the drawback may be computed on the total quantity of pig-iron, including pig-iron made as aforesaid, entering into such exported goods.
Would the minister state just what that change is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I explained the reasons for this legislation upon the occasion of the Budget speech, but I have prepared a succinct statement, which is as follows:
The object of this amendment is to enable drawback to be paid on pig-iron used in articles exported, but not exceeding the weight imported, and entered for duty.
When manufacturing the same article for export and for home consumption, it is found impracticable to keep the melts of foreign and domestic iron separate, so that only foreign pig-iron will be used in the article exported, and domestic pig-iron in the like article for home consumption.
The proposed amendment is designed to enable drawback to be paid to the extent of the weight of pig-iron used in the exported article, but not in excess of the quantity imported, and on which duty has been paid.
Section 288 of the Customs Act, which is amended, is as follows:
The Governor in Council may, under regulations made for that purpose, allow on the exportation of goods which have been imported into Canada, and on which a duty of customs has been paid, a drawback equal to the duty so paid with such deductions therefrom as is provided in such regulations.
In the administration of this drawback provision the Customs Department has found itself confronted with a difficulty which really makes it in the interest of Canadian manufacturers who manufacture for export as well as for home consumption to purchase all their pig-iron abroad. I can best illustrate to the House by a concrete example. Let us say that a manufacturer of articles into which pig-iron enters, for home consumption as well as for export, requires 30,000 tons of pig-iron during the year for his entire business, both domestic and export. Let us say that he buys 10,000 tons of pig-iron from the United States and 20,000 tons of domestic pig-iron; and let us assume that he exports
10,000	tons of manufactured product made from pig-iron. He is entitled to a drawback in respect of duties paid upon pig-

iron which has entered into his export product, 10,000 tons. The Customs Department will not allow him a drawback to the amount of the duty paid upon the 10,000 tons of pig-iron which he has imported from the United States because, they say that in the melts (a technical term) in his manufacturing of both his domestic and his foreign products he has combined the .foreign pig-iron and domestic pig-iron in the proportion of one and two. They therefore will allow him only one-thirc^ of the duties which he' has paid upon the
10.000	tons of imported pig-iron by way of drawback; that is to say, they will allow him the duty paid in respect of 3,333 tons only, although he has melted 10,000 tons of American pig-iron and has imported
10.000	tons of his manufactured product.
The manufacturer, therefore, whose case we have under consideration, says; Well, I will buy all my pig-iron, the whole 30,000 tons, in the United States, because then no question can possibly arise as to confusion in the melts; I can buy the 20,000 tons in the United States just as cheaply as T can in Canada, and I can buy the 10,000 tons just as cheaply in the United States as	I can in Canada,	and	therefore I will	buy it	all	there.
He gets a drawback in respect of the duties paid on 10,000 tons, because he has used
10.000	tons of imported pig-iron in the product which he has exported, and no question arises as to the confusion of the metals in the melts. This matter was brought to our attention by the iron and steel companies of Canada. They said-and I think the matter is beyond question-'that by reason of the administration of the drawback provision by the Customs Department in the past, they had been debarred from making sales to manufacturers who use pig-iron in their production; they requested that this change be made whereby a rebate of duty will be given in respect of the entire amount of pig-iron imported from abroad, provided the drawback does not exceed the total amount of duty paid upon the pig-iron imported by a manufacturer and entering into his exported product.

At the present time the drawback regulations are to their disadvantage.
If that is the end the minister wishes to attain, he is not attaining it at all according to the explanation he has given to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why not?

Because my hon.
friend says that to-day the Cana-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
