speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is going there now; I want to make it in his interest not to go.

My hon. friend was dealing with a case in which a Canadian manufacturer was purchasing one-third of his necessities in the United States and two-thirds in Canada. He said that if the manufacturer did that he would only be able to get one-third of the duty lie had paid on 10,000 tons of pig-iron, taking the hypothetical case, whereas, under this new legislation he would be able to get the whole of the duty paid on the 10,000 tons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let us assume that the
manufacturer, as in the hypothetical case, purchased 20,000 tons of pig-iron in Canada and 10,000 in the United States and, as in the hypothetical case, got a drawback of duties in respect of only 3,333 tons; I would ask my hon. friend what he would do next year. Next year, after having bought
10,000	in the United States and 20,000 in Canada and finding that he only got a rebate of duty in respect to 3,333 tons, he would do precisely what the manufacturers are doing to-day; he would find that it paid him better to buy his entire 30,000 tons in the United States and he would do so.

My hon. friend has made clear what he failed to make clear before. My hon. friend takes the ground that, because of the administration of the Cu.s-

toms Department and interpretation of the law as to the proportion of drawback that he is entitled to upon the material that he lias purchased, the manufacturer has been induced to go to the United States in order that there might be no question as to the proportion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Exactly.

speechtext: In Hamilton.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

How does the Government establish the quantity of pig-iron that has been imported and which has entered into the manufacture of different articles which are exported? Does it take the manufacturer's word?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A customs officer visits the establishment of the manufacturer making application for drawback, examines his records, ascertains the amount of his export product, and the amount of raw material imported from various sources that has entered into that product, and makes the necessary calculation.

The more this matter is explained the more mysterious it seems to be. The present law is that the manufacturer who imports iron from the United States gets a drawback of one-third when manufactured and exported, and my hon. friend argues that he is encouraged to buy more iron in the United States. My hon. friend is going to prevent him now from doing that. He is going to take away the inducement to purchase iron in the United States by increasing the bounty from one-third to three-thirds. I do not know how that will work out, but it seems to me that it will work out according to ordinary rules of common sense. I do not object to the legislation of my hon. friend, because, like my hon. friend behind me (Air. Michael Glark), I am in favour of a low tariff, and if this contributes to a lowering of the tariff I shall not object to it. But, unfortunately, it is not the Cana-203
dian consumer who will benefit by it, but the foreign consumer.

Representing a county interested in the pig-iron industry, I have only one objection to this proposed legislation, and it is that it does not go far enough. I think that when you are granting a bonus, or a rebate, on articles manufactured out of Canadian iron and steel, you should also give a bonus of an equal amount for the whole of the pig-iron that is manufactured in Canada and goes into the construction of these implements.
Where will you get the money?

The money is easily got. Any man who understands the question thoroughly can easily see what the minister is trying to do by this legislation. For instance, if a manufacturer imports any number of tons of pig-iron for the manufacture of implements to be exported from Canada, he receives a bounty for exactly that amount. If, on the other hand, he imports only one-third of the iron entering into these implements, he only gets, under-the present regulation, one-third of the rebate. The distinction, is that the man importing the total amount of pig-iron entering into the exported articles receives under the present law 99 per cent of the customs duty paid by him on that imported pig-iron. Thus, the man who imports one-third of his pig-iron and uses two-thirds Canadian pig-iron, according to the legislation now in force, is handicapped as compared with the man who imports the whole quantity. That is ,the present situation, and these are the conditions that we have to meet. If a manufacturer, using 100,000 tons of pig-iron a year, imports that pig-iron from the United States, he gets a rebate on 100,000 tons. If, on the other hand, he uses
100,000	tons for export, of which any amount is purchased from Canadian smelters, he only gets a rebate for the amount on which he has paid duty, or, for the amount that he has purchased from the United States. This resolution, as I understand it, is to allow a man to receive -a rebate to the extent of his exported product. If he exports 10,000 tons of manufactured goods, and if he has imported -from the United States 10,000 tons of pig-iron, he receives a rebate upon the whole of it, notwithstanding the fact that he may have purchased 50,000 tons of Canadian ore in the meantime and used it in the production of



exactly similar implements. My only objection is. that I believe that any one engaged in exactly similar business, using exactly the same material, and manufacturing in all probability similar products, should receive exactly the same treatment as the man who imports from the United States, and that is all that the minister is asking for at the present time.
He is simply asking that the manufacturer who is honest enough, Canadian enough, to buy as much as possible in Canada should receive the same treatment as the manufacturer who imports entirely from the United States.
My hon. friend has forgotten the point that the manufacturer can solve the problem by not importing any of it from the United States. Then he will not require to ask for any drawback.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The price is better.

Then, how is my hon. friend to assist the manufacturer of pig-iron in Canada by giving the full drawback to the person who goes to the United States to purchase pig-iron, when he can get it cheaper there than in Canada, even when handicapped by the fact that he can get only one-third of the duty back? Under the existing legislation, the Internationa] Harvester Company, for example, if they want to encourage Canadian production of pig-iron, can go to my hon. friend's (Mr. Arthurs) constituency and buy it. If they buy it in the United States, they get only one-third of the drawback on the duty. My hon. friend is proposing to give back the whole of the duty. The consequence will be that if the manufacturers can get pig-iron cheaper in the United States, they will buy it in the United States. That is what the Massey-Harris people did. While clamouring for the maintenance of the duty on their products, and asserting that they could not make goods wholesale in Canada without the assistance of the duty, they were purchasing all, their raw material in the United States. If these manufacturers who purchase pig-iron for raw material are patriotic and Canadian enough to encourage Canadian industries, they will purchase all their pig-iron in Canada without asking my hon. friend to give them the whole drawback and thus remove all the impediments which lie between them and purchasing in the United States. When the Hon. Mr. Fielding was Minister of Finance, he had to defend the maintenance of bounties on pig-iron; and I heard many hon.

members from the province of Ontario denounce the then Government for giving bounties to that industry.
Is my hon. friend in favour of bounties now'?

I was in favour of a bounty on pig-iron at the time when my hon. friends were opposing it in this House, and were going up and down the province of Ontario saying that the revenues of Canada wmuld be used by the manufacturers of pig-iron to build private yachts. If my hon. friend will turn to 'Hansard' of 1900 he will find that several hon. members who have seats in the House to-day turned their eyes askance at any gentleman on this side who said anything in regard to a duty on iron, although their statements were not nearly so extreme as what my hon. friends said when the late Government's proposals in respect to iron were brought dowm. My hon. friend (Mr. White), in dealing with this question of the duty on iron, has made a tariff for a few friends of his in the province of Ontario.

abolish the duty on agricultural implements; and my hon. friend says by implication:	Let us raise the duty on raw materials for the manufacture of agricultural implements. He is what may be described as an incidental or casual or occasional Conservative. We on this side call ourselves Liberal-Conservatives. what is back of it all-and have favoured certain others engaged in the steel industry. My hon. friend does not understand-at least, if he does, he desires not to be understood as understanding. My hon. friend says:	If he can buy
cheaper in the United States, why will he not buy all his supply in the United States? I will tell him why. Take the case of a company in Hamilton, let us say, manufacturing both for export and for domestic consumption. They are entitled to a drawback upon duties paid in respect of foreign pig-iron entering into their exported products; they are not entitled to a drawback in respect of duties upon imported pig-iron entering into their products consumed at home, w'ith the exceptions which I have indicated to my hon. friend from Halifax. That company can buy cheaper in the United States if they are getting the drawback, but not if they have to pay the duty without receiving a drawback. In that situation, the question arises- whether it will pay them to import all their pig-iron by reason of the fact that they get a drawback upon that part of it, which they export. Let us assume that with the drawback allowed they can buy in the United States more cheaply than in Hamilton. It does not follow that they can buy all their pig-iron more cheaply than in Hamilton; if they could, of course they would not buy in Hamilton. Even if the manufactures can

buy some of their pig-iron as- cheaply in Canada as they can buy it in the United States, after payment of the freight and duty upon it, under the regulations that now exist it would pay them to buy all their pig-ron in the United States, both for home and for foreign trade. Under the- amendment which I am introducing to the Customs Act they will receive a drawback in respect of the pig-iron which they import from the United States, provided they export an amount of manufactured iron equivalent to the amount imported.

Does the hon. minister say that they can buy pig-iron in Canada more cheaply in Canada than they can buy in the United States and pay the duty?
Mr. WHITE. Not necessarily. There is usually a parity of price. Suppose the agricultural implement manufacturer in Hamilton could buy in Pittsburg at a price which, freight and duty paid, would lay the pig-iron down in Hamilton at $15 a ton. In that case, the Hamilton price would be about $15 a ton. It might be that they would lower the price to get the business. As a general thing, they cut a little below the price of the American product, plus the freight and duty, to get the market.

As the minister is changing the law with regard to drawback, I think he should change it so as to give no drawback. If he intends that the Canadian consumer shall use pig-iron produced in Canada, the obvious way is to refuse to give any drawback, and give no advantage on the exported article either. Suppose that this change is some advantage to the Canadian manufacturer of pig-iron, it is no advantage to the Canadian consumer. The only persons who get advantage, according to the minister, is the manufacturer who imports from abroad and the outside consumer of the manufactured article.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This relates only to export products.

Exactly so. The minister tells us that this change is designed to benefit the iron and steel manufacturers of Canada. But if that is his intention, I say he should give no drawback at all. If it is a benefit to the iron and steel producers that the user of the material should not be allowed a drawback on goods sold for home consumption, it would be a double benefit if no drawback were allowed in any case. Doesv the minister follow mg?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I follow you, but I do not agree with you.

The minister agrees with
me that it would be more to the advantage of the Canadian manufacturers of iron and steel if no drawback were allowed. If the object is to benefit the producer of iron and steel, why not then do away with the drawback altogether? When this resolution was first brought down, I said in my remarks on the Budget that the change would be injurious to the manufacturer of iron. If the minister is right in his contention, I can see where there is some advantage. But I go further and say that this change -does not benefit the Canadian consumer, so I think the minister has made a- mistake in not -doing away with drawbacks altogether, thus making the manufacturers buy pig-iron altogether from the producers of iron in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend surely is
not -serious, or, if serious, he has not considered the question. His suggestion is that there should be no drawback of -duties paid in respect of raw materials entering into products of Canadian manufacturers exported from Canada. Let me point out to what that would lead. The Canadian manufacturer, of course, in respect of his -export business, is in competition with the manufacturers of the world. Now, let me ask my hon. friend, who is a good business man, to -suppose for a moment that he is a manufacturer of -agricultural implements which he is selling in the markets of the world in competition with similar m-anu-facturors of the United States. And suppose he received no drawback on pig-iron bought in the United -States. The agricultural implement maker in the United -States would have his pig-iron at about $2.25 or $2.50 a ton cheaper than my hon. friend would have his pig-iron if he were forced to buy in Canada. The result would toe that because the cost of manufacture is so much less to the American manufacturer, my hon. friend could not compete in the markets of the world with the manufacturer of the United States, and he would have no export business at all. The provision as to drawback does not relate only to iron and steel;- it relates to all raw material imported toy Canadian manufacturers in respect of their export business, and the reason is that either they must be placed on an equality

with foreign manufacturers, who get their raw material cheaper, or they cannot compete. Surely that must be perfectly plain to my hon. friend. If they are not put on that same footing, the pig-iron manufacturer of Canada, who occasionally-but seldom, I admit-can sell his products to the manufacturer, even in respect of his export business, would be in a worse position to manufacture for export; in fact he would not be able t-o carry on business successfully at all.
What about manufactured articles exported to Great Britain? Does the Canadian manufacturer get his drawback there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Supposing the Canadian
manufacturer is competing with the British manufacturer in the market of free trade Great Britain. The British manufacturer gets his raw material free; the Canadian manufacturer has to pay for whatever raw material he imports to Canada a price determined to a certain extent iby the duty payable upon it. The Canadian manufacturer, therefore, could not compete with the British manufacturer at all. It is absolutely necessary that the Canadian manufacturer should have a drawback in respect of raw material if he wishes to be placed upon an equal footing with the foreign competitor.

When the minister made his statement to the House he said that this was to be done for the advantage of the steel manufacturers of this country. I want to draw the minister out and show that he is also benefiting the manufacturers of agricultural implements and of all other things that are manufactured from iron. If he had told the House that when he was making his statement he would have told the whole truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Every manufacturer in
Canada to-day gets a drawback in respect of the raw material that he imports or uses in his export business, so that there is absolutely no charge in that regard. The Massey-Harris Company and the International Harvester Company buy practically all their pig-iron in the United States, for the reasons which I have given, and what I desire to do in this legislation is to enable them to buy some of their pig-iron in Canada, and to prevent the pig-iron manufacturers of Canada from losing business by reason of the regulation of the Customs Department, which at present allows to manufacturers in respect of their
export products a drawback upon commodities to the percentage that the imported American pig-iron bears to the amount of the American and the Canadian pig-iron used in their product, both for domestic and foreign export trade.
The minister does not suppose they are going to buy it in Canada if they can get it cheaper in the United. States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. .
They can get it cheaper in the United States with the duty as it is now.
Does my hon. friend think this regulation will help the export trade to the United States of manufactured iron goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
It is not meant to do that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not expect that that will be its effect.
I would like to *understand exactly the attitude of the minister in the matter. He seems to be in favour of the export of these manufactured iron goods into the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend asks
whether I am in favour of manufacture in Canada for export to the United States, I say, of course.

I am surprised, because when I want some beneficial arrangement on behalf of the western wheat growers I get sermons the length of the minister's arm preached to me about the advantages of the home market. Why should not the hon. minister and his friends be content with-the home -market? Is not the sauce for the-western goose good enough for the Ontario-gander?

The hon. minister
complains that I did not make the few remarks which I did at some other time. I want to tell my hon. friend that I will trouble the House whenever it suits me to do so, not when it may happen to please my hon. friend. I said-and I repeat it- that in dealing with this iron and steel schedule during the present session of Parliament, the minister has had in view, with the single exception of the wire rod industry in Nova Scotia, solely the interests of some of his friends in the province of Ontario. My hon. friend did not venture to

question that statement; he did not meet that proposition and cannot meet it, because it is absolutely correct. This is not his time, he says, for a general revision of the tariff. My hon. friend knows that if he did not lead certain iron and steel people in this country after 1911 to believe that the alleged anomalies of the tariff with regard to iron and steel, would be removed at an early day, some of his colleagues did. My hon. friend knows that the iron and steel people in this country, particularly in Nova Scotia, were led to believe by some of his colleagues that the bounty which expired in 1911 with regard to pig-iron and certain other products would be renewed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend complaining that they were not renewed!

I am discussing my hon. friend's position as Minister of Finance and his relation to the iron and steel people; I will discuss my own attitude when it suits me to do so. My hon. friend need not to be alarmed about my attitude in this matter; when the responsibility is placed upon hon. gentlemen on this side they will give to Canada, in regard not only to iron and steel but to other items as well, such a reasonable tariff that Canada will prosper as she did when the Liberals were in power. They will not, as the hon. gentlemen have done, dilly-dally with the question for nearly three years, creating business uncertainty throughout the land, a lack of public confidence here and abroad, and a condition in Canada where in almost every industrial centre manufacturing establishments are closed and workingmen are walking the streets. It is the attitude of my hon. friend and the performances of his party that have to be considered. I repeat that in 1911 the iron and steel people of this country were led to believe that the bounties on iron and steel, which expired in that year, would be renewed.
Who did that?

My hon. friend knows who did it; my hon. friend knows that some of his colleagues made representations to men connected with the iron and steel industry. My hon. friends know what happened last year and the year before. They know the expectations that were raised in regard to this question and how they proved to be illusory. My hon. friend had not the nerve to tackle this question, and now he says: Oh, this is not the time for a general revision of the tariff; wait until two or three years have passed, and

we have dealt with this matter; then come around and criticise us when we have dealt with the whole thing. I say to my hon. , friend now that in so far as he has dealt with the iron and steel tariff he has dealt with it on local lines, dealt with it in such a manner that the men who expected a great deal from him had a right to be disappointed and are disappointed.

I do not wish
to interrupt the dispute between the hon. members from Ontario and Nova Scotia, but I am anxious to expedite the noncontentious business in order to get to the really contentious business of the session, and if possible reach an end. I only intervened to ask one of these hon. gentlemen who are conducting this interesting dispute to explain to me, as a resident of one of the other seven provinces of Canada, how the policy which they both seem to support, if it is applied only to the locality in which they are particularly interested, ever came to have or can in any way deserve the term 'national ' as applied to it. I do not care which hon. gentleman gives me the explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I should
say: after you my dear Alphonse, because my hon. friend is so much more eloquent than I am. I do not want to mar the humour of my hon. friend's remarks by any answer, and I am sure he will overlook the fact that an answer is not given. With regard to what the hon. member for Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) has said, he may know of some promises having been given with respect to bounties. Personally I know of none.
I said they were led to believe.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know by whom
they were led to believe. As far as I know, any promises that this party have given have been lived up to.
All?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am quite satisfied that no tariff promises were made on the eve of any election; at least, on the occasion of the election of 1911; I am not so sure about the promises of 1896. My hon. friend seems to be disappointed at something I have refrained from doing, and yet he does not put fonvard what that something is. I have a very great respect for my hon. friend and for his ability, and any time he will rise in the House and tell me precisely what he has to suggest in the way of increased

duties I will say to him What I do to every member of the House or the public who bring matters of that kind to iny attention: I shall be glad to give it careful and serious consideration. The complaint I have against my hon. friend is that while he does not agree with what I have done he does not make any suggestions which indicate his own views. If at any time he will tell me what he complains about I shall be glad to meet that complaint as far as I am able. He has put forward no representations; he has not asked for any increased duties. If he did he would find himself in conflict with distinguished gentlemen whom I see on the other side of the House, his friends and colleagues. Under these circumstances I must continue to do what I have done: administer the tariff according to my own best judgment-in view of the facts before me. I repeat, if my hon. friend has any specific complaint to make that we have not raised duties in respect of the products of any particular industry, local or otherwise, in which he is particularly interested, if he can tell me in specific language what he is complaining about, I shall be glad to take any statement and any representations he may make under my careful consideration.
That is very good of my hon. friend, hut he has not met my point.

Together- with the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) I am particularly interested in the manufacture of iron and steel, especially pig-iron, which is under discussion this afternoon. I would say to the minister that the producers of pig-iron in Canada are quite capable of supplying the legitimate demands of the manufacturers of Canada. I do not pretend to be an expert on questions of duty as applied to the subject matter before the committee, but, generally, I make the statement that I believe the large producers in Canada are to-day capable of producing pig-iron sufficient to supply the Canadian market, and if we are capable of supplying the market we are equally capable of supplying it with a first-class article. I speak particularly for the Dominion Steel Company at Sydney, and the Nova Scotia Iron and Steel Company, oparating in the county which I have the honour to represent. Taking for granted that we have a supply in Canada of a firstclass article suflicient to meet the demand, the question is why would not that article be purchased if it be purchasable at about the price at which the same article can be purchased from the United States? The theory of the National Policy of which we heard so much, with which I have grown up and of which I profess to know something, was that protection would enable us to manufacture our own products for our own use, and that local competition would give our people the manufactured article at a price not any higher than that of the foreign market. If that theory were carried out, then, of course, protection would have its uses. But we had to contend with such things as combines, when there was no local legitimate competition. When combines arose this local competition which was promised to us was destroyed and so we have not got the National Policy in this particular sense, and some other remedy should be applied. I wish to point out to the minister that I cannot see the difference between a drawback and free admission, as far as the article upon which the drawback is given Is concerned. I think it is as broad as it is long. If a man lias to go into the United States or any other foreign country and import a thousand tons of p'g-iron. paying duty of $2.50 a ton, knowing that under certain conditions he will get that money back, it is tantamount to free trade. If protection is worth anything at all, and of course so far as my own industries are concerned and because I understand those industries well, I am in favour of protection of the industry of the country from which I come-
Hear, hear.

I am always pleased
io get a cheer from my hon. friends opposite. I cannot understand why I get a cheer o,n this occasion, because I have spoken in this House a great many times in the last ten or twelve yeans and when iron and steel and coal were under discussion I was always a tried and true protectionist. There is no reason why I should he particularly congratulated upon my stand to-day, it is an old stand and until conditions are changed it is the position to which I propose to adhere. The fault I have to find with the policy of the Minister of Finance is that he gives this drawback at all. If protection is good, if it is given far the purpose of encouraging the production of pig-iron in

Canada, why give us the will o' the wisp of giving us protection and taking it away the moment it becomes of any service to us? J think the protection should stand there for the 'Canadian pig-iron producer, particularly when we produce a first class article and lay it down for the same price that pig-iron can be got elsewhere. In this way we would encourage the production of manufactured goods in Canada and encourage our own manufacturers to supply the local market. If the local producer's horizon is widened, if the places where he can sell in the West and elsewhere become more numerous, he is encouraged to go more fully into the manufacture of his article, which in turn encourages the parties who are producing the raw material. I do not profess to understand the nice mechanism of the resolution before the House. I find it almost as difficult to understand as Mr. Hennessy found Mr. Dooley's explanation of Kruger's franchise. I do not for a moment say that my hon. friend is of the same calibre or ingenuity as Kruger, but I find this resolution extremely difficult to follow. One thing, however, I do understand; I think it is for the purpose of making it easier for the Canadian manufacturer to get his raw material from the United States, and while he professes to be paying the duty, he is getting it back. Another thing, it encourages the home manufacturer to produce articles to be sent out of the country instead of to be sold in Canada, where they would have the effect of making things cheaper for our own people. In conclusion, my idea is that the $2.50, which we are told is a protection to the pigdron producer, should mean something and stay there as a permanent protection.	'
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. WHITE thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 171, to amend the Customs Act.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

On motion of Hon. L. P. PELLETIER (Postmaster General), the House went into Committee on Bill No. 146, to amend the Civil Service Act, Mr. Blain in the Chair.

On section 1-salaries increased from $500 to $600;. annual increase from $50 to $100.

This Bill was explained when we were in Committee on the resolution. This Bill affects the clerks in city post offices, the offices of the post office inspectors, the offices of the superintendents of the railway mail service and the money order exchange offices. It raises the initial salary from $500 to $600, and it raises the annual increase from $50 to $100. When the resolution was in Committee it had the concurrence of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux).

How many employees
will this affect, and how much money does it amount to in the aggregate?

I have sent for the
deputy minister, who has that information for me.

I understand that in
the West, when a man's salary reached a certain stage, his living allowance dropped; but I also understand that the Government has amended that so that a man's living allowance never recedes. Is that cUne by this Bill?
No; what we have arranged has been done by Order in Council.
I notice that the railway mail clerks are not included in this Bill?
No, they come under another Bill.
What class of officials does this affect?

The clerks in city
post offices, the offices of the post office inspectors, the offices of the superintendents of the railway mail service, and the money order exchange offices; in fact, it covers every clerk in the outside service except the railway mail clerks, who will be provided for in a Bill which comes after this.

Is there not another
class not included in city post offices or the offices of post office inspectors? For instance, there are certain post offices that are created city offices, although they may not be in cities. Then, there is another class of post office which does not come under that heading.
I

Like Brantford or
Brockville, for instance; that is what we call a semi-staff office.

It will not affect the
standing of those clerks?

The semi-staff offices
are on the same footing, as far as the payment of the clerks is concerned, as the city post offices.
By whom are the clerks engaged?

They are engaged by
the department.

Is the staff at Renfrew
engaged by the department or by the postmaster?

That is a revenue
office.

Will this Bill have the
effect of saying to the postmaster there: You must pay a certain salary to your staff?
These people in Renfrew will not be affected by this Bill, because the Renfrew office is a revenue office. Brockville is a semi-3taff office and Toronto a city office.
There is nothing in this Bill for the aid of employees at Renfrew or Arnprior?

No, these people are
employed by the postmaster himself, and he pays them out of his revenue.
Is it the intention of the minister to create Medicine Hat and Lethbridge city post offices? At present they do not rank as such.

These are semi-staff
offices.

Is it the intention of
the department to place them in the rank of city post offices?
The qmestion is under consideration.
Will there be anything in any Bill that will affect the staff in revenue offices?
Not in this Bill.

I know it is not in this Bill; but is it in the mind of the Postmaster General? Is he thinking of doing something of that kind? A clerk may do just as much
work in a post office in a town the size of Renfrew or Arnprior as another clerk will do in an office that is on a different status. There are certain post offices where the salaries are fixed and the appointments are made by the department. In post offices in towns like Renfrew or Arnprior the postmaster gets a certain salary from the revenue and engages his own staff. There seems to be somewhat of an anomaly. In one post office a clerk may be working for $400 a year; whereas in a post office in a neighbouring town, where possibly an equal amount of business is done, a clerk may be getting $600 a year from the department. I think there should be some way in. which the salaries of the staff can he regulated, even though the revenues alter.

The whole difference
is this, that in the revenue offices we do not control the salaries at all; the employees are not our employees; they are engaged and paid by the post-master. We have, therefore, nothing to say as to wThat their salaries shall be. If a post office were not kept properly, if the postmaster had not the necessary number of employees, we would hear complaints about it and probably would have to interfere; but s-o long as we hear no complaints, we take it for granted that the office is properly equipped and run to the satisfaction of the public, and we have nothing to say about the salaries which the postmaster pays to his employees.

Does the department
never intimate to the postmaster whom he ought to employ?
No.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-minimum salaries:

What is the length of
the probationary period?
Six months.
Will these salaries date from the 1st day of April, or is that merely the qualification of the employment?
The salaries will date from the first day of the financial year.

Section agreed to.	*
On section 3-(temporary clerks:
What is that?
It is the same thing -to put the initial salary at $600 instead of $500.
Section agreed to.

Bill reported.
On the motion of Mr. Pelletier for the third reading of the Bill:

Has my !hon. friend
not considered the advisability of bringing all these outside clerks under the Civil Service Commission?
That will not come under this Bill.
But has not the Government considered, as a matter of policy, the bringing of the outside civil servants in those large offices under the Civil Service Commission?
We cannot do anything for the Post Office Department unless we do it for all the departments.
What is to be the policy of the Government in the future?
That is under consideration for the moment.

We have discussed this question on several occasions, and I have always understood that the day is not far distant when the Government may bring those officers under the Civil Service Commission. It would be in the best interest of the service and in the interest of the Government to do so.

speechtext: It might not be practicable to bring them all under the Civil Service Commission in the near future, but some of them might be brought. Probably that matter will be discussed in connection with the Civil Service Bill.

On motion of Hon. L. P. PELLETIER (Postmaster General) the House went into Committee on Bill No. 147, to amend the Post Office Act, Mr. Blain in the Chair.
On section 1-Revised Statutes, c. 66, amended:
This is an amendment to the Revised Statutes of 1906. Will the Postmaster General tell us briefly what changes are to be effected?

The main object of the first change, that is, in paragraph (e), is to make it quite clear that the right of looking at newspapers, parcels and so on, is absolutely confined to those, and that there is no right to open letters. The sec-

tion, as it .stands at present, as my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) knows, leaves the question open as to whether or not it is right to open letters. I want to make it quite clear that that right does not exist.
We are amending the clause, so that there is no possibility of doubt, by inserting the words ' except in the case of letters.' So we keep the right to open all other mailable matter, to carry out the purpose and intention of the Act, but making it quite clear that there is no right whatever to open letters. There are other matters of detail, but this is the main object of this clause.
Is the regulation making it compulsory to register letters containing money still in force?

There is no obligation at all upon anybody to register letters. But we have complaints from a great many people that they had sent money through the mail in letters not registered, and that their money has been stolen. My hon. friend knows that it is impossible to follow' letters which aie not registered, and people are subject to loss of money on a great many occasions in this way. At the same time, we have found that it is a great temptation for clerks in some of the offices to examine unregistered letters and some of these clerks are very apt to guess that there might be money in these letters. We have found that it was therefore a suitable thing to try and protect the public, and also save these clerks from temptation by asking the people to have their letters registered if there is money in them. But we do not exact that. We have a regulation under which we impress upon the public that they should not send money in letters, containing over a dollar, without taking the precaution of registering them. But it is not compulsory.

I suppose this amendment is made in connection with the regulations concerning the parcel post. The department is aware that people are sending all sorts of things through the new channel, and there must he some regulation, in order to prevent, for instance, chemicals and things of that kind being sent through the mails. I do not know whether the Postmaster General has seen the item in the Montreal paper that white rats were sent by mail, and that the department decided that the white rats ought to pass. I believe that the regulation, provided that letters are not inter-

fered with, is desirable. The Postmaster General should have the authority to describe what kind of material should be handled. As regards the Sending of coins in letters, I cannot agree with the criticism that has been made against the regulation of the department a few days ago. I remember when I was Postmaster General, some institutions, especially religious institutions, were being constantly robbed of small sums that were sent to them in letters. It is very easy to detect whether an envelope contains a coin, and I know of one or two institutions in Ottawa-and the Postmaster General knows, too-whose money some clerks had been tempted into taking for months and years. Sometimes the money is lost through the breaking of the envelopes, and complaints are made to the post office. It is better, under the circumstances, that the department should give the public notice that it is taking great risk in sending money in coins in that matter. And the mode of registration is so easy, and after all so cheap, that the public should register their letters when sending money through the mails.

I should be against
any compulsory order to people to register their mail. I had correspondence with people in Cape Breton on this subject. They interpreted this as being compulsory, and I may tell tha Postmaster General that some country postmasters have assumed it to be compulsory.	[DOT]

My hon. friend may
tell people who ask him for information on the subject that it is not compulsory. The regulation is merely an effort to persuade the people of what they should do, but there is no sanction to it except that we hope to bring the people to the right point of view in this matter, as so well expressed by the hon. member for Eouville (Mr. Lemieux) a moment ago.

Another point I wish
to discuss with my hon. friend. Of course, the secrecy of correspondence is kept; that is a privilege which the public enjoy, high or low. At the same time, there is a regulation in the Post Office Department, which permits the Postmaster General to open letters In the case of what is called fraud order. The section under discussion would not affect that right on the part of the Postmaster General. The Postmaster General was away the other day-he was in Quebec I believe-when my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) brought to the notice of the Minister of Finance the
case of some lotteries which were making use of the mails in order to extract as much money as possible from the gullible people. He cited instances in his own county, in which large sums of money had been taken from the people by this improper use of the mails. My hon. friend (Mr. Pelletier) can refer to the report of that debate, and he will see that in one case at least the department some years ago took drastic measures to prevent a lottery from using the mails. I think the hon. Postmaster General will do well to look into it and prevent the improper use of the mail by lotteries.

I have had the Deputy Postmaster General take a note of the fact referred to. He will look into it. We are doing this every week or two-stopping fraudulent practices by mail. We will take special care to refer to the matter of which the hon. gentleman has spoken.

I desire to call the attention of the Postmaster General to a matter which may not have been mentioned in the House before. During past years the gentlemen who represent the people in this House have had the privilege while in the city of Ottawa of franking parcels sent through the mail. The hon. minister has recently adopted a system of parcel post, upon which I shall not make any comment at this moment, but why that should have been made the occasion of taking away the privilege which the representatives of the people formerly enjoyed is something which I do not understand. If there is any reason why the privilege of the franking of parcels should be taken away from members of the House, that reason existed, of course, before the parcel post system came into operation. There are many occasions when it is to the advantage of the constituents whom we represent that we should have that privilege. Very often we visit the Experimental Farm and are favoured with a sample of wheat or oats which we wish to send to our constituents, and now we have to pay postage upon any parcel containing such samples. I raise the question not as asking a favour; I suppose that any hon. gentleman can put his hand in his pocket and pay postage, but it is a matter of public policy, and, so far I have not learned any reason why we should not have the same privileges that we formerly enjoyed.

My hon. friend says
that members of the House should not be deprived of the privileges that they had

before. The Post Office Department has deprived itself of the very privilege to which my hon. friend refers. When the parcel post system was put into operation on February 10 last, we decided to make no exemption from the payment of postage; the Prime Minister of Canada and the Postmaster General have to pay postage on all parcels sent through the mails. Our experience shows that this is the best policy. The franking privilege has not been taken away from members of Parliament; they may continue to frank literature sent by book post as well as anything in the shape or form of a letter.
If anything is mailed in an envelope the frankifig privilege may be used?
Yes.

Many members who have clerical staffs in their home towns have been in the habit of' sending home envelopes to be addressed by their stenographers or .secretaries, who have the voters3 lists .and other information at hand; and the envelopes are returned to Ottawa when the work is completed. Under present conditions members have to send these envelopes home by express or by parcel post. I think the taking away of the franking privilege in regard to parcel post is not right. A great deal of the work we do while in this city we do because we are members; a great deal of the expense we incur is incurred because we are the people's representatives. I do not think the minister intended to be small, but I think it was a small piece of business to take this privilege away from members. The hon. Postmaster General .says that the Post Office Department has deprived itself of the privilege. To say the least, that is a shallow argument, for my hon. friend knows that with the department it is a mere matter of book-keeping. The department buys the stamps and gets the money that is paid for them; of course, no money is paid out, so that it is just the same as franking. The amount is credited to revenue, of course, and this helps to increase the revenue and to bolster up a surplus, although in these hard times . there should not be any surplus.
Why should members of Parliament be asked to pay postage upon parcels addressed to them which do not carry any or sufficient postage stamps?

That is a regulation that applies to everybody. The postmaster should not receive a parcel unless the proper amount of postage is paid and the necessary stamps are affixed thereon. The same thing applies to letters. When a letter arrives at the point of destination, if the necessary stamps have not been put on it, the man who receives it has to pay-double the amount of the postage due.

It appears that postmasters in the country receive parcels which are addressed to members of Parliament and are not properly franked. When' the members receive these parcels, they are asked sometimes to pay as much as forty cents for postage due. I think this is an injustice. If the postmasters in the country have not received instructions to refuse all parcels addressed to members of Parliament which do not bear the proper frank, we should not be asked to pay the cost of transporting them. I was asked to pay forty cents, I think it was, on a parcel. I did not know where it came from, and I refused to pay the amount. In this ease it turned out to be a model sent to me for the patent office. A month later the gentlemen who sent me the model, discovering that it had been lost, came to me and explained the whole matter. Certainly the postmaster should not have received the parcel, and I think that in such cases we should not be asked to pay postage.

My deputy informs
me that the postmasters have been duly informed of their duty in this respect. Probably some of them overlooked the instructions. We will see that this is remedied.

It has not been explained to me why the franking privilege with regard to parcel post has been taken away from members. As an individual member of Parliament I do not ask for the privilege of the free use of parcel post, but I have been a member of this House foT fifteen years, and certain small parcels are frequently sent me- by constituents. Why should the privilege be withdrawn because of the establishment of parcel post? If the motive is economy, I do not think the Post Office Department is as economical in other directions. If the principle is wrong, withdraw the franking -privilege from members; but surely no good reasons have been shown why the privilege heretofore accorded should be withdrawn at this time.

I do not object to this discussion, because it is only fair that

people should have a chance to ventilate that grievance,, if it is one, on the floor of this House; but I may say that this subject does not come within the scope of this Bill. I shall look further into it, and when the question comes up on the Estimates I shall be glad to say more to my hon. friends.

Perhaps the minister will note that in subsection (c) he is given power to establish rates of postage on all mailable matter not being letters. That is with respect to a regulation and he has made the application. Nowhere under the law has the privilege been withdrawn. If the hon. member can point out to me where there has been a change in the law I shall stand corrected; but the mere establishment of the parcel post system in no way changes the law as respects the franking privilege enjoyed by members of Parliament since 1867.

I would ask if there
has really been any departure' from the principle which was always recognized in this House? Has there been any taking away from the members of any privilege? I have always understood that when the House was in session a member of Parliament had a right to frank letters, books and certain parcels from this House; but I have always understood that the general public had the same privilege of sending letters, parcels, books, etc., to any member of this House. In what respect has the principle heen violated? We enjoy as members exactly the same privileges as the general public enjoy. Frequently I have had reference made to the franking privilege of members. My answer has been: You possess the same privilege I possess; while the House is in session you have the right to send any mailable matter to any member of Parliament; or to any department of Government at any time free. While the House is in session we have the privilege of sending, mail free so that we are on exactly the same footing with the general public. If we had the right of franking parcels from this House, which right was not enjoyed by the general public, it would be a departure from the principle which has always hitherto obtained.

The principle which the hon. member lays down is now as it always ha3 been, namely that the member and the constituents in the country have the same right. But to-day neither has the same right that was enjoyed before a certain day in February when the minister changed the whole system, as I stated, in an ultra
vires fashion. I have had constituents send me samples of their soil, from different points in my very large riding, to submit to the proper department and ascertain the properties of the soil%nd the way in which it should be treated. I have had men send me ore. The public have had the privilege of sending such things, but they have not that privilege any longer; they must now pay postage to swell the revenue of the Post Office Department. The only justification for taking away that privilege is penury, economy; and as long as the inspector of the Post Office Department at Sherbrooke can go gallivanting around the country in a $4,500 Packard car, I do not think that they need to economize as much as the minister says in reference to parcel post. I think the minister should reconsider this and not economize on this little matter, but restore to us, as the peoples' representatives, the privileges of the parcel post. I would like to know what the hon. member for Selkirk thinks of this. He is close to the Cabinet, not in it, but I hope he soon will be.

I have read on several occasions in the press a rumour that the Canadian rate of postage on newspapers was to be increased. I do not suppose this will be carried out. The rate is one-quarter of a cent per pound now. Not very long ago I learned that there were loud complaints against newspapers abusing that privilege. Papers were published at one cent per number which did not contain the average number of pages of editorial matter but which contained more or less advertising and stories. The Postmaster General has the right according to the Post Office Act, to decide what is a newspaper and what is not a newspaper, and I daresay he will have to exercise his judgment, because there are these loud complaints from newspapers that their rivals in the business are selling newspapers in Montreal, for instance, at one cent a copy, the annual subscription being $3.00, while the same newspapers, very heavy, containing any amount of advertising and stories, are sold all over the Maritime provinces, after they have passed a certain zone, at only $1 a year. It seems unfair to the regular newspapers that they should have to face such competition. AA7hilst I am speaking about newspapers, is the minister at present discussing with the British Postmaster General the question of renewing the post office arrangement which I made

in 1907 with the then British Postmaster General, Right Hon. Sydney Buxton, by which the rate of postage on British magazines and newspapers was reduced from four pence a pound to one penny a pound, or from eight cents to two cents a pound in our currency? The arrangement was made because at that time many British organizations and leagues were clamouring for a more widespread circulation of British and imperial news with the dominions. At that time British newspapers and magazines had a very limited circulation in the dominions because they were handicapped by the heavy postage, and as a result heTe in Canada we were flooded with American newspapers and magazines. The question of increasing the circulation of British publications in Canada came up at that time, notably in the Canadian Senate under the lead of the late Sir George Drummond. I decided to take up the matter with the British ..Postmaster General, and we came to an agreement whereby British magazines and newspapers should pay two cents a pound instead of eight cents from the British post office to Liverpool, the transit charge from Liverpool being borne by the Canadian post office. The result has been very gratifying indeed. I remember standing one day on the wharf at Liverpool a few months after that agreement came into force, and I asked the captain of the steamer to give me an idea of the increase that had taken place in the number of British magazines and newspapers coming to Canada. I was simply amazed to see the number of baskets and bags filled with newspapers and magazines as a result of that agreement. The figures have since been published, and are very gratifying indeed. In 1906, the year before that agreement came into force, the weight of British publications sent to Canada was comparatively infinitesimal, but the reduction in postage which took place in 1907 has borne fruit as follows:	In
1908 the weight of British publications coming to Canada was 2,328,000 pounds; in 1909, 2,910,000 pounds; in 1910,	3,836,000
pounds; in 1911, 4,747,000 pounds; in 1912,
5,785,000	pounds. Fancy what this means to this country where we have so many immigrants from the British Isles, especially in the West. By this arrangement, the newly-arrived immigrant can continue to receive papers from home at a very cheap rate; and besides that, not only our newspapers but our clubs, our associations, and our public men can afford to receive the news from the right centre. It was stated 
on many occasions when we were discussing in this House the reduction of the cable rates that nearly all our papers both in the West and the East received tainted news from American sources. Personally, I do not believe that the news service is
9 p.m. tainted, but yet if it comes via New York the news lias first been addressed to New York papers, or perhaps to Chicago, or S-an Francisco, through American agencies and for American consumption, and then it is served afterwards to the Canadian public. The difference in the news may not be great, but when you compare it with the British dailies that arrive a week or two afterwards you find quite a difference; and that is why, on both sides of the House, we have been endeavouring for the last few years to get better postal regulations and cheaper telegraphic communication between the mother country and Canada. I was reading the other day a letter in the London Times of Monday, 6th April, signed by Evelyn Wrench. I dare say Evelyn is a feminine name but there are so many strange names in English that I am not quite sure.
Mr. GEORGE E. FOSTER: It is not a feminine name in that ease.
Yes.

-if there are difficulties in coming to a satisfactory arrangement with the British post office, he will find means of continuing the service. I am not more British than the King, but still I am British enough to be willing to go at. least half way in this matter. When we took up this question in 1907 we found that in the mining camps at jCobakt and elsewhere our people were provided with very cheap magazines and with questionable newspapers. We thought that by facilitating the circulation of British newspapers and magazines we might perhaps render a real service to the Imperial cause in Canada. The arrangement has proven very successful indeed according to the figures I have quoted to the House and I sincerely hope that my hon. friend will do his best to induce the British authorities to renew it. It would be a great pity indeed if the Postmaster General in England were to re-enact the old prohibitive postal Tate as regards newspapers and magazines mailed to Canada. Quite a trade has been established in Canada. As this correspondent, Mr. Wrench, states in every little village, in every township in the West, you find "the board at the railway station with the announcement that the British mail has arrived, or will arrive at a certain date and there also you will find for sale, quite a collection of British magazines and newspapers. I think that my hon. friend should strain a point in order to meet the views of the British postmaster and see that there is a renewal of the arrangement.

The matter of which
my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has spoken is a very important one. I would not like to go into all the details at the present moment because the whole question is the subject matter of negotiations between the British and Canadian post office departments. I am heartily in sympathy with almost everything that my hon. friend has said on this subject, but I think that, whilst he has shown that he is well posted on nearly all the details, there is one aspect about it upon which he is mis-

taken. He says that the effort of the department should be to get the British Postmaster General to renew the agreement. It would be rather an easy matter indeed to do that. That is what he is asking for but I think that my.hon. friend will remember that what the Post Office Department did under his direction and guidance in this respect was not absolutely on the lines which he has indicated. The general outline of it is all right as expressed by my hon. friend but there are some details that are of importance. It is absolutely true, as my hon. friend has said, that before that change was adopted by the Canadian post office in 1907, American literature in the shape of magazines was coming into this country in large volume. We had few British magazines. My hon. friend, when he was Postmaster General, saw fit to enter into an arrangement- with the British post office by which, for a certain number of years, it was provided that British magazines should come into this country on most favoured terms. This arrangement was for a period of four years. It was entered into in 1907. It has been continued during the four years in question and after its expiration it was renewed for a further period of one year. After I came into office I thought that the policy adopted by my predecessor was a good one in many respects and I renewed the arrangement for a year. But when the arrangement was renewed the British post office was informed that when the year upon which we were then entering had expired probably some other arrangement would have to be made.
It is important for hon. members to know what those arrangements are, so that they may be able to form a correct opinion in regard to the matter. On the British magazines which come to Canada the British post office collects postage at the rate of one penny or two cents per pound to pay for their carriage from London to Liverpool, a distance of 210 miles. The British post office gets that money; whilst Canada takes these same magazines at Liverpool and carries them to any point in Canada, as far as Vancouver or Victoria, and gets absolutely nothing for so doing. The British post office gets two cents per pound for carrying these magazines 210 miles and we get nothing for carrying them five or six thousand miles. That is the present condition of affairs. I do not intend to pass any judgment on it or to ask the House to do so. The American magazines coming into this country pay a postage rate of four cents per pound or one cent for four ounces. We have suggested 
to the British post office that the penny which they collect should be divided between Great Britain and Canada-that they keep one cent- for their 210 miles and we get one cent for our five or six thousand miles. I think this is offering a pretty fair bargain. If we succeed in making that arrangement, the British magazines will continue to come into Canada for one-half of what it is costing the American magazines to come here. As a matter of fact, the object for which the old arrangement was entered into is exactly as stated by my hon. friend the member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), namely, to encourage British literature to come into this country, and this object has been attained. When this arrangement was entered into, there were less than 500,000 pounds of British magazines coming to Canada. My hon. friend from Rouville told the House that there were over 2,000,000 pounds at a certain time.
In 1908, 2,328,000 pounds, and in 1912, 5,785,000 pounds. The quantity is increasing all the time.

Who benefits by that increase? There is no question that Canada does; but the publishers of these magazines also reap a great benefit. The British post office has realized every year $100,000 for carrying these magazines from London to Liverpool; and it seems to me that we are very reasonable if, now that the object has been accomplished, now that we have succeeded in getting these magazines into Can- . ada, we ask the British post office to share with us the two cents postage.
The old arrangement was renewed in 1912 for a year. In 1913 the British post office asked us to continue it for another year. We said: In order to give you time to consider the matter, we will continue it for six months. The arrangement was accordingly continued up to the 1st of December last, and then the British post office asked ns to extend it for another period of six months. We said: We will extend it for another three months. When those three months were np, they asked us to extend it for another six months. ' It suits them very well to extend the arrangement from time to time, because during all that time they are collecting all the postage. We have again extended the arrangement for another period of three months, which will expire at the end of July. Meanwhile we hope-in fact, we are almost sure-that we shall come to some reasonable agreement under which these

magazines shall have a kind of preferential rate, because that is what they are getting to come to Canada. My hon. friend from Rouville knows that whatever we do in this matter is not in any way, shape or form going to hurt the editors of these magazines, because they do not pay us anything at all. They do not deal with us; they mail their productions in the post offices in Great Britain. The British post office pays the Canadian Government the international postal union rates on all mail matter which comes to Canada under the Canadian Government contract for the carrying of the ocean mail. If this temporary agreement had not been entered into, the British post office would have paid us on these productions the same rate as they paid on all other kinds of mailable matter. They have been exempted from doing so, and the whole question resolves itself into this: Will the British post office pay to the Canadian Government on these magazines, not the same amount as they pay on other available matter, but a proportion of it; or will Canada carry for nothing these magazines for all time to come? After all, the present arrangement is an encouragement to the editors of British magazines. We have gone very far to help them, and we are prepared again to help them; tout we would like the British post office to meet us and to come to some other arrangement which would continue the preference which these magazines get at present. We think that the British post office should come, not half-way, but some little distance, in order to meet us in this matter.

Is not the position in regard to this matter of postage on magazines exactly the same as the matter of postage on letters, namely, that each country collects its own postage on matter going to the	other country,
and carries the matter that comes from the other country free? I understand	that that is the principle.

Yes, but there is some distinction. When the letter is mailed in England, people put on their stamps there and that goes to the British post office, but the British post office pays the Canadian Government thirty-five cents a pound for all letters which come over on our steamers, while as for those magazines the British post office, under the present arrangement, has not paid one cent. That is the point of difference.

My hon. friend has
here an illustration of *what free trade means. He says we should get one cent out of the two cents a pound on newspapers and magazines collected by the British post office from London and Liverpool. But the British Postmaster General might perhaps 'answer my hon. friend: Well, when we send goods to Canada we meet with customs duties ranging from twenty-five to sixty per cent. Of course, you Canadians loye the mother country, you love the empire, but you tax the goods sent from England to Canada, while you send your manufactured goods and all your products to Britain without paying duties, and Britain is, after all, your best customer.
However, that is not the issue at the moment; I simply bring it in to show my hon. friend that the Postmaster General in England could make a very good rejoinder to his argument. He must not forget that special treatment was given to Canada by Great Britain, that is to say a special alteration in the postal laws wa:s made in England so as to meet the case of Canada.
Special treatment?

Yes. This arrangement does not exist with the other colonies or dominions, but only with Canada, and possibly Newfoundland. Therefore it was just to meet the special Canadian case. My hon. friend must not forget that if Sir William Mulock and the Canadian Government were able, in 1897, to obtain penny postage on letters addressed to any part of the empire, it was due to the bold action taken by the British postal authorities. Canada, of course, took the lead in that matter, and was foremost. The reduction from three cents to two cents had been promoted in Canada and by some parties in England, but unsuccessfully, for a period of ten or fifteen years. I remember reading the pro-ces verbal of the Imperial Conference discussion on that subject. If the hon. gentleman will refer to the reports of the various conferences he will see how reluctantly the British authorities yielded at last. But it was due to that acquiescence of the British post office that Canada obtained the reduced rate of postage throughout the whole of the British Empire. It was done at the request of Canada, it was given after a very able presentment of the case by Sir William Mulock. It was a masterly stroke, and no one will question to-day that this reduction in postal rates in all parts of the British Empire has created an immense



amount of good. Now, there is give and take in these matters. I know the post office in Canada loses some thousands of dollars-
Fifty thousand.

-but is it worth-while for the Postmaster General t.o destroy this intellectual preference between Great Britain and Canada because of the paltry sum of $50,000? When I tell him that we tax British goods while England accepts our products duty free, and when we know that England has yielded to the request of the Canadian post office to establish penny postage throughout the empire, should we not'compromise?	*

If the hon. gentleman will allow me, I will draw his attention to the fact that the amount of $50,000 would he the amount we would get if the two cents, which is now collected by the British post office, were divided between the British and Canadian post offices. But the amount which the British post office would have to pay the Canadian Government if the rates that apply to this class of business were collected is $235,000. That is the extent to which the British magazines benefit by the present postal arrangement. The only suggestion made now Js that instead of imposing the same rates as we do on foreign magazines, the amount that is collected should be divided between us. I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me that this is not a matter of trade arrangement between the home Government and our Government. I take it that this is purely and simply a matter of arrangement between the British and Canadian post offices. Of course, if we go further and say that since England takes our products without charging us duty we should therefore yield this benefit to England, I think that we are driving far afield from the real point at issue. England is a free trade country and does not charge high customs duties on Canadian products or on products from any other country in the world. This is not done as a special benefit to Canada; it is the free trade policy of England. It is for that reason, no doubt, that the British Government has not brought forward the argument mentioned by my hon. friend, and I do not expect they will do so in the future. I hope the new British Postmaster General *will be able to meet us and to make another kind of agreement which will be helpful and continue to be helpful to the British magazines, without leaving the poorer 
government of the two, that is the Canadian Post Office Department, to bear the whole cost without any remuneration whatever. That is the whole point at issue, and the only one. The hon. member suggests that tins should be an entirely one-sided arrangement. It has been so for seven years. The object has been attained, because we do not get now much more than the five or six million pounds to which the hon. gentleman referred as coming in in 1910. It is not increasing very much, and I take it that if we leave the foreign rate at four cents a pound and the rate for British magazines at two cents a pound, they will have had a full realization of the hopes they entertained at that time. The reasons for entering into that agreement are on record. It was stated that if this preference were given for three or four, years, the British magazines would be enabled to get a strong foothold in this country, and that they could then be put on the same footing as the others. They now have a strong foothold in Canada, and I hope that hon. gentlemen on both sides will join with me in trying to meet the new situation which is thus created. We have had to increase the ocean mail subsidies by a large amount, and we have had to increase the amount paid the railway companies for the transportation of our mails. They carry our mails on a ear mile basis. Under the new arrangements we are going to' carry
6,000,000 lb. of British magazines a year, and we will have to pay the railways sixteen cents a car mile or nine cents a car mile, as the case may be, for the carrying of this mail matter. Under these circumstances I think that the British Post Office Department should meet us, and I hope they will. The British publishers oif these periodicals had a meeting with, the Right Hon. Mr. Hobhouse the other day in London. Some of them told him that the Canadian post office was right in its contention. They said that they appreciated what the Canadian Government had done. The English press-the Times, for instance-say that the Canadian Post Office Department is taking a reasonable view of this- matter. The answer Mr. Hobhouse made to the publishers was that they might increase to a very small extent the subscription prices of their publications. They in turn tried to put the shoe on the other foot; they told Mr. Hobhouse that he should consent to our request without asking for any increase in the charges. In a matter like this all the members of the Canadian Parliament should be of one mind, and while

we do desire to continue to give preference to the British magazines, the Canadian post office should not bear all the burden; the British post office should do its share.

*very moderate proposition that has been put 'to him by our Postmaster General. Where -we carried almost nothing a number of years ago we are now carrying six million pounds of magazines. We are carrying these absolutely at our own cost and charges. I am quite willing that we should carry that and twice as much as that at our own cost and charges if it is necessary; but I would like the arguments and the views to be put as strongly as possible in the mother country that the imperial sentiment is as much to them as to us, and that therefore they ought to be willing to bear their fair share of the burden.

The Postmaster General
gave us information that the letter postage from Great Britain to Canada paid thirty-five cents a pound for the ocean transport.

To the Canadian
authorities?

To the Canadian
authorities. Does not the Postmaster General think that the price is fairly high? It seems to me that thirty-five cents a pound for the transport of the mail matter across the ocean, when the freight rate is exorbitant at one cent a pound, is really not helping out the transport of information across the ocean.
These are the Postal Union rates.
I am only saying that is not a low rate and the country is not losing anything on that side of the transaction, or if it is it ought not to be.
We lose heavily.

Under what circumstances and conditions do we pay this amount? I understand the British Post Office Department pays our department and our department pays the steamship lines. To whom do we pay more than thirty-five cents a pound for the carriage of our mails across the ocean?

To the steamship
companies.
What companies?
Four.

Are these the same
steamship companies that we pay a million dollars a year subsidy to? [DOT]

That is the amount
we pay for the transportation of our mail, one million dollars; that covers every-
JMr. G. E. Poster.]
thing. That is the amount of the contract. There are four companies, the Allan, the Canadian Pacific railway, the White Star and the Canadian Northern railway lines have entered into a contract with us under which we pay to the whole of them one million dollars a year for transportation of all mails from Canada to Great Britain and the return mail from Great Britain to Canada.

Therefore, really it does
not make any difference to us whether we carry one ton or one hundred tons of mail matter or what rate we may be charged for it; we pay a fixed amount to the steamship companies, and we get such service as they give us for that.

My hon. friend is
mistaken in that last statement. This year the steamship companies have approached the Post Office Department, and I think the Department of Trade and Commerce, . and they have told us that the increase in the amount of mail matter is such that we would have to increase our price. But there is' another more tangible point. When we come to take these magazines at Halifax or St. John in winter and to Quebec or Montreal in summer we pay for the transportation of these six million pounds sixteen cents a car mile.

I am only getting down
to the ocean transport, and it is still in my mind that although, as a matter of bookkeeping, we are paying 35 cents a pound for the carriage of the mail, as a matter of fact we are not paying anything; we are paying a million dollars a year for the purpose of establishing a steamship monopoly between Canada and England. We are not paying anything for the carrying of mail; the carriage of mail is an incident subordinate to the payment of subsidy, which we pay whether they carry a pound of mail or not.

We have the right to put all our mail and all United States mail which may go through Canada on board these steamers, and they are obliged to carry all the mail from Great Britain or other European countries to this country. That is a flat rate arrangement. It covers the whole world.

If we were not sending
or receiving a pound of mail by any of the steamers of either of these four lines we
