would be'paying one million dollars just the same.

But we would not
make the contract.

The contract being as it
is, whether they bring a pound of mail or not, they would get the one million dollars.

It is a mail subsidy
we are giving these companies.

As a matter of fact, it
does not make any difference to the Canadian Government in cash whether they bring five million pounds of magazines or not, it is costing not one cent for ocean transport over what would be paid whether the magazines came or not.

It does not look like
that to me. The proposition of the hon. member for Edmonton is one that cannot happen. The British magazines that come from the old country have their subscribers in this country, and there is always a certain amount of this matter to Ibe carried. The amount of mail coming over is almost as regular as clockwork, except that it seems to increase in weight and size. The amount of mail matter carried in steamers has increased immensely. We have not seen as yet-and I do not think we ever shall see-any one of those steamers coming in without any mail. If the hon. member for Rouville could see the mail being landed at Rimouski or Halifax or Quebec he would be amazed at the large amount of mail matter brought by every one of those steamers. At Quebec, in the summer time, I have seen as many as twelve or fourteen full carloads unloaded * from the steamers.

We need not dispute about that; we know the mail comes on those steamers, but I was wishing to get clear in my mind the point the hon. minister was making that we were sacrificing in cash a large amount for the benefit of the English magazines, which cost should be borne by the British post office. I am only wanting to get clear in my own mind and in the mind of Parliament that as a matter of actual fact the coming of these British magazines does not cost the Dominion of Canada one cent, so far as their transportation across the Atlantic is concerned. The British Post Office Department does not pay the Canadian Government 35 cents a pound as it does in the case of letters.
In my humble judgment, the Canadian Post Office, in the slang of the day, is ' putting one over ' the British Post Office-Department when it charges 35 cents a pound for mail matter carried on these steamers. But we will not find fault with that; we are glad to see the Post Office-Department showing a due dilligence in the collection of revenue, especially revenue that is not collected from the Canadian people. We do not wish the argument to be made, however, that Canada is actually making a sacrifice in cash when, as a matter of fact, she is not making any such sacrifice. In regard to transportation of mail by rail in Canada I wish to deal with the subject matter of this section, and there is some little connection between the point I had primarily in mind and this carriage of English magazines. We pay a certain rate to the railway companies for carrying our mail matter through Canada. Do we pay by the pound or by the car mile?
By the car mile.
And it works out something on the same principle as in the case of the steamers. If we have no mail matter to load, we pay just the same as if the car were'full. Is that correct?

No. We pay by the
car mile, but if we need only half a car we pay for only half a car; that
10 p.m. is, we pay for the space we use.
So, whatever the worth of my hon. friend's argument in the case of sea transit, he will have some trouble in arriving at the same conclusion in regard to mail carried by rail.

I just wanted t-o get the facts clear in my mind. I wish to deal with the matter of newspaper transportation, which was brought up by my hon. friend from Rouville. I notice that the section of the Bill gives authority to the minister to establish the rates of postage on all mailable matter 'not being letters and prescribe the terms and conditions, etc.' I am sure the question has been before the Postmaster General very frequently, and as he must have come to some conclusion on the matter, I think it is inorder that he should tell the House what his conclusion is. He is asking for power; let us know how he proposes to exercise-that power.	*
That is in the old law..

It is not the old law, but the new conditions that are the question.

The Law expressly places the responsibility on the Postmaster General, and gives him due authority, and we would like to know how the minister proposes to deal with this question. I am speaking of a question that I am sure has been brought to the attention of the (minister very frequently, that is, as to the postal rates on newspapers of different classes, and the question of drawing a distinction between newspapers which aTe published primarily for the purpose of carrying advertising, and newspapers which are published primarily for the purpose of distributing news.

I have not reached any conclusion so far, but the matter has been the subject of a good deal of thought and care. We have taken this matter up with the Canadian Press Association, and have asked them to meet us with the view of coming to some arrangement. We are very desirous to arrange this matter by consent, and I must say that the Canadian Press, Limited, and the Canadian Press Association have shown a good deal of the right spirit in this matter. They have sent delegations to us, and have .appointed a committee to look into the matter. That committee has made a report to them, which they have adopted. They have sent a second delegation to the Post Office Department to try to come to some conclusion. We have not been able yet to come to a complete agreement, but I may say we have agreed on certain points of detail, and we hope to be able to come to a complete agreement some time after tbe session. I have had no time lately to devote to the matter, but when you realize that in this country the newspapers only pay one-quarter of a cent per pound for postage to be carried all the way from Vancouver to Halifax, or vice versa, and that in England they pay one cent per copy-

Ours is the cheapest
rate in the world.

My hon. friend who has been Postmaster General knows that. There is not a country in the world where such rates are in existence. The rates do not begin to pay for the cost. In the United States the rate is one cent per pound. I may say to the credit of tihe newspaper men that they agree that our rates are not high enough, and they have admitted that in black and white in their report, which is now on file in the Department. We have gone pretty far in the way of effecting an 
agreement when they have reached the conclusion that the present state of things cannot continue. Just what changes will be made, is another question. Some newspaper proprietors suggest that we should increase the rates in a certain way, and others suggest a different way. I would like to say that the different suggestions .which have been made wonld be to the greater or less benefit of the owners in question. They have however shown a good deal of public spirit in the matter. The rates will be and I hope it will be done with the consent of the newspapers. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) will realize that it would :be a somewhat difficult matter for the Postmaster General to antagonize all the newspapers in the country and it is not a very desirable thing to do, although, if it should come to that, I want it to be understood that as a matter of public duty I would' not hesitate to do it. But, I prefer doing it with their consent. However, I am happy to say, that they have met us fairly, and I think that next session I will be able to tell this House that we have reached a certain point and that we have made some progress.

I do not wish to delay
the committee on this question but I wish to state the views which I hold. The newspaper rate of postage i,n Canada is no doubt very low. It was made low in order that the literary matter published by the newspapers might reach as large a proportion, of the population as possible. It was recognized that it was a country of vast area with a comparatively small population .and that the conditions being exceptional it was desirable to disseminate the newspapers at the lowest possible cost. As my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has spoken of the arrangement in regard to British magazines, it was understood to be an intellectual preference. At this time conditions have changed. We have entered upon an era of newspaper publication wherein, from year to year, the newspaper is published rather as a vehicle of advertising than as a means of disseminating news and opinions. Just in proportion as the newspaper expands as an advertising medium, as compared with ita value as a news service, it departs from; the conditions that warranted the low postal rate that was given to newspapers in the earlier days.. I do not think that a newspaper which is published primarily as an advertising medium is. entitled to the rate of postage it

would have been entitled to if it were published primarily as a vehicle of news oir opinion. I would be sorry that any increase in the postal rate should apply to newspapers published primarily as newspapers. I think it would only be just to the country and to the newspapers that are published as newspapers rather than, as advertising mediums that there should be a difference of treatment between these two classes of so-called publications. I do not lay down any rule, I do not suggest any division, I quite appreciate the difficulties that will have to be met, but as one who has published newspapers for a long time I would resent very much any increase in the burden of legitimate newspapers whereby they were compelled to carry that burden which is levied by the Post Office Department by reason of these papers published as advertising- mediums rather than as newspapers.
The low rate that was given to newspapers was given as an intellectual preference and so, if the department is carrying that quantity of paper under the name of newspapers which are really advertising mediums at a price much below the cost, my hon. friend has no very good case to demand with -any serious strength a radical revision of the rates in regard to the British magazines. Let us put our own house on a business basis before we undertake to dictate to the people across the water how they must do business. I was more than astonished to hear some gentlemen who so eloquently and so vociferously undertook a year ago to insist upon making a free gift of $35,000,000 to the Government of Great Britain to-night protest that it was necessary as a matter of good business that the British Post Office Department should pay, or help to pay, for the carriage of British magazines across the ocean when that carriage does not cost this Dominion of Canada one extra cent.

My hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) is more inaccurate than usual in the statement he has made just now. The $35,000,000 that we proposed last year was to be used for the construction of ships^ to remain in the ownership of the Canadian people, and to be placed at the disposal of His Majesty for the common defence of the empire until recalled. As far as his argument is concerned in regard to some other matters that he mentioned, he might as well say that we could carry all the letters
and other mail matter from the United
States to Great Britain without charging anything for it and not be out of pocket, as to make the argument that he has made in regard to these magazines. As I understand, the Canadian post office, in respect to the transmission of mails across the Atlantic, acts as a courier, and charges the United States Government, for example, certain rates, not rates fixed by the IPost Office Department, but fixed by an international arrangement, and charges the British Government or any other Government, for these mails, the transportation of which is arranged for by this Government through a mail subsidy of $1,000,000. While in one sense, of course, if we did not charge the British Government, the United States Government, or any other Government, we would not be out of pocket if we should continue to pay that $1,000,000; still it would hardly 'be a very good argument that we should give up charging any of the nations of the world for the transmission of their mail matter across the Atlantic. The magazines that have been alluded to by my hon. friend the Postmaster General are precisely in the same category as any other mail matter. The Postmaster General -has merely suggested to the British Postnfaster General that, inasmuch as a penny a pound is charged upon these magazines, a reasonable proportion which he has suggested to be a half, should be paid to the Canadian Government for the transmission of these mails by the Post Office Department of Canada as a courier across the Atlantic and by other means throughout our territory as a reasonable compensation for that carriage.

On the
item before the House we have been discussing the franking privilege, the character of the literature that goes through the post office, and mailing privileges generally. Therefore I think I am in order if I ask the Postmaster General whether or not the sheet called The Liberator, with which he is familiar, published in the city of Ottawa, is accorded the privilege of the mails. I am not a subscriber to that paper, but I receive it regularly through the post office here. I do not know whether postage is paid on it or not. The reason I ask that question is that I observed in the last issue that the editor or publisher had some fears of the present Postmaster General. The paper stated editorially that the present Postmaster General was watching it pretty closely, and that there was some diabolical influence behind him that was likely to make trouble for it whenever the Post-

master General could screw up enough courage to make the attack. So far as the editor of that paper is concerned, it seems to me, in view of the courage and strength and forcefulness which the Postmaster General displayed with reference to the sheet called the Menace, which is characterized as scurrilous, indecent and immoral, that there should be no cause for anxiety or misgiving in the breast of Mr. Morgan at all. I would like, however, to have some official statement from the minister as to whether or not this paper has the privileges of the mails. I know it does not have very much circulation outside the city of Ottawa, but in Ottawa it is known and has been denounced by all the leading clergymen of the city.

The Liberator, published in Ottawa, does not go very much through the mails; its circulation is almost entirely in the city. I understand from the deputy minister that this paper has been warned that it must not publish any immoral literature, and on that condition the privileges of the mails have been given to it. I have not the pleasure of reading that paper as carefully as my hon. friend; but P hear from him to-night that it says that it is being watched. It is not being watched by me at all events; but there are officers in the department whose duty it is to watch all that is going through the mails, not from the point of view of religion, but from the point of view of decency and public morals, and the Liberator or any other paper, whether Protestant or Catholic, which does not come within that rule, will be dealt with in the same manner.

Since the Menace has been mentioned, and as it was I who first placed the question on the Order Paper, I wish to ask the minister why he ruled first that the Canadian Menace should not be allowed, and later ruled that it should be allowed, the privileges of the mails. I am not at the moment asking him to enter into a dissertation as to the merits of the Menace or as to his own personal view of it or as to the view of his deputy minister or of any one in his department, although in one of his letters he hid behind the fact that his deputy minister happened to be a Protestant. It is not a matter of concern to us what is the religion of the deputy minister or whether he has any religion. We vote the deputy minister his salary; and, as we all have troubles of our own, we have not the time to consider the religion of the deputy minister. In answer to my question 
the minister said that the Menace of Aurora, Ontario, was denied the mails for the same reason that the Menace of Aurora, Missouri, had been denied, namely, because it was scurrilous and indecent and immoral. I wish to ask him, because I think the public have a right to knew the reason, why later on he admitted the Canadian Menace to the privileges of the mails.

I gave a full and complete answer to that question only a few days ago. My answer will be found on ' Hansard ' and I would like my hon. friend to read it. The reason for which the Canadian Menace was refused the privileges of the mails in the first instance was that it was going to be a Canadian edition of the scurrilous sheet published at Aurora, Missouri. Later on the Canadian Menace acknowledged that we were right in our contention that it had no right to publish dirt and filth, and promised not to do so; consequently it was given the privileges of the mails.

Some time ago the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) stated that the paper, the Liberator, published in Ottawa, came through the mails and was put into our boxes. The Postmaster General very frankly said at that time that this matter did not come under his supervision, but was under the control of the Speaker. If I remember aright, the Speaker told us at the time that he would see that this would [DOT] not occur again. We have been surprised to see that this paper, though without any franking privileges at all, is placed in our boxes. I would like to know if the Speaker has forgotten or if he is going to give new orders. We do not want to see this paper in our boxes.

I did not make that

But what I should like to know is bow it happens that this paper is placed in our boxes, not franked, with nothing to show from what source it comes c<r by whom it is placed in, our boxes. Is the responsibility on the Postmaster Gen-

I think the House will see that a radical change is made as regards the insurance of letters. I do not wish to delay the committee, but I think the House is entitled to the information.

We have the power of insurance now. We are making a distinction between the power of registration and the power to insure. The two are now mixed up. We are limiting it now to $25, as compensation which people who register mail matter should have the right to claim as a result of the loss. This is carrying into effect a proposal which I explained last year, and it will enable those who wish to do so to insure their parcels going through the mails. This is done, if I mistake not, in all countries where parcel post exists. We thought, and I still think, that we might have that power, but there was some doubt expressed about it, so we thought it best to come to Parliament and have the whole thing on the statutes so that there might be no mistake. We are going to keep to the five cents for registration fee. We will make the charge for insurance of parcels not lairge, but we may have to charge a little more for insurance purposes.-Our present intention, as advised by the officers of the department, is that -the proper limit would be $50.

Insurance brokers are
taking advantage of the Post Office Department in this way: they insure parcels, so to speak, and really they do not insure them, but they profit by the registration of the post office and are satisfied with paying the small amount of five cents instead of paying for the regular insurance, and in that way they are taking away the money due the Post Office Department. I understand that the amendment is to cover that point.

The hon. gentleman
has put it exactly as it is. I was coming to that point. Money is taken by some companies and for it a receipt is given, and they undertake to carry it to the point of destination. What do they do? There are some

If the minister is not

The Orange Sentinel does not take the same view with regard to the action taken by the Postmaster General as he himself has taken. The Sentinel says that the reason he turned rightabout face was that the Orange lodges made him do so. I do not know either Orangeman or Catholic so far as this House goes, or so

far as the public business goes; but I know the Postmaster General as a man responsible to this House for the discharge of his duties, and it is scarcely right that a paper of wide circulation like the Sentinel should make the charge that the Postmaster General had changed his views-which we must assume were conscientious because the Sentinel and his friends made him do so, and that no explanation should be given. The Sentinel says;
The ban on the Canadian Menace has been raised. Hon. Mr. Pelletier has seen a new light and has conceded interim postal privileges. So long as the Menace refrains from imitation of the paper of the same name in the United States, it is likely to be allowed to pass through the mails.
Credit for the vindication of the liberty of the press is largely due- to Orangemen. Thousands of them protested in vigorous terms against Rome's attempt to establish herself as press censor and allowed it to be known that they would break party affiliations rather than endure a violation of the Protestant principles.
Had the Orange Association and its official organ been less influential, Canada would still be disgraced by the State's suppression of a publication disliked by Rome. No one can tell what the end would have been.
The lesson for our members is that if they will get all their friends to read the Sentinel and succeed in inducing them to join the Order, and fight for equal rights and one school, one flag, and one language, it will not be long before Orangeism is triumphant all along the line.
It is time all Protestants got up on the band wagon.
Now, one of two things is correct: Either this paper has committed a gross libel upon the minister-and it is not becoming the dignity of this House that one of our members should be so libelled-or we are in the hands of a Postmaster General who would have done us a wrong, unless the Sentinel and its Orange friends had in some divine way come to our assistance. Either one of these is an unfortunate position, and I think it is the minister's duty to straighten the matter out.

My hon. friend is very witty and draws a great many smiles from his friends around him: Why he is bringing this matter up and putting it before the committee I do not know, but I would advise him to consult some of his friends on the other side as to whether they think the matter to which he has referred is a good and proper one to bring before the House in the way he is bringing it. So far as I am concerned it is not a question of my doing what I am told by the Orange Lodges, by the Catholic Church or by anybody else;

what I try to do is that which I think is right; that is my only guide. That is what I am going to continue to do, whether it pleases the one church or the other, and whether my hon. friend from the West is satisfied or not.

I want to speak of the proposed changes in newspaper rates in so far as they concern newspapers published in western Canada, and I would like to place before the Postmaster General some views in that regard based upon practical experience. If there is to be an increase in postal rates, special consideration should be given .to the newspapers of western Canada on account of the extent to which the cost of production exceeds that of eastern newspapers. I have some figures here which I prepared last session when this matter was under consideration, and which I did not place before the House. In the first place, I would like the minister to consider that the field covered by the western daily newspaper is very wide compared with that covered by the eastern newspaper. .For instance, there is no daily newspaper between Moosejaw and Medicine Hat and there is no daily newspaper between Medicine Hat and Calgary; consequently the newspapers in those western cities cover a very large territory.
This is not the case in Ontario, where daily newspapers are published in nearly every incorporated city and in some of the towns. What I want to emphasize is the fact that the cost of publication in western Canada is much heavier-much more so, perhaps, than the Postmaster General realizes- than it is in eastern Canada. Apart from the matter of high telegraph and cable tolls and from the question of wages-and wages in western Canada are considerably higher than they are in the East-the cost of publication is higher in the West than in the East and higher in Winnipeg than in the cities of Minneapolis and St. Paul. Dealing with the item of freight rates on the paper on which newspapers are printed, I would like to quote these figures: Winnipeg papers pay 61 cents a hundred pounds; Regina, 99 cents; Calgary, 81.32; Edmonton, $1.32; Lethbridge, $1.27; Saskatoon, 1.09; Nelson, B.C., $1.71; Rossland, $1.71; Minneapolis and St. Paul, 10. cents; eastern Canadian newspapers, from 10 to 20 cents. It will be observed that the cost of production in the West is very much larger than in the East, in respect of the one item of freight rates, upon paper. The newspapers of western Canada have been of

great value to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior in providing a great deal of publicity, for the western Canadian newspapers circulate not only in their own respective districts, but very largely in the United States and Great Britain. They are of value also in developing a strong Canadian and British sentiment in this country, and that is very important in a new part of the country like western Canada. I hope that the Postmaster General will take up the case of the newspapers of western Canada which, I believe, has been presented to him by influential western publishers, and give it the serious consideration which I feel sure it deserves.
The remarks of the hon. gentleman are worthy of attention, and they will, be taken into serious consideration when we take up this matter at the end of the present session.

On section 4-temporary appointments:

When this Bill was before the committee in the shape of a resolution, some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House asked my hon. friend for an explanation with regard to this section. A partial explanation was given, but, with all respect to my hon. friend, I must say that' he did not satisfy this side of the House that he was not taking power under
these amendments to appoint without examination a host of political friends, who will serve as travelling political agents for the Government of which my hon. friend is a valued and useful member. If my hon. friends on this side of the House who have been complaining about dismissals will apply their attention to this section and observe the difference between it and the provisions of the section for which it is a substitute, they will readily understand what has become of many of their political friends of whose dismissals they have previously complained. One remarkable feature of subsection 3 of this section is that it is retro active; it is to be effective frpm March 12, 1912. It provides among other things that persons who were then in the employ of the railway mail service shall be continued in the service, irrespective of age, and notwithstanding the fact that they have not passed the Civil Service examinations.
It then makes a further amendment of the previously existing law, which declared that such persons shall not be eligible for an increase until they pass the Civil Service examination, while the new section provides that they shall be eligible for an annual increase until their salaries amount to $1,000 so they may be continued for an indefinite length of time in the service without examination and have their salaries increased to $1,000. After that the new section provides that they shall not be eligible for an increase above $1,000 until they have passed the qualifying examination. - Perhaps the minister can give me some explanation.

There is no such radical change in the Bill, as my hon. friend may learn from the hon. member for Rou-ville. Clerks are taken on as temporary employees not only in the post office but in all the departments. Before the date mentioned in that section, that is, the 12th * of March, 1912, under the law as it then existed the Post office Department had the right to appoint these employees as they were appointed; but subsequently we ourselves passed a law under which it became necessary to pass certain examinations. Thus, instead of relaxing the rigorous state of the law, we have made it more rigorous.
Not by this amendment.

This amendment is
not as my hon. friend read it. The only thing whidh this Bill provides which is a

change from the present law is that these people, if they are satisfactory, may get their increases like everyone else. There is no such radical change as he suggests.

My hon. friend has referred to some subsequent legislation. I do not know whether he referred to chapter 41, of the statutes of 1912, or to' some Act subsequent to that. If his reference is to chapter 41 of the statutes of 1912, I would submit that the observations I have made are entirely borne out by this amendment. This amendment is doing precisely what I stated a few moments ago it is intended to do.

There is now a law in existence under which railway mail clerks can be kept as temporary employees for more than twelve months. They have then to pass the preliminary examination, or they have to go; even if we wanted to keep them the Auditor General would not pay them. When an employee has passed the preliminary examination he can be kept, but his salary does not go beyond a certain limit until he has passed the qualifying examination. Some of the temporary clerks in the Post Office Department have had no increase because they did not pass the preliminary examination at the end of the first year of their appointment, and did not pass it because they were not then obliged by law to pass it. Then the law came into force saying that no increase would be given to those who had not passed the examinations. The law discriminated against these clerks, and we are taking care of this special condition by this clause. My hon. friend will see that this Bill makes no great change.
What I see is the reverse of what the hon. gentleman has stated. Under subsection 3 surely my hon. friend will not contend that he has not taken power to appoint.
The clause only refers to those appointed before the 12th of March, 1912. The clause does not refer to future appointments.

I am not speaking about the future, but about people who have been in the service. My statement is that the intention is to make them practically permanent officials, turning them from temporary into permanent employees without examination.

But this does not give me the power to make temporary appointments, as my hon. friend says, he speaks of
[Mr. Pelletier.!
political agents going around the country It refers to appointments made prior to the 12th of March, 1912. These people have been in the service during all that time, and we would like those who are qualified for the work and who are recommended by their superior officers, to have the increases to which they would have been entitled if they had been appointed under the same circumstances as the others who were appointed since that date. That is all the clause provides for.

In other words, the law says that no man can be appointed railway mail clerk until he has passed certain examinations and not if he is over thirty years of age. My hon. friend has not been able, as I was not able, to find young men of less than thirty years who would be willing to accept the paltry sum of $500 to serve as railway mail clerks and he has appointed, under the name of labourers, many mail clerks over thirty years, some fifty years of age and probably some sixty. My hon. friend wishes to put these men regularly in the service but he gives them a little salve because under the existing law unless they pass the qualifying examination he would be unable to give them a salary beyond $1,000.
Can my hon. friend tell the committee to how many employees this will apply?

That question was put by the hon. member for Oxford, and I have the information here, as to the number of people affected and the amount involved. By reason of the annual increase from $50 to $100 for the people now in the service it will cost $66,200.

This gives the information for the Bill we have passed and the Bill we are now engaged on. To raise the salaries of permanent clerks from $500 to $600 will cost $38,300. The total number of persons affected is as follows: Temporary cleTks who will be raised from $500 to $600, 89; permanent clerks who will be raised from $500 to $600, 126; clerks who will receive an annual increase of $100 instead of $50, 490; altogether 705 people will come under the preceding Bill and the Bill we are now discussing.
Seven hundred and five will be made permanent.

No, that relates to
salary. The figures I have given include railway mail clerks, who are provided for by this Bill, employees in the city post offices, and in the other offices.
How many will be made permanent?

I have not that
information, but there are not many.

About 90?

No, that is the number of temporary clerks who will be raised from $500 to $600.

I do not wish t<s
delay the passage of this very important Bill, but there is a matter which I think is deserving of the attention of the Postmaster General, and that is in connection with the maximum salary of the railway mail clerks. Every .member of the House realizes that the employees of the railway mail service are subject to very many casualties. Employees in that branch probably run greater risks than in any other branch of the Government service, and I am pleased to see that the Postmaster General has seen fit to recognize the railway mail Service by raising the minimum and maximum salaries. clerk who lives in my town who was appointed to the service in 1884, and it was only last year, after being thirty years in the service, that he reached his maximum. However, the present legislation making the annual increase $100 instead of $50 will enable clerks in this particular branch to reach their maximum much more rapidly. Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: I do not think this legislation is quite as innocent as the Postmaster General tries to make it appear. There is no objection, of course, to raising the minimum salary to $600. Five hundred dollars may appear low; in fact it is low. If $500 was a proper salary ten or twenty years ago, $600 is low enough to-day. This section provides:
3. Any person employed temporarily as a railway mail clerk on the twelfth day of March, 1912, may, if his services have been satisfactory-
Who is to be the judge?
-and if recommended by the superintendent and the controller of the railway mail service, be appointed to the permanent staff at a salary not exceeding the amount he is then receiving, irrespective of age and notwithstanding the fact that he has not passed the Civil Serviec examination.

Next thing the committee takes him in hand and says: We will appoint you to the railway mail service. by	an	independent and	competent

Those who were appointed before the date mentioned in that clause. At that time it was not necessary for these people to pass an examination.

I wish to bring to the minister's attention a matter that has been the subject of a resolution of the Association of Railway Mail Clerks in my own city. Among other things they asked the department that they might use their good offices to secure for railway mail clerks transportation privileges while they are on their holidays. At the present time railway mail clerks, although they are very closely indentified with the transportation system of the country, have to pay out of their own pockets for their transportation while on vacation. They have, by a formal resolution, asked that the Government

might use its good offices to get railway transportation for them during their holidays. The Government is very close to the railway companies and especially the railway mail service branch of the Post Office Department. Immense sums are paid to the railway companies by the Post Office Department and there seems to be a great deal of pith in what any constituents say that the influence of the Postmaster General would be very great with the railway companies in securing this concession. I am told that the employees of the express companies get this privilege to which I am referring. The department might accomplish this end, if in no other way, by allowing railway mail clerks to travel in the mail car itself which would not do any harm inasmuch as the men engaged in that service might very well be trusted to travel in the mail car. If the minister would be kind enough to assure me that he would do his utmost with the railway companies to come to an understanding with them that they would grant vacation passes such as they grant to their own employees I am sure it would be quite satisfactory to the railway mail clerks. I think they might grant such passes not only to the railway mail clerk but to the railway mail clerk and his wife. I would commend this to his favourable consideration.

My hon. friend certainly overestimates the power which the Postmaster General has with the railways. If he could only have been present at the numerous interviews which were held in order to come to a settlement of the vexed question of the increase of the rates he would have known that the railway companies are not so willing to give the PostOffice Department favours as he supposes. Instead of giving us a pass for the railway mail clerk going on his vacation with his wife, his children and maybe his cousins, his aunts, -his friends, or his lady friend-

That was on the ground of morality, I suppose.
Mr. PELLETIER-I do not know; some of these people stand on very high ground, I understand. They even contended that we had no right to send a second clerk on duty on the postal car and that if we did so we had to pay for his passage. My hon. friend sees that instead of giving us passes for the railway mail clerks going away on their vacations they are so exacting in that respect that we would have very little chance of securing such a concession. We had to take the stand that the railway mail
clerks who were on the mail car on duty should not be called upon to pay anything for their passage. I do not at all agree with the policy of the minister in taking power to himself to make regulations for the postage of newspapers without the direct sanction of Parliament. The postal rates are provided at present by the sections that are being repealed. I think postal rates should be established by authority of Parliament and should be embodied in the statute. I do not agree that it is proper legislation or a proper discharge of the responsibilities of this House merely to authorize the Postmaster General to fix any rate of postage that he may think fit. The rule that has prevailed in the past, whereby the rate of postage is -set down in the statute on the responsibility of Parliament as recommended by the Government, is the proper way and the only way in which that matter should be dealt with.

Does the minister
provide under that section to blot out the statute regulation in regard to newspapers and to take the whole thing into his own hands? What ground does he give for taking such powers?

We have it in everything else; it is a matter of regulation. If one reads the law as it exists at present, one- -may reach the conclusion tha-t we have that power at the present time, whereas another may reach a different conclusion; but it has been considered by me as a matter of regulation in the department. We are desirous to reach an agreement with the newspaper owners to increase the rates of postage on newspapers. If we cannot make this a matter of regulation, our hand's will be paralyzed. Under the Parcel Post Act we have the power to make the rates as they are ; we have the power to increase or to decrease them.
That is an experimental proposition.

We are about to
change the ra-tes on newspapers and we expect to do it with the consent of the newspaper owners.
Will there be an increase?

The rates may not be increased in all eases. The press associations have admitted that the rates should be increased but they propose, not the same zones, -but the same system of zones as exist for parcel post. They say that we

should ask a higher rate of postage for newspapers beyond.a certain distance. If this has all to be put into the law by Parliament, our hands will be tied and we shall not be able to make any such arrangement with the newspapers owners. This power exists for parcel post and for everything else. Last year we were told, when parcel post came up, that we should take that power and fix the rates. We cannot do that except by regulations which are adopted, which have to be published in the official Gazette, and which come into force only after being so published. These rates, of course, can be recalled. For parcel post, to which the same principle applies absolutely, if we had had to wait for Parliament to fix these rates, we could not have prepared as we did; and if in the course of our experience in Tegard to parcel post, we see that these rates may be decreased for the benefit of the public, we can do it without coming to Parliament for sanction. It is all a question as to whether or not the officers of the department, in whose hands this matter lies to a great extent, can be trusted to do what is right in the matter. There never has been a complaint in regard to the matter, and I do not think there ever will be.

Has the minister
nothing to do with these things himself?

I take a great interest in these matters as I do in all matters concerning my department. I have met the newspaper editors several times and have discussed this matter with them. They have been good enough to tell me that I have met them in the proper spirit and that they are willing to do all they can to meet my views, because they think I am right, at least to a certain extent. I do not think there is any great danger in this section.

I can say to my hon.
friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that the minister is right in his explanation. The Postmaster General, if you read his powers in the Post Office Act, can himself make all these regulations for newspapers, for parcel post and so on.

The Postmaster
General says that he does not look after these matters; that it is his officials who do so.

My hon. friend can
trust the Postmaster General not to quarrel with the newspapers. I can credit him to be an astute enough politician to play fair with them.

On some occasions
lately I have found my hon. friend the Postmaster General to be a gentleman of wonderfully fertile resources. He is very plausible in regard to this proposition concerning the newspapers, but he 'has a -way of putting his officials in front of him when there is anything for which he does not want to assume the responsibility, and he tells us that is all right. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is a newpaper man, and he has rather impressed me with his argument in regard to the matter. If my hon. friend the minister finds it necessary in the carrying on of the business of his department to deal with matters of detail, and if he is going to take the power-and he has made an argument to impress the House that he ought to have the power- to negotiate and do all these things between sessions, there ought to be an ultimate reference to Parliament when changes are to be made.

I agree with my hon. friend; but the revising power of Parliament exists even if I do not reserve it in this case. If I make an arrangement with the newspaper editors and owners which is not suitable to Parliament, hon. members can tell "me so at the next session. I think I understand what my hon. friend has in mind. I am not asking for powers to make the Liberal newspapers pay a certain rate and the Conservative newspapers pay another rate.
I never would have thought that at all.	.

I am asking that the same rates shall apply to all newspapers, and no Postmaster General would think of doing anything else than that. Under the circumstances, as my hon. friend from Rouville has very properly said, there are a great many guarantees that this matter will be approached in the right spirit. I think we can accomplish some good if there is no doubt about these powers being vested in the Postmaster General. I am of the opinion that these powers are at present vested in the Postmaster General but there is some doubt in regard to the matter and I would like to make it clear, so that there will be no question about it.

This question of zone, of which my hon. friend has spoken, cannot be operated generally so as to be satisfactory. But let me point out the difference. It is all right where the newspaper is 205
located with a country surrounding it o'n all sides. But take newspapers published along the frontier, the circulation of which is in Canada alone, they have only half a zone in which to circulate. Now, unless provision is made to make the centre of their zone somewhere else than the place of publication, they are at a disadvantage. I have had a good deal of correspondence with newspaper men on this subject, and I said that if there was the change proposed it would be unfair to the newspapers on the frontier. Heretofore, the place of publication was at the edge of the zone, Which was fair. But the change that is proposed will take away a quarter of the privilege of these newspapers.	.

I hold no brief for the newspapers, but I hope no regulation will be made to make it difficult for people in the country to get a cheap newspaper. It is a great advantage that the Montreal Star, the Toronto Globe, and other large newspapers can go out to distant places in the country at cheap rates. The farmers will not pay a big price for a daily paper, but it certainly makes a country district a better place to live in if its people have access to daily newspapers, even though they be three or four days old. We are all agreed that rural life should be made more attractive, and cheap newspapers is one of the means to that end. If the Postmaster General takes away from the country people the opportunity to get newspapers at cheap rates, he will strike a heavier blow at the welfare of the country than he thinks. I hope he will give the matter very serious consideration.

I desire to protest as emphatically as I can, without delaying the committee, against the position of the Postmaster General that this should be by regulation. I say emphatically that it should not be by regulation, but by statute. It has always been by statute and is so now. But the minister proposes to strike that provision out of the statute and take power to regulate as he may please. The minister has given no reason so far to justify that position. It is right that associations of newspaper men should meet the officers of the department and discuss the proposed changes with them, and it is entirely desirable that they should reach an amicable conclusion. But that does not alter the fact that changes in such an important service as the postal rates on newspapers should be at the discretion of Parliament, and of Parliament alone. It is



not a matter that should be fixed between my hon. friend's department and an association of newspaper publishers; it is a matter that should foe set right on the floor of the House, not in the interest of the newspaper publishers and the officials of the department, but in the interest of the people of Canada who are interested in the newspapers and in the postal service. There is a very material reason from the newspaper publisher's point of view why this matter should be by statute and not by regulation. The newspaper postage, although it is small on each number of the paper, is, in the aggregate, a very important part of the charges upon any considerable newspaper enterprise, and it is important to the enterprise, wherever it may be located and whether large or small, that it should know that that feature of its existence and this limitation of its opportunities should not be subject to change without due notice and without the fullest consideration.
This does not interfere with all that.

If postal charges are to be subject to change simply at the will of the department, after consultation with this, that, or the other association of newspapers, there is no reasonable assurance of permanence in the regulations of the newspaper publishers at large, such as there would be if there could foe change only by Parliament only after full discussion on the floor of this House. From that standpoint, the practical effect of my hon. friend making the change from statute to regulations, is entirely against the material interest of the newspaper publishers.	.	j ,,
The Postmaster General has instanced the case of the parcel post rates as provided by regulation. He received authority from Parliament at the last session to establish a parcel post system with rates and regulations such as he should fix. And he concludes that because he was given that authority at that time therefore he should be given this authority now. Without introducing controversial matters, I say that for my part, as a representative of the people, as a member of this Parliament, I am responsible, measurably responsible, for m/ hon. friend's parcel post system and the rates he levied. Now, I am not in agreement with his parcel post system or the rates he levied; I do not think the system 
is well-conceived or well carried out, and I do not think it is fair to me or to members of this House that I have no opportunity to give my opinion with regard to that matter. So, his instance of the parcel post system is unfortunate fro-m my point of view. This is a matter of very great importance to the people of Canada, and the representatives of the people of Canada in Parliament assembled should have the deciding vote.

On section 9-letter carriers on electric railways:

I would suggest to the minister that he strike out the words 'except municipally owned electric railways.' In the city of Guelph in my riding the electric railway is municipally owned. It was a stock company; the city acquired the stock, and it is operated under a commission named by the council. I do not think that any arrangement has ever been made with them for the carrying of letter-carriers. I notice in the section that the Postmaster General proposes that letter-carriers shall be conveyed on every electric railway in Canada except municipally owned railways, on such terms and conditions and under such regulations as are made by the Postmaster General. Why make au exception of the municipally owned railways? If they will not make terms, the. Postmaster General can set the price. I think that should apply to municipalities as well as to companies. Nearly all electric companies are provincial companies, and the Postmaster General assumes under the section the right to prescribe rates for these companies. Municipal institutions are provincial institutions; if the Postmaster General can prescribe rates for the one he can prescribe them for the other. It would be a hardship to twelve or fifteen young men in the town where distances are long, and a hardship to the public as well, if they cannot get and deliver the letters as speedily as they could if they were permitted to use this electric road. I have heard it said that the Railway Commission at Guelph is exorbitant in its requests. I do not know what those requests are, but I think that the Postmaster General should take action at once to fix a price, and if he will strike out the words which I have indicated he will be able to fix a price.
For what reason are municipally owned railways excluded?

In all our experience we have had no trouble whatever with the 2054
municipally owned electric railways. I was asked by them: have you any reason to complain about us? I told them: no, you have been very decent about it. They said: if so, why put us on the same footing as the others who .are so exacting? I thought they were right:	The letter carriers in
every city would like to enjoy this privilege, which is now so general; but in many cases they are prevented from doing so oil account of the prohibitive price which certain tramway companies endeavour to exact from the department. In the case of Guelph or other towns where there are municipally owned railways we have authorities who will help us to come to terms and -to meet the views of the letter carriers in a fair way, and those are the reasons why we have not included the municipally-owned railway. Have the Guelph
people done so?

I am not in a position to tell my hon. friend about it just at the moment, but if the matter is not settled by the Guelph people on proper lines my hon. friend can count on me to do what is right in the matter. If that tramway in Guefph is the property of the corporation, probably we cannot reach them under this clause, tout if it is in the hands of a company we can reach them. I have put this section in in order to show the other companies with which we have been having so much trouble-companies which are making enormous profits and which have no consideration for employees who are obliged to walk the streets with their loads-to show them that we intend to make a distinction between them and those companies which offer us fair terms. I want to make a clear distinction between the people who act in a fair way in the matter and those who demand from us prohibitive rates and, if they do not get them, decline to take care of the transportation of the men. We have been unable to come to terms with the company in Moosejaw; that is one of the few places in the West where we have been unable to come to a reasonable arrangement with the company.

I cannot recall the figures, but I offered the same rates as are paid all over corresponding area in the West. They admitted that the other

-companies were prepared to accept the rates offered, but they said: We will not accept them; we will get more. I would say to my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that I would Tather have this legislation passed as it is and if there is one case that is left out I shall tell this corporation that we have passed this' law for this year and that they may be one of the exceptions among all municipally owned railways, but if they do not agree to it, another law will be enacted so as to reach them. I want to see all letter carriers taken care of in this respect and these tramway companies should do it. If they do not wish to do so I will see that they do.

I am glad to have that assurance from the hon. Postmaster General. I am afraid there may be some difficulty in coming to terms with the Guelph electric railway. That is an ordinary provincial electric company. The city bought a controlling interest in its stock and operates it through a controlling commission which is elected, but it is just in the same position as an ordinary privately owned company. I cannot see why the words ' except municipally owned railways' should not be omitted. The present condition is unfair to the letter carriers but to the citizens of Guelph because they are kept waiting for their mail. If the words referred to were struck out the Postmaster General would have power to control the Guelph company and secure a reasonable rate there.

I wish to give credit to the people who are entitled to it. These people have acted in the proper spirit and I told them that when I asked Parliament to enact that clause they would be given this consideration. I would like to keep faith with them, but I can tell the hon. member for South Wellington that I am quite prepared to do for Guelph what I am doing at the present time for Moosejaw, if the letter carriers there are in the same position and if the company is not willing to do what it ought to do. The letter carriers in Moosejaw are satisfied with the arrangement and it is at their request that I am doing it. I do not remember having received any communications from the letter carriers of Guelph.
I have received them.
If my hon. friend will tell the letter carriers in Guelph to send me a representation to that effect I will take it up and see they are treated fairly.
I am glad to hear it.
The Guelph railway is a company but the majority of the stock in the company is owned by the city. In Moosejaw it may happen that the municipality owns some of the stock of the company.
That is a corporation.

It is a corporation in Guelph only the city of Guelph owns practically all the stock. But that does not take it away from the operation of this clause. Has the minister satisfied himself that this Parliament has power to pass this legislation?
Oh, yes.

Take the Moosejaw or Toronto street railway companies incorporated 'by provincial legislatures, their rates are subject to whatever 'bodies the legislature may create in the shape of a provincial railway commission. I very much question if this House has power to say to a provincially created company: You will carry people for a certain price. We might as well say we have power to compel a three cent rate in Toronto. I question if the minister has power to pass the legislation.

This Bill was presented last year, not the whole of it, but this clause, and this question was raised. Some of the most important companies, , one in particular, were trying to hold us up. The question whether we had this power was raised. We were at the tail end of the session and we were not able to come to an agreement with the company in question. Finally, I succeeded in making an arrangement. So I told that Parliament that I would drop the Bill for last year. The Department of Justice have been consulted in this matter. They have gone thoroughly into it and have told us that the Bill was well intra vires of the powers of this Parliament. If there was any doubt about it I think we might fairly run that little risk in order to see that we are not imposed upon by certain companies who think they can exact 'anything from the public and who are not desirous of helping the public as they ought to. At all events, the Department of Justice having fully considered

the question, I do not venture to offer my own opinion about it. If I were to do so, I might. Under the circumstances I think this is a Bill very much in the public interest, and one for the assistance of the letter-carriers who are doing a great deal of good work and ought to be protected against the exaction of some of the corporations.

On motion of Hon. W. J. Roche (Minister of the Interior), Bill No. 136, to amend the Dominion Lands Act, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blain in the Chair.

This Bill provides for two principal amendments:, one is in reference to the matter of pre-emptions, and the other is in reference to proving up on homestead pre-emptions, and purchased homesteads that are not suitable for agricultural purposes, by keeping a certain number of stock. When I was in the West last summer, and since then, a great many representations were made to me that people in the pre-emption area are labouring under certain disabilities in the matter of pre-emptions, which they desire to see removed. The first request was that they would not be charged interest the first three years. The present Act provides that interest shall be charged during the first three years, but not collected until the end of the third year, when the homestead patent has been earned, Although they ate charged interest during that time, they are not allowed to pay either interest or any portion of the principal until the expiration of the three years. We are making provision to throw off the interest for the first three years. The preemption area is located in what was formerly known as a semi-arid district, and it was considered by the minister who created this pre-emption area that 320 acres in that particular district would not do more towards sustaining a farmer than 160 acres in a more productive part of the country. For that reason the lands were sold at |3 per acre, interest to be charged from the first. The first request made to me was to throw off the three years' interest. As time went on the requests became a little more drastic in character, and we have been asked to throw off the principal as well as the
interest, allowing them to spend the same amount of money on fencing and to keep a certain number of stock. The third request was that we should treat the preemptions exactly as we treat the homesteads; that is that we should charge them nothing for them and give a refund to those who had already paid up in whole or in part. That was rather too radical a step, as it would mean the refunding of upwards of two or three million dollars to those who had already paid for their pre-emptions, in whole or in part. However, I am taking power under the amendments to shorten the time in which they may receive patents for their pre-emptions. By doing their cultivation and residential duties they may, if they desire to pay up m full, obtain their pre-emption patents at the same time they are entitled to receive homestead patents, or at any time between the three years and the six years as at present. These are the principal amendments. In connection with the amendment relating to stock, we are merely taking power to allow them to prove up by keeping a certain number of stock on lands not suitable for cultivation purposes. There was a time in the history of the Land Act when we had a stock provision, but it was abolished some years ago-possibly for good reasons. I have no doubt it was abused to a certain extent. ' However, we are safeguarding as far as we possibly can against abuses like occurred in the past. There are other minor amendments, not very important, to which I shall not refer to-night.
